paragraphs: Many learning models use changes in activity over time as part of their calculations. Those changes may be expressed as discrete temporal differences or continuous-time derivatives. This paper examines what happens when such models represent neural communication through individual pulses, instead of describing it only through a firing rate or activation value.

The motivation is that pulse-based communication can affect processing and learning in ways that a rate abstraction hides. The authors reformulate existing temporal-difference and temporal-derivative approaches in a pulse-coded system. They report that computing these changes becomes easier and more stable under this more neuronally realistic representation.

The significance is that the choice of neural representation affects the behavior of the learning computation itself. Individual pulses are therefore relevant to evaluating these models, beyond their resemblance to biological signaling. The authors use this reformulation to seek closer connections between models of learning expressed through behavior over time and models of the biological circuitry underlying learning and memory.
summary.tldr: Expressing temporal-change learning models through discrete neural pulses makes their calculations easier and more stable.

title: Learning with Temporal Derivatives in Pulse-Coded Neuronal Systems

paragraphs: The paper asks whether early retinal processing can be understood as optimal estimation under very dim light. In dark-adapted vision, thermal noise in rod photoreceptors limits reliable photon detection. The authors design a signal processor that estimates changing light intensity from rod signals, using the signal and noise properties to determine the required computation.

They show that the first processing stage is a linear filter whose characteristics are fixed by the rod signal and noise spectra. The authors describe this stage as general to visual processing at low photon flux. They then identify its output with the voltage response of bipolar cells, connecting the optimal computation to the first anatomical stage after photoreceptors.

Using tiger salamander photoreceptor data, they derive parameter-free quantitative predictions for bipolar-cell responses to a dim, diffuse flash. The reported agreement with experiment is essentially perfect. The result links measured receptor properties to downstream neural dynamics, supporting an account in which the retina’s early processing closely matches an optimal filtering computation.
summary.tldr: An optimal filter derived from rod signal and noise predicts salamander bipolar-cell flash responses with essentially perfect agreement.

title: Optimal Filtering in the Salamander Retina

abstract: Product units provide a method of automatically learning the higher-order input combinations required for efficient learning in neural networks. However, we show that problems are encountered when using backpropagation to train networks containing these units. This paper examines these problems, and proposes some atypical heuristics to improve learning. Using these heuristics a constructive method is introduced which solves well-researched problems with significantly less neurons than previously reported. Secondly, product units are implemented as candidate units in the Cascade Correlation (Fahlman & Lebiere, 1990) system. This resulted in smaller networks which trained faster than when using sigmoidal or Gaussian units.

This paper examines these problems, and proposes some atypical heuristics to improve learning. Using these heuristics a constructive method is introduced which solves well-researched problems with significantly less neurons than previously reported. Secondly, product units are implemented as candidate units in the Cascade Correlation (Fahlman & Lebiere, 1990) system. This resulted in smaller networks which trained faster than when using sigmoidal or Gaussian units.

paragraphs: The paper studies product units, which allow a neural network to learn higher-order combinations of its inputs. Such combinations can express interactions that are useful for efficient learning. However, the authors show that ordinary backpropagation encounters difficulties when training networks containing these units, making their representational promise difficult to realize directly.

They investigate those learning problems and propose unconventional heuristics to improve training. Using the heuristics, they introduce a constructive method that builds networks capable of solving well-studied problems with substantially fewer neurons than previously reported. The result connects training choices to the compactness of the resulting representation.

The authors also add product units as candidate units within Cascade Correlation, allowing the constructive system to consider them as it grows a network. In this setting, the networks are smaller and train faster than versions using sigmoidal or Gaussian units. The findings suggest that product units become more useful when paired with learning procedures suited to their particular training behavior.
summary.tldr: Specialized training heuristics and constructive learning make product units yield smaller networks, with faster training in Cascade Correlation.

title: Learning with Product Units

abstract: Intermediate and higher vision processes require selection of a subset of the available sensory information before further processing. Usually, this selection is implemented in the form of a spatially circumscribed region of the visual field, the so-called "focus of attention" which scans the visual scene dependent on the input and on the attentional state of the subject. We here present a model for the control of the focus of attention in primates, based on a saliency map. This mechanism is not only expected to model the functionality of biological vision but also to be essential for the understanding of complex scenes in machine vision.

paragraphs: Visual processing often requires choosing a portion of the available information for further analysis. This paper addresses how that choice can be controlled in primates. It treats attention as a spatially bounded region of the visual field, or focus of attention, that moves through a scene according to the incoming information and the subject's attentional state.

The proposed model uses a saliency map to control this focus. Such a map provides a spatial representation for deciding where attention should be directed. This makes the selection of a location an explicit part of the visual-processing system: before higher-level analysis proceeds, the controller determines which region receives further processing.

The work presents this mechanism as an account of biological visual attention and as a potentially useful component of machine vision. Its significance lies in connecting scene analysis with control over where analysis occurs. The abstract frames understanding complex scenes as depending on this selection process and proposes the model as a way to study that relationship.
summary.tldr: A saliency-map model controls where visual attention moves, linking spatial selection to biological and machine scene understanding.

title: Control of Selective Visual Attention: Modeling the "Where" Pathway

abstract: AdaBoost and other ensemble methods have successfully been ap(cid:173) plied to a number of classification tasks, seemingly defying prob(cid:173) lems of overfitting. AdaBoost performs gradient descent in an error function with respect to the margin, asymptotically concentrating on the patterns which are hardest to learn. For very noisy prob(cid:173) lems, however, this can be disadvantageous. Indeed, theoretical analysis has shown that the margin distribution, as opposed to just the minimal margin, plays a crucial role in understanding this phe(cid:173) nomenon. Loosely speaking, some outliers should be tolerated if this has the benefit of substantially increasing the margin on the remaining points. We propose a new boosting algorithm which al(cid:173) lows for the possibility of a pre-specified fraction of points to lie in the margin area Or even on the wrong side of the decision boundary.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a boosting algorithm motivated by the behavior of ensembles on noisy classification problems. AdaBoost increasingly concentrates on examples that are hardest to learn. That emphasis can be disadvantageous when some difficult examples are outliers, because improving their treatment may compete with obtaining stronger separation for the other examples.

The authors frame the issue through classification margins, which describe how securely examples sit on the appropriate side of a decision boundary. They emphasize the distribution of margins across the dataset rather than only the smallest margin. The underlying tradeoff is that tolerating some outliers may be worthwhile if it substantially improves margins for the remaining points.

The proposed algorithm permits a prespecified fraction of examples to occupy the margin region or even lie on the incorrect side of the boundary. This builds tolerance for problematic examples into the boosting formulation. The contribution is a method designed around that tradeoff, translating the concern about noisy data into an explicit allowance for a controlled fraction of poorly separated points.
summary.tldr: v-Arc modifies boosting to tolerate a prespecified fraction of poorly separated or misclassified examples in pursuit of better margins elsewhere.

title: v-Arc: Ensemble Learning in the Presence of Outliers

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a grid-based map using a robot with noisy sensors and actuators. We compare two approaches: online EM, where the map is treated as a fixed parameter, and Bayesian inference, where the map is a (matrix-valued) random variable. We show that even on a very simple example, online EM can get stuck in local minima, which causes the robot to get "lost" and the resulting map to be useless. By contrast, the Bayesian approach, by maintaining multiple hypotheses, is much more ro(cid:173) bust. We then introduce a method for approximating the Bayesian solution, called Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering. We show that this approximation, when coupled with an active learning strategy, is fast but accurate.

We compare two approaches: online EM, where the map is treated as a fixed parameter, and Bayesian inference, where the map is a (matrix-valued) random variable. We show that even on a very simple example, online EM can get stuck in local minima, which causes the robot to get "lost" and the resulting map to be useless. By contrast, the Bayesian approach, by maintaining multiple hypotheses, is much more ro(cid:173) bust. We then introduce a method for approximating the Bayesian solution, called Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering. We show that this approximation, when coupled with an active learning strategy, is fast but accurate.

paragraphs: A robot building a grid map must interpret measurements while its sensors and actions are noisy. The paper compares two ways to represent the map during learning. Online expectation-maximization treats it as a fixed parameter to estimate, while Bayesian inference treats the entire map as a random variable with multiple possible values.

The authors show that online expectation-maximization can become trapped in a local minimum even in a simple example. In that case, the robot loses track of where it is and produces an unusable map. The Bayesian approach is much more robust because it maintains competing hypotheses instead of relying on a single map estimate.

To make the Bayesian approach practical, the paper introduces an approximation called Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering. Combined with an active learning strategy, this approximation is reported to be both fast and accurate. The contribution connects the benefits of preserving uncertainty with a computational method for using those benefits during map learning; the reported efficiency and accuracy apply to the combined approach.
summary.tldr: Maintaining multiple map hypotheses improves robustness, and an approximate Bayesian method with active learning is reported to be fast and accurate.

title: Bayesian Map Learning in Dynamic Environments

abstract: We present a class of approximate inference algorithms for graphical models of the QMR-DT type. We give convergence rates for these al(cid:173) gorithms and for the Jaakkola and Jordan (1999) algorithm, and verify these theoretical predictions empirically. We also present empirical re(cid:173) sults on the difficult QMR-DT network problem, obtaining performance of the new algorithms roughly comparable to the Jaakkola and Jordan algorithm.

We give convergence rates for these al(cid:173) gorithms and for the Jaakkola and Jordan (1999) algorithm, and verify these theoretical predictions empirically. We also present empirical re(cid:173) sults on the difficult QMR-DT network problem, obtaining performance of the new algorithms roughly comparable to the Jaakkola and Jordan algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper develops a class of approximate inference algorithms for two-layer graphical models of the QMR-DT type. Inference is the task of drawing probabilistic conclusions within a model. The contribution addresses how this computation can be approximated for the network family under study, with particular attention to understanding algorithmic convergence.

The authors give convergence rates for their algorithms and for the existing Jaakkola and Jordan algorithm. A rate describes how convergence proceeds, adding information beyond whether an algorithm converges at all. They also test the theoretical predictions empirically, linking the mathematical analysis to observed computational behavior.

Experiments on the difficult QMR-DT network problem find that the new algorithms perform roughly comparably to the Jaakkola and Jordan method. The stated result supports them as alternatives with analyzed convergence behavior, rather than as a demonstrated performance breakthrough over that method. The paper's value lies in combining a new algorithm family, rate analysis covering both new and existing approaches, and empirical checks on a challenging inference problem.
summary.tldr: New approximate inference algorithms for QMR-DT-type networks have analyzed convergence rates and empirically comparable performance to an existing method.

title: Approximate Inference A lgorithms for Two-Layer Bayesian Networks

abstract: We present a new method for the blind separation of sources, which do not fulfill the independence assumption. In contrast to standard methods we consider groups of neighboring samples ("patches") within the observed mixtures. First we extract independent features from the observed patches. It turns out that the average dependencies between these features in different sources is in general lower than the dependencies be(cid:173) tween the amplitudes of different sources. We show that it might be the case that most of the dependencies is carried by only a small number of features. Is this case - provided these features can be identified by some heuristic - we project all patches into the subspace which is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by the "correlated" features. Standard ICA is then performed on the elements of the transformed patches (for which the independence assumption holds) and ro(cid:173) bustly yields a good estimate of the mixing matrix.

paragraphs: The paper tackles blind source separation when the sources do not satisfy the independence assumption used by standard independent component analysis. Instead of considering individual sample amplitudes alone, it groups neighboring samples into patches. It first extracts independent features from observed patches, seeking a representation in which cross-source dependencies are easier to isolate.

The authors find that average dependencies between corresponding features across sources are generally lower than dependencies between source amplitudes. They also show that much of the remaining dependence may be concentrated in only a few features. If those features can be identified heuristically, the method projects patches away from the subspace they span.

Standard ICA is then applied to the transformed patches, whose elements satisfy the independence assumption in the described case. The authors report that this robustly estimates the mixing matrix. The approach depends on dependence being concentrated in identifiable features: it offers a conditional route from correlated sources to a representation suitable for conventional ICA.
summary.tldr: Patch-based feature removal can enable ICA for correlated sources when their dependence is concentrated in a small, identifiable feature subspace.

title: Multi Dimensional ICA to Separate Correlated Sources

abstract: Even under perfect ﬁxation the human eye is under steady motion (tremor, microsaccades, slow drift). The “dynamic” theory of vi- sion [1, 2] states that eye-movements can improve hyperacuity. Accord- ing to this theory, eye movements are thought to create variable spatial excitation patterns on the photoreceptor grid, which will allow for better spatiotemporal summation at later stages. We reexamine this theory us- ing a realistic model of the vertebrate retina by comparing responses of a resting and a moving eye. The performance of simulated ganglion cells in a hyperacuity task is evaluated by ideal observer analysis. We ﬁnd that in the central retina eye-micromovements have no effect on the perfor- mance. Here optical blurring limits vernier acuity. In the retinal periph- ery however, eye-micromovements clearly improve performance. Based on ROC analysis, our predictions are quantitatively testable in electro- physiological and psychophysical experiments.

We reexamine this theory us- ing a realistic model of the vertebrate retina by comparing responses of a resting and a moving eye. The performance of simulated ganglion cells in a hyperacuity task is evaluated by ideal observer analysis. We ﬁnd that in the central retina eye-micromovements have no effect on the perfor- mance. Here optical blurring limits vernier acuity. In the retinal periph- ery however, eye-micromovements clearly improve performance. Based on ROC analysis, our predictions are quantitatively testable in electro- physiological and psychophysical experiments.

paragraphs: The eye continues to move slightly even during steady fixation. A dynamic theory of vision proposes that these movements can improve fine visual discrimination by shifting spatial excitation across photoreceptors. Later processing could combine the resulting patterns across space and time. This paper reexamines that proposal with a realistic model of the vertebrate retina.

The authors compare a resting eye with a moving eye and evaluate simulated ganglion-cell responses in a hyperacuity task. Ideal-observer analysis assesses how much task-relevant information those responses provide. This makes the comparison about the usefulness of the retinal signals for discrimination, rather than simply whether movement changes the signals.

The results depend on retinal location. In the central retina, micro-movements do not improve performance because optical blur limits vernier acuity in the model. In the peripheral retina, they clearly improve performance. ROC analysis yields quantitative predictions that could be tested electrophysiologically and psychophysically. The findings therefore support a location-dependent benefit in simulation and specify a route to experimental testing.
summary.tldr: Retinal simulations predict that tiny eye movements improve peripheral hyperacuity but provide no central benefit where optical blur limits performance.

title: Eye Micro-movements Improve Stimulus Detection Beyond the Nyquist Limit in the Peripheral Retina

abstract: In this paper we propose to combine two powerful ideas, boosting and manifold learning. On the one hand, we improve A DA B OOST by incorporating knowledge on the structure of the data into base classifier design and selection. On the other hand, we use A DA B OOST’s efficient learning mechanism to significantly improve supervised and semi-supervised algorithms proposed in the context of manifold learning. Beside the specific manifold-based penalization, the resulting algorithm also accommodates the boosting of a large family of regularized learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose to combine two powerful ideas, boosting and manifold learning. On the one hand, we improve A DA B OOST by incorporating knowledge on the structure of the data into base classifier design and selection. On the other hand, we use A DA B OOST’s efficient learning mechanism to significantly improve supervised and semi-supervised algorithms proposed in the context of manifold learning. Beside the specific manifold-based penalization, the resulting algorithm also accommodates the boosting of a large family of regularized learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper connects boosting with manifold learning by allowing information about the structure of the data to influence the classifiers that boosting uses. In AdaBoost, base classifiers are the components from which the combined classifier is built. The proposed approach brings structural knowledge into both the design of those components and their selection.

The connection also works in the other direction. The authors use AdaBoost's efficient learning mechanism to improve supervised and semi-supervised methods developed in the manifold-learning setting. Their approach therefore treats data structure and the boosting procedure as interacting parts of learning: the structure guides the available classifiers, while boosting provides a mechanism for using them.

A manifold-based penalty is one concrete form of regularization within the resulting algorithm. The framework also accommodates boosting a large family of regularized learning algorithms, giving it a scope beyond that particular penalty. The abstract reports improvements to both AdaBoost and manifold-learning methods, with the broader contribution being a shared framework for combining boosting and regularization.
summary.tldr: The paper combines boosting with data-structure-based regularization to improve AdaBoost and manifold-learning methods.

title: Boosting on Manifolds: Adaptive Regularization of Base Classifiers

abstract: Reinforcement learning models have long promised to unify computa- tional, psychological and neural accounts of appetitively conditioned be- havior. However, the bulk of data on animal conditioning comes from free-operant experiments measuring how fast animals will work for rein- forcement. Existing reinforcement learning (RL) models are silent about these tasks, because they lack any notion of vigor. They thus fail to ad- dress the simple observation that hungrier animals will work harder for food, as well as stranger facts such as their sometimes greater produc- tivity even when working for irrelevant outcomes such as water. Here, we develop an RL framework for free-operant behavior, suggesting that subjects choose how vigorously to perform selected actions by optimally balancing the costs and beneﬁts of quick responding. Motivational states such as hunger shift these factors, skewing the tradeoff. This accounts normatively for the effects of motivation on response rates, as well as many other classic ﬁndings. Finally, we suggest that tonic levels of dopamine may be involved in the computation linking motivational state to optimal responding, thereby explaining the complex vigor-related ef- fects of pharmacological manipulation of dopamine.

paragraphs: The paper asks how reinforcement learning can explain the speed and intensity with which animals work for rewards. Free-operant conditioning experiments measure response rates, yet the existing models discussed by the authors lack a notion of vigor. This leaves them unable to address how motivational states such as hunger change the amount of work animals perform.

The proposed framework treats vigor as a choice governed by the costs and benefits of responding quickly. Motivation changes those factors and therefore shifts the preferred response rate. This gives a normative account of why an animal might work harder when hungry, including findings in which increased productivity extends to outcomes such as water.

The framework accounts for effects of motivation on response rates and several other classic findings. The authors further suggest that tonic dopamine may participate in the computation linking motivational state to optimal responding. That proposed neural role offers an explanation for complex effects of dopamine manipulation, while remaining a hypothesis about the underlying computation.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning account treats response vigor as a cost-benefit choice and proposes a possible computational role for tonic dopamine.

title: How fast to work: Response vigor, motivation and tonic dopamine

abstract: Humans make optimal perceptual decisions in noisy and ambiguous conditions. Computations underlying such optimal behavior have been shown to rely on probabilistic inference according to generative models whose structure is usually taken to be known a priori. We argue that Bayesian model selection is ideal for inferring similar and even more complex model structures from experience. We ﬁnd in experiments that humans learn subtle statistical properties of visual scenes in a completely unsupervised manner. We show that these ﬁndings are well captured by Bayesian model learning within a class of models that seek to explain observed variables by independent hidden causes.

Computations underlying such optimal behavior have been shown to rely on probabilistic inference according to generative models whose structure is usually taken to be known a priori. We argue that Bayesian model selection is ideal for inferring similar and even more complex model structures from experience. We ﬁnd in experiments that humans learn subtle statistical properties of visual scenes in a completely unsupervised manner. We show that these ﬁndings are well captured by Bayesian model learning within a class of models that seek to explain observed variables by independent hidden causes.

paragraphs: Probabilistic explanations of visual perception often assume that the observer already has a generative model with the right structure. This paper asks how such structure could be acquired through experience. It shifts attention from using a model to interpret uncertain visual input toward learning which model can explain that input.

The authors argue that Bayesian model selection offers an appropriate account of this process, including the acquisition of more complex structures. Their experiments find that people learn subtle statistical properties of visual scenes without supervision. This makes the learning question relevant to behavior: the observers acquire information about scene statistics without being explicitly taught those properties.

The experimental findings are well captured by Bayesian model learning within a class of models that explain observed variables through independent hidden causes. The result supports this particular account of how perceptual models can be learned from experience. It connects unsupervised visual learning with probabilistic structure discovery, extending the explanatory role of Bayesian inference beyond decisions made with a predetermined model.
summary.tldr: Experiments on unsupervised visual learning are well explained by Bayesian learning of models built from independent hidden causes.

title: Bayesian model learning in human visual perception

abstract: We determine the asymptotic limit of the function computed by support vector machines (SVM) and related algorithms that minimize a regularized empirical convex loss function in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the Gaussian RBF kernel, in the situation where the number of examples tends to infinity, the bandwidth of the Gaussian kernel tends to 0, and the regularization parameter is held fixed. Non-asymptotic convergence bounds to this limit in the L2 sense are provided, together with upper bounds on the classification error that is shown to converge to the Bayes risk, therefore proving the Bayes-consistency of a variety of methods although the regularization term does not vanish. These results are particularly relevant to the one-class SVM, for which the regularization can not vanish by construction, and which is shown for the first time to be a consistent density level set estimator.

Non-asymptotic convergence bounds to this limit in the L2 sense are provided, together with upper bounds on the classification error that is shown to converge to the Bayes risk, therefore proving the Bayes-consistency of a variety of methods although the regularization term does not vanish. These results are particularly relevant to the one-class SVM, for which the regularization can not vanish by construction, and which is shown for the first time to be a consistent density level set estimator.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what support vector machines and related kernel methods approach as the amount of training data grows. It studies algorithms that minimize a regularized empirical convex loss using a Gaussian radial basis function kernel. The central question is whether keeping regularization fixed can still permit statistically consistent estimation.

The analysis considers a specific limiting regime: the number of examples grows without bound, the kernel bandwidth shrinks toward zero, and the regularization parameter stays fixed. Under this regime, the authors identify the limiting learned function and provide finite-sample bounds on convergence in squared-integral distance. They also bound classification error and show convergence to the Bayes risk, the best achievable classification error for the underlying distribution.

The result establishes Bayes consistency for a variety of methods despite nonvanishing regularization. It is especially relevant to the one-class SVM, whose regularization cannot vanish by construction. The paper shows that this method consistently estimates density level sets, giving its identification of regions of a distribution a precise asymptotic justification under the stated regime.
summary.tldr: With shrinking Gaussian kernel bandwidth and increasing data, several regularized methods remain consistent even when regularization stays fixed.

title: Consistency of one-class SVM and related algorithms

abstract: Fusing multiple information sources can yield signiﬁcant beneﬁts to suc- cessfully accomplish learning tasks. Many studies have focussed on fus- ing information in supervised learning contexts. We present an approach to utilize multiple information sources in the form of similarity data for unsupervised learning. Based on similarity information, the clustering task is phrased as a non-negative matrix factorization problem of a mix- ture of similarity measurements. The tradeoff between the informative- ness of data sources and the sparseness of their mixture is controlled by an entropy-based weighting mechanism. For the purpose of model se- lection, a stability-based approach is employed to ensure the selection of the most self-consistent hypothesis. The experiments demonstrate the performance of the method on toy as well as real world data sets.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to cluster data using several sources of similarity information. Each source supplies information about which items resemble one another, and the task is to combine these sources without class labels. The approach brings information fusion into an unsupervised setting where the usefulness of a source must be handled within clustering.

The authors express clustering as non-negative matrix factorization of a mixture of similarity measurements. An entropy-based weighting mechanism controls the balance between how informative the sources are and how sparse their mixture is. This makes the allocation of weight across sources an explicit part of the method rather than treating every source identically.

For model selection, the method uses stability to choose the most self-consistent hypothesis. The authors demonstrate its performance on both toy and real-world datasets. The contribution combines three decisions in one approach: representing clusters through factorization, weighting multiple similarity sources, and choosing a clustering hypothesis through consistency. Together, these components provide a way to use several information sources when labeled guidance is unavailable.
summary.tldr: The method combines multiple similarity sources for clustering using non-negative matrix factorization, entropy-based weights, and stability-based model selection.

title: Fusion of Similarity Data in Clustering

abstract: In many modern large-scale learning applications, the amount of unlabeled data far exceeds that of labeled data. A common instance of this problem is the transductive setting where the unlabeled test points are known to the learning algorithm. This paper presents a study of regression problems in that setting. It presents explicit VC-dimension error bounds for transductive regression that hold for all bounded loss functions and coincide with the tight classification bounds of Vapnik when applied to classification. It also presents a new transductive regression algorithm inspired by our bound that admits a primal and kernelized closedform solution and deals efficiently with large amounts of unlabeled data. The algorithm exploits the position of unlabeled points to locally estimate their labels and then uses a global optimization to ensure robust predictions. Our study also includes the results of experiments with several publicly available regression data sets with up to 20,000 unlabeled examples. The comparison with other transductive regression algorithms shows that it performs well and that it can scale to large data sets.

paragraphs: Transductive regression predicts values for test points that are already visible to the learning algorithm, although their labels are unknown. This paper studies how to use that information when unlabeled data greatly outnumber labeled examples. Knowing the test inputs creates an opportunity to make their locations part of the learning process.

The authors derive explicit error bounds based on VC dimension for all bounded loss functions. When applied to classification, the bounds coincide with Vapnik's tight classification bounds. They also develop a regression algorithm inspired by the analysis. It first uses the locations of unlabeled points to estimate labels locally, then applies a global optimization to produce robust predictions.

The algorithm has closed-form solutions in both primal and kernelized forms and is designed to handle large quantities of unlabeled data efficiently. Experiments on public regression datasets include up to 20,000 unlabeled examples. Comparisons with other transductive regression methods show good performance and scalability in those evaluations, connecting the theoretical analysis to a computationally practical prediction method.
summary.tldr: The paper develops error bounds and a scalable transductive regression algorithm that combines local label estimates with global optimization.

title: On Transductive Regression

abstract: In this paper, we study the manifold regularization for the Sliced Inverse Regression (SIR). The manifold regularization improves the standard SIR in two aspects: 1) it encodes the local geometry for SIR and 2) it enables SIR to deal with transductive and semi-supervised learning problems. We prove that the proposed graph Laplacian based regularization is convergent at rate root-n. The projection directions of the regularized SIR are optimized by using a conjugate gradient method on the Grassmann manifold. Experimental results support our theory.

We prove that the proposed graph Laplacian based regularization is convergent at rate root-n. The projection directions of the regularized SIR are optimized by using a conjugate gradient method on the Grassmann manifold. Experimental results support our theory.

paragraphs: The paper adds manifold regularization to Sliced Inverse Regression, or SIR. Its purpose is to make the method account for the local geometry of the data when finding projection directions. Nearby relationships among observations therefore become part of the information used to determine the resulting representation.

The regularization is based on a graph Laplacian. Beyond incorporating geometry, the authors show that it enables SIR to handle transductive and semi-supervised learning problems. These settings broaden the role of the available data beyond fully labeled training examples. The projection directions are optimized with a conjugate-gradient method on the Grassmann manifold, a geometric space for representing subspaces.

The theoretical contribution is a root-n convergence result for the proposed graph-Laplacian regularization. The authors also report experimental results that support their theory. The work thus combines a statistical guarantee with an optimization method for the regularized projections. Its significance is that local data geometry becomes usable within SIR while retaining a stated convergence rate and extending the learning settings it can address.
summary.tldr: Graph-Laplacian regularization adds local geometry and semi-supervised capabilities to SIR, with a proven root-n convergence rate.

title: Manifold Regularization for SIR with Rate Root-n Convergence

abstract: The worst-case complexity of general decentralized POMDPs, which are equivalent to partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) is very high, both for the cooperative and competitive cases. Some reductions in complexity have been achieved by exploiting independence relations in some models. We show that these results are somewhat limited: when these independence assumptions are relaxed in very small ways, complexity returns to that of the general case.
originalAbstract: The worst-case complexity of general decentralized POMDPs, which are equivalent to partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) is very high, both for the cooperative and competitive cases. Some reductions in complexity have been achieved by exploiting independence relations in some models. We show that these results are somewhat limited: when these independence assumptions are relaxed in very small ways, complexity returns to that of the general case.

paragraphs: Decentralized control studies decision problems involving multiple agents that do not have complete information. The paper considers decentralized partially observable Markov decision processes and their equivalent game formulation. General versions have very high worst-case computational complexity, whether the agents cooperate or compete. This makes restricted models especially important for understanding when planning becomes more manageable.

Some earlier reductions in complexity rely on independence relationships within the model. Such assumptions remove particular dependencies from the decision problem. The paper examines how much those simplifications depend on preserving the assumptions precisely, rather than treating independence as an approximately satisfied property.

The central finding is that very small relaxations of the studied independence assumptions can restore the complexity of the general problem. Thus, the easier special cases have boundaries that can be computationally consequential. This is a worst-case result about classes of problems: it shows that the earlier complexity reductions do not necessarily extend to closely related models. Its significance is to clarify how narrowly some tractable or less difficult formulations must be interpreted.
summary.tldr: Small relaxations of certain independence assumptions can make decentralized control as computationally difficult as the general case.

title: Complexity of Decentralized Control: Special Cases

abstract: For many real-world applications, we often need to select correlated variables---such as genetic variations and imaging features associated with Alzheimer's disease---in a high dimensional space. The correlation between variables presents a challenge to classical variable selection methods. To address this challenge, the elastic net has been developed and successfully applied to many applications. Despite its great success, the elastic net does not exploit the correlation information embedded in the data to select correlated variables. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel hybrid model, EigenNet, that uses the eigenstructures of data to guide variable selection. Specifically, it integrates a sparse conditional classification model with a generative model capturing variable correlations in a principled Bayesian framework. We develop an efficient active-set algorithm to estimate the model via evidence maximization. Experiments on synthetic data and imaging genetics data demonstrated the superior predictive performance of the EigenNet over the lasso, the elastic net, and the automatic relevance determination.

paragraphs: Selecting useful variables is difficult when a high-dimensional dataset contains strongly correlated measurements. The paper motivates this problem with genetic and imaging features associated with Alzheimer's disease. Although elastic net addresses correlated-variable selection, the authors identify an opportunity to use the correlation structure embedded in the data more directly.

It combines a sparse conditional classification component with a generative component that represents correlations among variables. The classification component connects selected variables to prediction, while the generative component brings information about how those variables vary together into the same framework.

The authors develop an efficient active-set algorithm that estimates the model through evidence maximization. Experiments on synthetic and imaging genetics data show better predictive performance than lasso, elastic net, and automatic relevance determination in the comparisons reported. The findings support using the data's correlation structure to guide sparse prediction, with the demonstrated advantage tied to those experiments.
summary.tldr: EigenNet combines Bayesian classification and correlation modeling to guide sparse variable selection and improve prediction in the reported experiments.

title: EigenNet: A Bayesian hybrid of generative and conditional models for sparse learning

abstract: We develop convergent minimization algorithms for Bethe variational approximations which explicitly constrain marginal estimates to families of valid distributions. While existing message passing algorithms define fixed point iterations corresponding to stationary points of the Bethe free energy, their greedy dynamics do not distinguish between local minima and maxima, and can fail to converge. For continuous estimation problems, this instability is linked to the creation of invalid marginal estimates, such as Gaussians with negative variance. Conversely, our approach leverages multiplier methods with well-understood convergence properties, and uses bound projection methods to ensure that marginal approximations are valid at all iterations. We derive general algorithms for discrete and Gaussian pairwise Markov random fields, showing improvements over standard loopy belief propagation. We also apply our method to a hybrid model with both discrete and continuous variables, showing improvements over expectation propagation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses instability in approximate probabilistic inference based on the Bethe free energy. Existing message-passing procedures seek stationary points, but their updates do not distinguish minima from maxima and may fail to converge. In continuous problems, this instability is connected to invalid intermediate probability estimates, including Gaussian distributions assigned negative variances.

The proposed approach treats inference as constrained minimization. It uses multiplier methods with established convergence properties and bound projections that keep marginal approximations within valid distribution families at every iteration. Validity therefore becomes an explicit part of the optimization process, addressing a concrete failure mode of the message-passing dynamics.

The authors derive algorithms for discrete and Gaussian pairwise Markov random fields and report improvements over standard loopy belief propagation. They also evaluate a model combining discrete and continuous variables, reporting improvements over expectation propagation. The contribution brings convergent optimization and valid intermediate estimates together; its stated convergence result does not imply that every solution is a global minimum.
summary.tldr: Constrained Bethe minimization keeps intermediate probability estimates valid and provides convergent alternatives to unstable message-passing updates.

title: Minimization of Continuous Bethe Approximations: A Positive Variation

abstract: Recently, it has become evident that submodularity naturally captures widely occurring concepts in machine learning, signal processing and computer vision. In consequence, there is need for efficient optimization procedures for submodular functions, in particular for minimization problems. While general submodular minimization is challenging, we propose a new approach that exploits existing decomposability of submodular functions. In contrast to previous approaches, our method is neither approximate, nor impractical, nor does it need any cumbersome parameter tuning. Moreover, it is easy to implement and parallelize. A key component of our approach is a formulation of the discrete submodular minimization problem as a continuous best approximation problem. It is solved through a sequence of reflections and its solution can be automatically thresholded to obtain an optimal discrete solution. Our method solves both the continuous and discrete formulations of the problem, and therefore has applications in learning, inference, and reconstruction. In our experiments, we show the benefits of our new algorithms for two image segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Submodular functions appear in learning, signal processing, and computer vision, but minimizing them can be computationally challenging. This paper develops an approach that exploits existing decomposability in the function being optimized. Its aim is an exact, practical procedure that is easy to implement and parallelize without cumbersome parameter tuning.

The central step reformulates discrete submodular minimization as a continuous best approximation problem. A sequence of reflections solves this continuous formulation. Its solution can then be automatically thresholded to produce an optimal discrete solution, linking continuous computation directly to the original discrete optimization task.

Because the method solves both formulations, it has applications in learning, inference, and reconstruction. Experiments on two image segmentation tasks demonstrate benefits of the proposed algorithms. The important structural condition is the decomposability the method exploits: the contribution uses that available organization to obtain a practical optimization route. The automatic thresholding also makes the continuous solution useful without giving up optimality in the discrete problem.
summary.tldr: Reflection-based optimization exploits decomposability to solve submodular minimization exactly through a continuous formulation and automatic thresholding.

title: Reflection methods for user-friendly submodular optimization

abstract: We consider the online Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for contaminated samples (containing outliers) which are revealed sequentially to the Principal Components (PCs) estimator. Due to their sensitiveness to outliers, previous online PCA algorithms fail in this case and their results can be arbitrarily bad. Here we propose the online robust PCA algorithm, which is able to improve the PCs estimation upon an initial one steadily, even when faced with a constant fraction of outliers. We show that the final result of the proposed online RPCA has an acceptable degradation from the optimum. Actually, under mild conditions, online RPCA achieves the maximal robustness with a $50\%$ breakdown point. Moreover, online RPCA is shown to be efficient for both storage and computation, since it need not re-explore the previous samples as in traditional robust PCA algorithms. This endows online RPCA with scalability for large scale data.

paragraphs: Online principal component analysis estimates important directions in data as samples arrive sequentially. Outliers can make previous online PCA estimates arbitrarily poor. This paper develops an online robust PCA algorithm designed to improve an initial estimate steadily even when a constant fraction of the incoming observations are outliers.

The authors show that the final estimate has a controlled degradation from the optimum. Under mild conditions, the method attains a 50% breakdown point, described as maximal robustness. A breakdown point concerns how much contamination an estimator can withstand before its behavior can become arbitrarily bad, so the stated conditions matter to interpreting this robustness claim.

The algorithm also avoids revisiting earlier observations, unlike traditional robust PCA methods that re-explore previous samples. This supports efficiency in both storage and computation and makes the approach suitable for large datasets. The contribution combines resistance to contamination with sequential processing: it aims to improve principal-component estimates without repeatedly processing the full history of data.
summary.tldr: Online robust PCA improves estimates despite outliers, avoids revisiting past samples, and reaches a 50% breakdown point under mild conditions.

title: Online PCA for Contaminated Data

abstract: How are firing rates in a spiking network related to neural input, connectivity and network function? This is an important problem because firing rates are one of the most important measures of network activity, in both the study of neural computation and neural network dynamics. However, it is a difficult problem, because the spiking mechanism of individual neurons is highly non-linear, and these individual neurons interact strongly through connectivity. We develop a new technique for calculating firing rates in optimal balanced networks. These are particularly interesting networks because they provide an optimal spike-based signal representation while producing cortex-like spiking activity through a dynamic balance of excitation and inhibition. We can calculate firing rates by treating balanced network dynamics as an algorithm for optimizing signal representation. We identify this algorithm and then calculate firing rates by finding the solution to the algorithm. Our firing rate calculation relates network firing rates directly to network input, connectivity and function. This allows us to explain the function and underlying mechanism of tuning curves in a variety of systems.

paragraphs: Predicting how often neurons fire is difficult because individual spiking mechanisms are nonlinear and connected neurons strongly influence one another. This paper studies that problem in optimal balanced networks, where excitation and inhibition dynamically balance. These networks combine optimal spike-based signal representation with activity resembling cortical spiking.

The authors’ central move is to interpret the network dynamics as an algorithm that optimizes signal representation. They identify that algorithm and derive firing rates by finding its solution. This connects the calculation to what the network computes, giving a way to relate firing rates directly to the incoming signal, the connectivity, and the network’s function.

The resulting calculation is used to explain tuning curves in a variety of systems, connecting patterns of response to both their function and their underlying mechanism. The scope is the particular class of optimal balanced networks considered in the paper. Within that class, the approach shows how a computational objective can make strongly interacting spiking dynamics more accessible to firing-rate analysis.
summary.tldr: Treating optimal balanced network dynamics as an optimization algorithm yields firing-rate predictions linked directly to input, connectivity, and computational function.

title: Firing rate predictions in optimal balanced networks

abstract: Based on a new atomic norm, we propose a new convex formulation for sparse matrix factorization problems in which the number of nonzero elements of the factors is assumed fixed and known. The formulation counts sparse PCA with multiple factors, subspace clustering and low-rank sparse bilinear regression as potential applications. We compute slow rates and an upper bound on the statistical dimension of the suggested norm for rank 1 matrices, showing that its statistical dimension is an order of magnitude smaller than the usual l_1-norm, trace norm and their combinations. Even though our convex formulation is in theory hard and does not lead to provably polynomial time algorithmic schemes, we propose an active set algorithm leveraging the structure of the convex problem to solve it and show promising numerical results.
originalAbstract: Based on a new atomic norm, we propose a new convex formulation for sparse matrix factorization problems in which the number of nonzero elements of the factors is assumed fixed and known. The formulation counts sparse PCA with multiple factors, subspace clustering and low-rank sparse bilinear regression as potential applications. We compute slow rates and an upper bound on the statistical dimension of the suggested norm for rank 1 matrices, showing that its statistical dimension is an order of magnitude smaller than the usual l_1-norm, trace norm and their combinations. Even though our convex formulation is in theory hard and does not lead to provably polynomial time algorithmic schemes, we propose an active set algorithm leveraging the structure of the convex problem to solve it and show promising numerical results.

paragraphs: Sparse matrix factorization seeks factors with limited numbers of nonzero entries. This paper introduces a convex formulation based on a new atomic norm, assuming those numbers are fixed and known. Potential applications include sparse PCA with multiple factors, subspace clustering, and low-rank sparse bilinear regression.

The authors derive slow rates and bound the norm's statistical dimension for rank-one matrices. They report a statistical dimension an order of magnitude smaller than that of the usual l1 norm, trace norm, and their combinations. This theoretical comparison concerns rank-one matrices and indicates the value of designing a norm specifically around the assumed sparse-factor structure.

Convexity does not make this formulation computationally easy: the problem remains theoretically hard, and the paper does not obtain a provably polynomial-time solution scheme. Instead, the authors propose an active-set algorithm that exploits the convex problem's structure and report promising numerical results. The contribution therefore combines a statistically attractive formulation with a practical algorithm, while explicitly retaining a distinction between its statistical properties and computational guarantees.
summary.tldr: A new atomic norm improves rank-one statistical-dimension bounds for sparse factorization, although solving the convex formulation remains theoretically hard.

title: Tight convex relaxations for sparse matrix factorization

abstract: The presence of noise and small scale structures usually leads to large kernel estimation errors in blind image deblurring empirically, if not a total failure. We present a scale space perspective on blind deblurring algorithms, and introduce a cascaded scale space formulation for blind deblurring. This new formulation suggests a natural approach robust to noise and small scale structures through tying the estimation across multiple scales and balancing the contributions of different scales automatically by learning from data. The proposed formulation also allows to handle non-uniform blur with a straightforward extension. Experiments are conducted on both benchmark dataset and real-world images to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. One surprising finding based on our approach is that blur kernel estimation is not necessarily best at the finest scale.

We present a scale space perspective on blind deblurring algorithms, and introduce a cascaded scale space formulation for blind deblurring. This new formulation suggests a natural approach robust to noise and small scale structures through tying the estimation across multiple scales and balancing the contributions of different scales automatically by learning from data. The proposed formulation also allows to handle non-uniform blur with a straightforward extension. Experiments are conducted on both benchmark dataset and real-world images to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. One surprising finding based on our approach is that blur kernel estimation is not necessarily best at the finest scale.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a difficulty in blind image deblurring: noise and fine image structures can badly distort estimation of the blur kernel. Because recovering the image depends on estimating that blur, errors at this stage can undermine the whole process. The authors approach the problem by examining deblurring across image scales.

They introduce a cascaded scale-space formulation that connects estimation at multiple scales. The method learns from data how to balance the contribution of each scale automatically. This supplies a way to use cross-scale information while reducing the influence of noise and small structures that can interfere with kernel estimation. The formulation also admits a straightforward extension to spatially non-uniform blur.

Experiments on a benchmark dataset and real-world images validate the method's effectiveness. One finding is that the finest scale does not necessarily produce the best blur-kernel estimate. This supports treating scale as something to balance during estimation, rather than assuming that the most detailed image representation must always be the most useful for recovering blur.
summary.tldr: Learning how to combine blur estimates across scales improves blind deblurring, with experiments showing that the finest scale is not always best.

title: Scale Adaptive Blind Deblurring

abstract: We improve a recent gurantee of Bach and Moulines on the linear convergence of SGD for smooth and strongly convex objectives, reducing a quadratic dependence on the strong convexity to a linear dependence. Furthermore, we show how reweighting the sampling distribution (i.e. importance sampling) is necessary in order to further improve convergence, and obtain a linear dependence on average smoothness, dominating previous results, and more broadly discus how importance sampling for SGD can improve convergence also in other scenarios. Our results are based on a connection we make between SGD and the randomized Kaczmarz algorithm, which allows us to transfer ideas between the separate bodies of literature studying each of the two methods.
originalAbstract: We improve a recent gurantee of Bach and Moulines on the linear convergence of SGD for smooth and strongly convex objectives, reducing a quadratic dependence on the strong convexity to a linear dependence. Furthermore, we show how reweighting the sampling distribution (i.e. importance sampling) is necessary in order to further improve convergence, and obtain a linear dependence on average smoothness, dominating previous results, and more broadly discus how importance sampling for SGD can improve convergence also in other scenarios. Our results are based on a connection we make between SGD and the randomized Kaczmarz algorithm, which allows us to transfer ideas between the separate bodies of literature studying each of the two methods.

paragraphs: The paper improves convergence guarantees for stochastic gradient descent on smooth, strongly convex objectives. These assumptions describe a setting in which the objective has controlled variation and sufficient curvature. Within that setting, the authors sharpen an existing linear-convergence result, reducing its quadratic dependence on the strong-convexity quantity to a linear dependence.

They then examine how changing the sampling probabilities can improve convergence further. This reweighting, called importance sampling, gives different parts of the stochastic computation different chances of being selected. The authors show that it is necessary for the further improvement they study and obtain a bound with linear dependence on average smoothness, improving on previous results.

The analysis comes from a connection between stochastic gradient descent and the randomized Kaczmarz algorithm. Establishing that relationship lets the authors transfer ideas between two bodies of research. They also discuss benefits of importance sampling in other settings. The contribution makes sampling distribution a central part of convergence analysis, alongside the curvature and smoothness assumptions that support the stated guarantees.
summary.tldr: Connecting SGD with randomized Kaczmarz yields sharper convergence guarantees and identifies importance sampling as necessary for the further improvement studied.

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent, Weighted Sampling, and the Randomized Kaczmarz algorithm

abstract: We investigate the problem of learning an unknown probability distribution over a discrete population from random samples. Our goal is to design efficient algorithms that simultaneously achieve low error in total variation norm while guaranteeing Differential Privacy to the individuals of the population.We describe a general approach that yields near sample-optimal and computationally efficient differentially private estimators for a wide range of well-studied and natural distribution families. Our theoretical results show that for a wide variety of structured distributions there exist private estimation algorithms that are nearly as efficient - both in terms of sample size and running time - as their non-private counterparts. We complement our theoretical guarantees with an experimental evaluation. Our experiments illustrate the speed and accuracy of our private estimators on both synthetic mixture models and a large public data set.

Our goal is to design efficient algorithms that simultaneously achieve low error in total variation norm while guaranteeing Differential Privacy to the individuals of the population.We describe a general approach that yields near sample-optimal and computationally efficient differentially private estimators for a wide range of well-studied and natural distribution families. Our theoretical results show that for a wide variety of structured distributions there exist private estimation algorithms that are nearly as efficient - both in terms of sample size and running time - as their non-private counterparts. We complement our theoretical guarantees with an experimental evaluation. Our experiments illustrate the speed and accuracy of our private estimators on both synthetic mixture models and a large public data set.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate an unknown probability distribution over a discrete population from random samples while protecting the individuals represented in those samples. Its goal combines three requirements: low estimation error, efficient computation, and differential privacy. Accuracy is measured in total variation, which compares the estimated probability distribution with the true one.

The authors propose a general approach for a broad range of structured distribution families. Their estimators are computationally efficient and use nearly the smallest possible number of samples. The theoretical results show that, for many such families, private estimation can come close to the sample requirements and running times of estimation without privacy protection.

Experiments on synthetic mixture models and a large public dataset illustrate the estimators' speed and accuracy. The significance is that distributional structure can make privacy compatible with strong statistical and computational performance. The near-equivalence to non-private estimation is established for the structured families covered by the results, rather than asserted for every possible discrete distribution.
summary.tldr: For many structured discrete distributions, private estimators nearly match non-private methods in sample requirements and computation.

title: Differentially Private Learning of Structured Discrete Distributions

abstract: Information diffusion in online social networks is affected by the underlying network topology, but it also has the power to change it. Online users are constantly creating new links when exposed to new information sources, and in turn these links are alternating the way information spreads. However, these two highly intertwined stochastic processes, information diffusion and network evolution, have been predominantly studied separately, ignoring their co-evolutionary dynamics.We propose a temporal point process model, COEVOLVE, for such joint dynamics, allowing the intensity of one process to be modulated by that of the other. This model allows us to efficiently simulate interleaved diffusion and network events, and generate traces obeying common diffusion and network patterns observed in real-world networks. Furthermore, we also develop a convex optimization framework to learn the parameters of the model from historical diffusion and network evolution traces. We experimented with both synthetic data and data gathered from Twitter, and show that our model provides a good fit to the data as well as more accurate predictions than alternatives.

This model allows us to efficiently simulate interleaved diffusion and network events, and generate traces obeying common diffusion and network patterns observed in real-world networks. Furthermore, we also develop a convex optimization framework to learn the parameters of the model from historical diffusion and network evolution traces. paragraphs: COEVOLVE models a feedback loop in social networks: existing connections influence how information spreads, while exposure to information can lead users to create new connections. Those new links then change future diffusion. The paper argues that studying diffusion and network growth separately leaves out this interaction between two evolving processes.

The authors represent both processes with a temporal point process model. Its key feature is that the intensity of either process can be influenced by the other, allowing information events and link-creation events to develop together. The model supports efficient simulation of their interleaved histories and can generate traces with diffusion and network patterns commonly observed in real networks.

The paper also supplies a convex optimization framework for estimating model parameters from historical records of both kinds of events. Experiments on synthetic data and Twitter data show good fit and more accurate predictions than the alternatives considered. These findings support modeling the coupled dynamics when both information activity and changing connections are available, rather than treating network structure as merely a fixed backdrop.
summary.tldr: COEVOLVE jointly models information spreading and link creation, capturing their feedback and improving predictions in the reported experiments.

title: COEVOLVE: A Joint Point Process Model for Information Diffusion and Network Co-evolution

abstract: A cluster tree provides an intuitive summary of a density function that reveals essential structure about the high-density clusters. The true cluster tree is estimated from a finite sample from an unknown true density. This paper addresses the basic question of quantifying our uncertainty by assessing the statistical significance of different features of an empirical cluster tree. We first study a variety of metrics that can be used to compare different trees, analyzing their properties and assessing their suitability for our inference task. We then propose methods to construct and summarize confidence sets for the unknown true cluster tree. We introduce a partial ordering on cluster trees which we use to prune some of the statistically insignificant features of the empirical tree, yielding interpretable and parsimonious cluster trees. Finally, we provide a variety of simulations to illustrate our proposed methods and furthermore demonstrate their utility in the analysis of a Graft-versus-Host Disease (GvHD) data set.

paragraphs: A cluster tree summarizes how high-density groups are organized within a probability distribution. In practice, researchers estimate that tree from a finite sample, so some apparent features may reflect sampling variation. This paper asks how to quantify uncertainty in the estimated tree and assess which parts have statistical support.

The authors first study several ways to measure differences between trees, examining their properties and suitability for inference. They then construct and summarize confidence sets for the unknown true cluster tree. These sets express uncertainty about the overall structure, making the analysis broader than simply returning one estimated hierarchy.

A newly introduced partial ordering provides a way to prune some statistically insignificant features from the empirical tree. The aim is a simpler, more interpretable result whose retained structure is better supported by the data. Simulations illustrate the methods, and an analysis of a Graft-versus-Host Disease dataset demonstrates their utility. The contribution brings uncertainty assessment and principled simplification into the interpretation of density-based cluster hierarchies.
summary.tldr: Confidence sets and statistically guided pruning help distinguish supported cluster-tree structure from features caused by sampling uncertainty.

title: Statistical Inference for Cluster Trees

abstract: We study dual volume sampling, a method for selecting k columns from an n*m short and wide matrix (n <= k <= m) such that the probability of selection is proportional to the volume spanned by the rows of the induced submatrix. This method was proposed by Avron and Boutsidis (2013), who showed it to be a promising method for column subset selection and its multiple applications. However, its wider adoption has been hampered by the lack of polynomial time sampling algorithms. We remove this hindrance by developing an exact (randomized) polynomial time sampling algorithm as well as its derandomization. Thereafter, we study dual volume sampling via the theory of real stable polynomials and prove that its distribution satisfies the “Strong Rayleigh” property. This result has numerous consequences, including a provably fast-mixing Markov chain sampler that makes dual volume sampling much more attractive to practitioners. This sampler is closely related to classical algorithms for popular experimental design methods that are to date lacking theoretical analysis but are known to empirically work well.

For an n-by-m matrix, it selects k columns with n ≤ k ≤ m. The authors then analyze the sampling distribution using real stable polynomials and establish that it has the Strong Rayleigh property.

It supplies another computational route to the distribution, backed by an analysis of convergence. The sampler is also closely related to classical experimental-design algorithms that work well empirically but lack theoretical analysis, connecting the new guarantees with established practical methods.
summary.tldr: Exact polynomial-time algorithms and a Strong Rayleigh analysis make dual volume sampling computationally accessible and yield a fast-mixing sampler.

title: Polynomial time algorithms for dual volume sampling

abstract: Steganography is the practice of concealing a secret message within another, ordinary, message. Commonly, steganography is used to unobtrusively hide a small message within the noisy regions of a larger image. In this study, we attempt to place a full size color image within another image of the same size. Deep neural networks are simultaneously trained to create the hiding and revealing processes and are designed to specifically work as a pair. The system is trained on images drawn randomly from the ImageNet database, and works well on natural images from a wide variety of sources. Beyond demonstrating the successful application of deep learning to hiding images, we carefully examine how the result is achieved and explore extensions. Unlike many popular steganographic methods that encode the secret message within the least significant bits of the carrier image, our approach compresses and distributes the secret image's representation across all of the available bits.

paragraphs: Steganography conceals information inside an ordinary-looking message or image. Common image-based approaches hide a relatively small message in a larger carrier. This paper investigates a more demanding task: placing an entire color image inside another image of the same dimensions, then recovering the hidden image through a matching learned process.

The hiding and revealing networks are trained together and designed to function as a pair. This joint design lets the representation produced by the hiding process work with the corresponding recovery process. Training uses randomly selected ImageNet images, and the authors report that the resulting system works well on natural images drawn from a broad variety of sources.

The paper also examines how the hiding mechanism works and explores extensions. Instead of restricting the secret to the carrier’s least significant bits, the learned approach compresses its representation and spreads it across all available bits. This finding explains the approach’s distinctive use of the carrier: the hidden image is represented throughout it, with recovery handled by the jointly trained revealing network.
summary.tldr: Jointly trained neural networks hide and recover a full-size color image by distributing its compressed representation throughout another image.

title: Hiding Images in Plain Sight: Deep Steganography

abstract: Mainstream captioning models often follow a sequential structure to generate cap- tions, leading to issues such as introduction of irrelevant semantics, lack of diversity in the generated captions, and inadequate generalization performance. In this paper, we present an alternative paradigm for image captioning, which factorizes the captioning procedure into two stages: (1) extracting an explicit semantic representation from the given image; and (2) constructing the caption based on a recursive compositional procedure in a bottom-up manner. Compared to conventional ones, our paradigm better preserves the semantic content through an explicit factorization of semantics and syntax. By using the compositional generation procedure, caption construction follows a recursive structure, which naturally fits the properties of human language. Moreover, the proposed compositional procedure requires less data to train, generalizes better, and yields more diverse captions.

paragraphs: Image captioning requires deciding what an image contains and expressing that content in language. The paper argues that conventional sequential caption generators can introduce irrelevant meaning, produce limited variety, and generalize inadequately. It proposes separating the identification of semantic content from the construction of the sentence that describes it.

The method first extracts an explicit semantic representation of the image. It then builds a caption through a recursive, bottom-up composition process. Rather than treating caption construction solely as a sequence of successive outputs, this procedure organizes language through repeated composition. The explicit separation between meaning and syntax is intended to help preserve the image’s content during generation.

The paper reports that this compositional procedure requires less training data, generalizes better, and generates more diverse captions than conventional approaches. Its contribution is a different organization of the captioning task: an intermediate representation carries the visual meaning, while recursive construction handles its linguistic expression. The stated benefits connect that architectural separation to both semantic fidelity and learning efficiency.
summary.tldr: Separating visual meaning from recursive sentence construction improves image captioning’s semantic fidelity, diversity, and data efficiency.

title: A Neural Compositional Paradigm for Image Captioning

abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization method for differential neural architecture search, based on the theory of prediction with expert advice. Its optimization criterion is well fitted for an architecture-selection, i.e., it minimizes the regret incurred by a sub-optimal selection of operations. Unlike previous search relaxations, that require hard pruning of architectures, our method is designed to dynamically wipe out inferior architectures and enhance superior ones. It achieves an optimal worst-case regret bound and suggests the use of multiple learning-rates, based on the amount of information carried by the backward gradients. Experiments show that our algorithm achieves a strong performance over several image classification datasets. Specifically, it obtains an error rate of 1.6% for CIFAR-10, 23.9% for ImageNet under mobile settings, and achieves state-of-the-art results on three additional datasets.
