XNAS develops an optimization method for differentiable search using the theory of prediction with expert advice. Its criterion minimizes regret from suboptimal operation choices, giving the search process an objective directly concerned with the quality of those selections.

The method dynamically removes inferior architecture options and strengthens better ones. The authors establish an optimal worst-case regret bound and motivate using multiple learning rates according to the information carried by backward gradients. These are guarantees and design choices for the architecture-selection process; the empirical classification results provide a separate assessment of the architectures obtained.

Experiments report strong image-classification performance across several datasets. The stated error rates are 1.6% on CIFAR-10 and 23.9% on ImageNet under mobile settings, alongside state-of-the-art results on three additional datasets. The paper therefore connects a theoretically motivated selection rule to practical architecture search, with reported evidence that this way of allocating emphasis among candidate operations can produce competitive networks.
summary.tldr: XNAS uses expert-advice theory to guide differentiable architecture selection, combining an optimal regret bound with strong reported classification results.

title: XNAS: Neural Architecture Search with Expert Advice

abstract: In safety-critical applications a probabilistic model is usually required to be calibrated, i.e., to capture the uncertainty of its predictions accurately. In multi-class classification, calibration of the most confident predictions only is often not sufficient. We propose and study calibration measures for multi-class classification that generalize existing measures such as the expected calibration error, the maximum calibration error, and the maximum mean calibration error. We propose and evaluate empirically different consistent and unbiased estimators for a specific class of measures based on matrix-valued kernels. Importantly, these estimators can be interpreted as test statistics associated with well-defined bounds and approximations of the p-value under the null hypothesis that the model is calibrated, significantly improving the interpretability of calibration measures, which otherwise lack any meaningful unit or scale.

paragraphs: A probabilistic classifier should express uncertainty accurately, especially when its predictions inform consequential decisions. In classification with several possible classes, checking only the probability assigned to the most confident choice can leave important aspects of calibration unexamined. This paper develops a broader framework for measuring calibration across multiclass predictions.

The proposed measures generalize several existing approaches, including expected calibration error, maximum calibration error, and maximum mean calibration error. For a particular family built using matrix-valued kernels, the authors propose and empirically evaluate consistent and unbiased estimators. The framework therefore connects familiar calibration summaries with a more general mathematical treatment.

A central contribution is interpreting these estimators as statistical test quantities under the hypothesis that the model is calibrated. The authors provide bounds and approximations for the associated p-values. This gives calibration measurements a clearer statistical meaning than an isolated score with no natural scale, helping readers assess evidence of miscalibration rather than relying solely on the numerical size of an error measure.
summary.tldr: A unified framework turns multiclass calibration measures into statistically interpretable tests of predictive uncertainty.

title: Calibration tests in multi-class classification: A unifying framework

abstract: We study the problem of fitting an ultrametric distance to a dissimilarity graph in the context of hierarchical cluster analysis. Standard hierarchical clustering methods are specified procedurally, rather than in terms of the cost function to be optimized. We aim to overcome this limitation by presenting a general optimization framework for ultrametric fitting. Our approach consists of modeling the latter as a constrained optimization problem over the continuous space of ultrametrics. So doing, we can leverage the simple, yet effective, idea of replacing the ultrametric constraint with a min-max operation injected directly into the cost function. The proposed reformulation leads to an unconstrained optimization problem that can be efficiently solved by gradient descent methods. The flexibility of our framework allows us to investigate several cost functions, following the classic paradigm of combining a data fidelity term with a regularization. While we provide no theoretical guarantee to find the global optimum, the numerical results obtained over a number of synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the good performance of our approach with respect to state-of-the-art agglomerative algorithms. This makes us believe that the proposed framework sheds new light on the way to design a new generation of hierarchical clustering methods. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/PerretB/ultrametric-fitting.

This paper develops an optimization framework for fitting an ultrametric distance to a graph of dissimilarities. summary.tldr: An unconstrained reformulation of ultrametric fitting enables gradient-based hierarchical clustering with flexible objectives and promising empirical results.

title: Ultrametric Fitting by Gradient Descent

abstract: We introduce a lifelong language learning setup where a model needs to learn from a stream of text examples without any dataset identifier. We propose an episodic memory model that performs sparse experience replay and local adaptation to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in this setup. Experiments on text classification and question answering demonstrate the complementary benefits of sparse experience replay and local adaptation to allow the model to continuously learn from new datasets. We also show that the space complexity of the episodic memory module can be reduced significantly (~50-90%) by randomly choosing which examples to store in memory with a minimal decrease in performance. We consider an episodic memory component as a crucial building block of general linguistic intelligence and see our model as a first step in that direction.

paragraphs: The paper studies language learning from a continuing stream of text without labels identifying which dataset each example belongs to. In this setting, a model must absorb new examples while retaining useful knowledge from earlier ones. The central problem is catastrophic forgetting: learning new material can damage performance on previously learned material.

The proposed model uses an episodic memory with two mechanisms, sparse experience replay and local adaptation. Replay brings stored experiences back into learning, while local adaptation provides another way to use memory as the model encounters examples. Experiments on text classification and question answering show complementary benefits from the two mechanisms, supporting their combination for continued learning across datasets.

The authors also examine how much memory the approach needs. Randomly selecting which examples to retain reduces the memory module’s space complexity by approximately 50–90%, with only a minimal performance decrease in the reported experiments. This makes the memory component less costly while preserving much of its benefit. The authors position episodic memory as a step toward broader linguistic intelligence, rather than claiming that goal is achieved.
summary.tldr: An episodic memory combines sparse replay and local adaptation to reduce forgetting during continuous language learning without dataset identifiers.

title: Episodic Memory in Lifelong Language Learning

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically applied to static graphs that are assumed to be known upfront. This static input structure is often informed purely by insight of the machine learning practitioner, and might not be optimal for the actual task the GNN is solving. In absence of reliable domain expertise, one might resort to inferring the latent graph structure, which is often difficult due to the vast search space of possible graphs. Here we introduce Pointer Graph Networks (PGNs) which augment sets or graphs with additional inferred edges for improved model generalisation ability. PGNs allow each node to dynamically point to another node, followed by message passing over these pointers. The sparsity of this adaptable graph structure makes learning tractable while still being sufficiently expressive to simulate complex algorithms. Critically, the pointing mechanism is directly supervised to model long-term sequences of operations on classical data structures, incorporating useful structural inductive biases from theoretical computer science. Qualitatively, we demonstrate that PGNs can learn parallelisable variants of pointer-based data structures, namely disjoint set unions and link/cut trees. PGNs generalise out-of-distribution to 5x larger test inputs on dynamic graph connectivity tasks, outperforming unrestricted GNNs and Deep Sets.

Pointer Graph Networks address this problem by adding a sparse, adaptable set of inferred connections to sets or graphs.

The findings show the value of supervised, adaptable pointers for the evaluated algorithmic tasks and larger-input generalization.
summary.tldr: Supervised dynamic pointers give graph networks a sparse learned structure that generalizes to larger inputs on connectivity tasks.

title: Pointer Graph Networks

abstract: Multi-Source Domain Adaptation (MSDA) deals with the transfer of task knowledge from multiple labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain, under a domain-shift. Existing methods aim to minimize this domain-shift using auxiliary distribution alignment objectives. In this work, we present a different perspective to MSDA wherein deep models are observed to implicitly align the domains under label supervision. Thus, we aim to utilize implicit alignment without additional training objectives to perform adaptation. To this end, we use pseudo-labeled target samples and enforce a classifier agreement on the pseudo-labels, a process called Self-supervised Implicit Alignment (SImpAl). We find that SImpAl readily works even under category-shift among the source domains. Further, we propose classifier agreement as a cue to determine the training convergence, resulting in a simple training algorithm. We provide a thorough evaluation of our approach on five benchmarks, along with detailed insights into each component of our approach.

paragraphs: Multi-source domain adaptation transfers knowledge from several labeled data domains to a target domain without labels. Differences between domains make that transfer difficult. This paper starts from the observation that training deep models with label supervision can implicitly align domains, creating an opportunity to use that behavior directly for adaptation.

The proposed method, Self-supervised Implicit Alignment or SImpAl, uses target samples assigned pseudo-labels and enforces classifier agreement on those labels. It aims to exploit implicit alignment without adding separate distribution-alignment objectives. Agreement also serves as a cue for deciding when training has converged, linking the adaptation mechanism with a practical training decision.

The authors find that SImpAl also works when the source domains differ in their category composition. They evaluate the method on five benchmarks and examine the contributions of its components. The reported findings support a comparatively simple adaptation procedure centered on supervised classification, target pseudo-labels, and classifier agreement, including settings where source-domain categories are not all the same.
summary.tldr: SImpAl uses target pseudo-labels and classifier agreement to exploit implicit domain alignment for multi-source adaptation.

title: Your Classifier can Secretly Suffice Multi-Source Domain Adaptation

abstract: We present Graph-Q-SAT, a branching heuristic for a Boolean SAT solver trained with value-based reinforcement learning (RL) using Graph Neural Networks for function approximation. Solvers using Graph-Q-SAT are complete SAT solvers that either provide a satisfying assignment or proof of unsatisfiability, which is required for many SAT applications. The branching heuristics commonly used in SAT solvers make poor decisions during their warm-up period, whereas Graph-Q-SAT is trained to examine the structure of the particular problem instance to make better decisions early in the search. Training Graph-Q-SAT is data efficient and does not require elaborate dataset preparation or feature engineering. We train Graph-Q-SAT using RL interfacing with MiniSat solver and show that Graph-Q-SAT can reduce the number of iterations required to solve SAT problems by 2-3X. Furthermore, it generalizes to unsatisfiable SAT instances, as well as to problems with 5X more variables than it was trained on. We show that for larger problems, reductions in the number of iterations lead to wall clock time reductions, the ultimate goal when designing heuristics. We also show positive zero-shot transfer behavior when testing Graph-Q-SAT on a task family different from that used for training. While more work is needed to apply Graph-Q-SAT to reduce wall clock time in modern SAT solving settings, it is a compelling proof-of-concept showing that RL equipped with Graph Neural Networks can learn a generalizable branching heuristic for SAT search.

paragraphs: SAT solvers search for an assignment satisfying a Boolean formula or establish that no such assignment exists. Their branching choices influence the work required. Graph-Q-SAT learns these choices using value-based reinforcement learning and a graph neural network, with the aim of making better early decisions when conventional heuristics are still warming up.

The learned heuristic examines each problem's structure and is trained through interaction with MiniSat. It preserves solver completeness: the resulting solver still produces a satisfying assignment or a proof of unsatisfiability. The authors report data-efficient training without elaborate dataset preparation or feature engineering, and reductions of two to three times in the iterations needed to solve problems.

The reported generalization includes unsatisfiable instances, problems with five times as many variables as training examples, and positive transfer to a different task family without additional training. On larger problems, fewer iterations also reduce elapsed solving time. The authors nevertheless frame this as a proof of concept, with further work needed to reduce wall-clock time in modern SAT solving settings.
summary.tldr: Graph-Q-SAT learns branching decisions that reduce SAT search iterations and show transfer while preserving solver completeness.

title: Can Q-Learning with Graph Networks Learn a Generalizable Branching Heuristic for a SAT Solver?

abstract: A popular approach to learning encoders for lossy compression is to use additive uniform noise during training as a differentiable approximation to test-time quantization. We demonstrate that a uniform noise channel can also be implemented at test time using universal quantization (Ziv, 1985). This allows us to eliminate the mismatch between training and test phases while maintaining a completely differentiable loss function. Implementing the uniform noise channel is a special case of the more general problem of communicating a sample, which we prove is computationally hard if we do not make assumptions about its distribution. However, the uniform special case is efficient as well as easy to implement and thus of great interest from a practical point of view. Finally, we show that quantization can be obtained as a limiting case of a soft quantizer applied to the uniform noise channel, bridging compression with and without quantization.

paragraphs: Neural lossy compression often trains with additive uniform noise because it gives a differentiable approximation to quantization. At test time, actual quantization replaces that approximation, creating a mismatch between training and use. This paper shows that universal quantization can implement a uniform noise channel at test time as well, aligning the two phases.

That alignment preserves a fully differentiable training loss while making the training-time channel realizable in the deployed compression procedure. The authors place the construction within the broader problem of communicating a sample. They prove that this general problem is computationally hard when no assumptions are made about the sample's distribution.

The uniform case remains efficient and straightforward to implement, making it a useful exception to the general difficulty. The paper also shows that ordinary quantization arises as a limiting case of a soft quantizer applied to the uniform noise channel. These results connect noise-based and quantized compression within one framework and explain how a common training approximation can become part of the actual compression mechanism.
summary.tldr: Universal quantization implements the training-time uniform noise channel at test time, removing a mismatch in neural lossy compression.

title: Universally Quantized Neural Compression

abstract: Triplet loss with batch hard mining (TriHard loss) is an important variation of triplet loss inspired by the idea that hard triplets improve the performance of metric leaning networks. However, there is a dilemma in the training process. The hard negative samples contain various quite similar characteristics compared with anchors and positive samples in a batch. Features of these characteristics should be clustered between anchors and positive samples while are also utilized to repel between anchors and hard negative samples. It is harmful for learning mutual features within classes. Several methods to alleviate the dilemma are designed and tested. In the meanwhile, an element-weighted TriHard loss is emphatically proposed to enlarge the distance between partial elements of feature vectors selectively which represent the different characteristics between anchors and hard negative samples. Extensive evaluations are conducted on Market1501 and MSMT17 datasets and the results achieve state-of-the-art on public baselines.

paragraphs: Person re-identification learns representations that bring images of the same person together and separate different people. TriHard loss emphasizes difficult triplets, including negatives that resemble the anchor. This paper identifies a tension in that strategy: the same visual characteristics may help identify a person while also appearing in a hard negative.

Training then asks those shared characteristics to support both attraction and separation. The authors argue that this conflict harms the learning of common features within a class. They investigate several ways to alleviate it and emphasize an element-weighted TriHard loss that selectively increases distances along feature-vector elements representing differences between anchors and hard negatives.

The intended effect is to direct separation toward distinguishing characteristics while reducing conflict around shared ones. Extensive evaluations on Market1501 and MSMT17 achieve state-of-the-art results on the public baselines considered. The findings support refining how a hard negative contributes to the loss: identifying a difficult example is useful, and choosing which parts of its representation to separate can further improve learning.
summary.tldr: An element-weighted TriHard loss selectively separates distinguishing features to reduce conflicting training signals in person re-identification.

title: The Dilemma of TriHard Loss and an Element-Weighted TriHard Loss for Person Re-Identification

abstract: One-stage detector basically formulates object detection as dense classification and localization (i.e., bounding box regression). The classification is usually optimized by Focal Loss and the box location is commonly learned under Dirac delta distribution. A recent trend for one-stage detectors is to introduce an \emph{individual} prediction branch to estimate the quality of localization, where the predicted quality facilitates the classification to improve detection performance. This paper delves into the \emph{representations} of the above three fundamental elements: quality estimation, classification and localization. Two problems are discovered in existing practices, including (1) the inconsistent usage of the quality estimation and classification between training and inference, and (2) the inflexible Dirac delta distribution for localization. To address the problems, we design new representations for these elements. Specifically, we merge the quality estimation into the class prediction vector to form a joint representation, and use a vector to represent arbitrary distribution of box locations. The improved representations eliminate the inconsistency risk and accurately depict the flexible distribution in real data, but contain \emph{continuous} labels, which is beyond the scope of Focal Loss. We then propose Generalized Focal Loss (GFL) that generalizes Focal Loss from its discrete form to the \emph{continuous} version for successful optimization. On COCO {\tt test-dev}, GFL achieves 45.0\% AP using ResNet-101 backbone, surpassing state-of-the-art SAPD (43.5\%) and ATSS (43.6\%) with higher or comparable inference speed.

On COCO test-dev, the method reaches 45.0% average precision with a ResNet-101 backbone, compared with 43.5% for SAPD and 43.6% for ATSS, at higher or comparable inference speed. The result supports changing both the prediction representation and its training objective together: the loss makes it possible to learn quality-aware class scores and more flexible box-location distributions.
summary.tldr: Generalized Focal Loss trains joint class-quality predictions and distributed box locations, improving the reported detection accuracy without sacrificing inference speed.

title: Generalized Focal Loss: Learning Qualified and Distributed Bounding Boxes for Dense Object Detection

abstract: Novel view synthesis is a long-standing problem in machine learning and computer vision. Significant progress has recently been made in developing neural scene representations and rendering techniques that synthesize photorealistic images from arbitrary views. These representations, however, are extremely slow to train and often also slow to render. Inspired by neural variants of image-based rendering, we develop a new neural rendering approach with the goal of quickly learning a high-quality representation which can also be rendered in real-time. Our approach, MetaNLR++, accomplishes this by using a unique combination of a neural shape representation and 2D CNN-based image feature extraction, aggregation, and re-projection. To push representation convergence times down to minutes, we leverage meta learning to learn neural shape and image feature priors which accelerate training. The optimized shape and image features can then be extracted using traditional graphics techniques and rendered in real time. We show that MetaNLR++ achieves similar or better novel view synthesis results in a fraction of the time that competing methods require.

paragraphs: Novel view synthesis creates images of a scene from viewpoints beyond those already available. Neural scene representations have made substantial progress in visual quality, but training and rendering can be slow. MetaNLR++ targets both costs by learning a scene representation quickly and making the optimized result suitable for real-time rendering.

The approach combines a neural representation of shape with image features extracted by a two-dimensional convolutional network. These features are aggregated and re-projected as part of the rendering approach. Meta-learning supplies learned priors for both shape and image features, accelerating the process of fitting the representation and bringing convergence times down to minutes.

Once optimized, the shape and image features can be extracted using traditional graphics techniques and rendered in real time. The authors report novel-view results that are similar to or better than competing methods while requiring a fraction of their time. The contribution connects faster representation learning with an output that can also be displayed efficiently, addressing two distinct sources of delay.
summary.tldr: MetaNLR++ uses meta-learned shape and image-feature priors to train scene representations in minutes and support real-time novel-view rendering.

title: Fast Training of Neural Lumigraph Representations using Meta Learning

abstract: We theoretically analyze the typical learning performance of $\ell_{1}$-regularized linear regression ($\ell_1$-LinR) for Ising model selection using the replica method from statistical mechanics. For typical random regular graphs in the paramagnetic phase, an accurate estimate of the typical sample complexity of $\ell_1$-LinR is obtained. Remarkably, despite the model misspecification, $\ell_1$-LinR is model selection consistent with the same order of sample complexity as $\ell_{1}$-regularized logistic regression ($\ell_1$-LogR), i.e., $M=\mathcal{O}\left(\log N\right)$, where $N$ is the number of variables of the Ising model. Moreover, we provide an efficient method to accurately predict the non-asymptotic behavior of $\ell_1$-LinR for moderate $M, N$, such as precision and recall. Simulations show a fairly good agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental results, even for graphs with many loops, which supports our findings. Although this paper mainly focuses on $\ell_1$-LinR, our method is readily applicable for precisely characterizing the typical learning performances of a wide class of $\ell_{1}$-regularized $M$-estimators including $\ell_1$-LogR and interaction screening.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether sparse linear regression can recover the interaction structure of an Ising model despite using a misspecified model. It analyzes typical learning behavior with the replica method from statistical mechanics. The main theoretical setting is typical random regular graphs in the paramagnetic phase.

Within that setting, the authors estimate the sample requirements of ℓ1-regularized linear regression and find it is consistent for model selection. Its sample complexity has the same logarithmic order in the number of variables as ℓ1-regularized logistic regression. This result concerns identifying interactions: a model’s mismatch to the data-generating mechanism does not necessarily prevent successful structure recovery in the analyzed regime.

The authors also provide an efficient way to predict finite-size behavior, including precision and recall for moderate sample counts and numbers of variables. Simulations agree fairly well with those predictions, even for graphs containing many loops. Although the analysis emphasizes linear regression, the method also applies to a broader class of ℓ1-regularized estimators, including logistic regression and interaction screening.
summary.tldr: For typical random regular Ising graphs in the paramagnetic phase, sparse linear regression can consistently recover structure with logarithmic-order sample complexity.

title: Ising Model Selection Using $\ell_{1}$-Regularized Linear Regression: A Statistical Mechanics Analysis

abstract: In this paper, we comprehensively reveal the learning dynamics of normalized neural network using Stochastic Gradient Descent (with momentum) and Weight Decay (WD), named as Spherical Motion Dynamics (SMD). Most related works focus on studying behavior of ``effective learning rate" in ``equilibrium" state, i.e. assuming weight norm remains unchanged. However, their discussion on why this equilibrium can be reached is either absent or less convincing. Our work directly explores the cause of equilibrium, as a special state of SMD. Specifically, 1) we introduce the assumptions that can lead to equilibrium state in SMD, and prove equilibrium can be reached in a linear rate regime under given assumptions; 2) we propose ``angular update" as a substitute for effective learning rate to depict the state of SMD, and derive the theoretical value of angular update in equilibrium state; 3) we verify our assumptions and theoretical results on various large-scale computer vision tasks including ImageNet and MSCOCO with standard settings. Experiment results show our theoretical findings agree well with empirical observations. We also show that the behavior of angular update in SMD can produce interesting effect to the optimization of neural network in practice.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes normalized neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, momentum, and weight decay. Earlier discussions often examined an equilibrium where the weight norm stays constant. The authors instead investigate why that equilibrium can arise, treating it as a particular state within what they call Spherical Motion Dynamics.

They introduce assumptions that lead to equilibrium and prove a linear-rate convergence regime under those assumptions. They also propose angular update as an alternative to effective learning rate for describing the dynamics. This quantity focuses on how weight direction changes, and the authors derive its theoretical value at equilibrium.

Experiments on large-scale vision tasks, including ImageNet and MSCOCO with standard settings, test the assumptions and theoretical predictions. The reported observations agree well with the theory. The paper also shows that angular-update behavior can affect practical network optimization. Its contribution is a conditional account of how equilibrium develops and a different quantity for tracking training motion, rather than simply assuming that a stable weight norm has already been reached.
summary.tldr: Spherical Motion Dynamics explains equilibrium in normalized-network training under stated assumptions and uses angular updates to characterize that behavior.

title: Spherical Motion Dynamics: Learning Dynamics of Normalized Neural Network using SGD and Weight Decay

abstract: We study acquisition functions for active learning (AL) for text classification. The Expected Loss Reduction (ELR) method focuses on a Bayesian estimate of the reduction in classification error, recently updated with Mean Objective Cost of Uncertainty (MOCU). We convert the ELR framework to estimate the increase in (strictly proper) scores like log probability or negative mean square error, which we call Bayesian Estimate of Mean Proper Scores (BEMPS). We also prove convergence results borrowing techniques used with MOCU. In order to allow better experimentation with the new acquisition functions, we develop a complementary batch AL algorithm, which encourages diversity in the vector of expected changes in scores for unlabelled data. To allow high performance text classifiers, we combine ensembling and dynamic validation set construction on pretrained language models. Extensive experimental evaluation then explores how these different acquisition functions perform. The results show that the use of mean square error and log probability with BEMPS yields robust acquisition functions, which consistently outperform the others tested.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive labels so that a classifier can learn effectively. This paper studies that choice for text classification. It starts from Expected Loss Reduction, which uses a Bayesian estimate of how much a label would reduce classification error, and changes the objective used to judge a candidate example.

The proposed BEMPS framework estimates improvements in strictly proper scores, including log probability and negative mean square error. The authors prove convergence results using techniques associated with Mean Objective Cost of Uncertainty. They also introduce a batch selection algorithm that encourages diversity in the expected score changes across unlabeled data, so selection considers differences in anticipated learning effects.

For experiments with pretrained language models, the approach combines ensembles with dynamically constructed validation sets. The evaluation compares acquisition functions within this broader setup. BEMPS using mean square error and log probability consistently outperforms the other functions tested. These findings support selecting examples through expected improvements in probabilistic scores, with batch diversity providing a complementary way to organize the labeling decisions.
summary.tldr: BEMPS selects text examples by expected improvements in proper probabilistic scores and outperforms the other acquisition functions tested.

title: Diversity Enhanced Active Learning with Strictly Proper Scoring Rules

abstract: Capturing accurate uncertainty quantification of the prediction from deep neural networks is important in many real-world decision-making applications. A reliable predictor is expected to be accurate when it is confident about its predictions and indicate high uncertainty when it is likely to be inaccurate. However, modern neural networks have been found to be poorly calibrated, primarily in the direction of overconfidence. In recent years, there is a surge of research on model calibration by leveraging implicit or explicit regularization techniques during training, which obtain well calibration by avoiding overconfident outputs. In our study, we empirically found that despite the predictions obtained from these regularized models are better calibrated, they suffer from not being as calibratable, namely, it is harder to further calibrate their predictions with post-hoc calibration methods like temperature scaling and histogram binning. We conduct a series of empirical studies showing that overconfidence may not hurt final calibration performance if post-hoc calibration is allowed, rather, the penalty of confident outputs will compress the room of potential improvements in post-hoc calibration phase. Our experimental findings point out a new direction to improve calibration of DNNs by considering main training and post-hoc calibration as a unified framework.

paragraphs: A well-calibrated predictor should express confidence that matches how often its predictions are correct. Neural networks often express excessive confidence, motivating training methods that penalize confident outputs. This paper asks whether improving calibration during training also produces the best result after a separate calibration step.

The authors distinguish current calibration from calibratability: how effectively a model's predictions can be calibrated afterward. Their empirical studies find that regularized models can be better calibrated initially yet harder to improve using methods such as temperature scaling and histogram binning. Suppressing confidence during training can reduce the room available for these later adjustments.

The experiments suggest that overconfidence may not harm final calibration when post-hoc calibration is allowed. This is a conditional empirical finding, rather than a claim that confidence is always harmless. Its practical implication is to assess training and subsequent calibration together. A model that looks less reliable before adjustment can still provide a useful starting point for the full calibration procedure, so initial calibration alone may not identify the strongest final approach.
summary.tldr: Reducing overconfidence during training can hinder later calibration, suggesting that training and post-hoc adjustment should be evaluated together.

title: Rethinking Calibration of Deep Neural Networks: Do Not Be Afraid of Overconfidence

abstract: We propose a novel Frank-Wolfe (FW) procedure for the optimization of infinite-dimensional functionals of probability measures - a task which arises naturally in a wide range of areas including statistical learning (e.g. variational inference) and artificial intelligence (e.g. generative adversarial networks). Our FW procedure takes advantage of Wasserstein gradient flows and strong duality results recently developed in Distributionally Robust Optimization so that gradient steps (in the Wasserstein space) can be efficiently computed using finite-dimensional, convex optimization methods. We show how to choose the step sizes in order to guarantee exponentially fast iteration convergence, under mild assumptions on the functional to optimize. We apply our algorithm to a range of functionals arising from applications in nonparametric estimation.

Our FW procedure takes advantage of Wasserstein gradient flows and strong duality results recently developed in Distributionally Robust Optimization so that gradient steps (in the Wasserstein space) can be efficiently computed using finite-dimensional, convex optimization methods. paragraphs: Some optimization problems choose an entire probability distribution rather than a finite vector of parameters. Their objectives are functionals: quantities that assign values to distributions. Such problems arise in areas including variational inference and generative adversarial networks. This paper proposes a modified Frank-Wolfe procedure for working in that infinite-dimensional setting.

The method combines Wasserstein gradient flows with strong duality results from distributionally robust optimization. These ingredients allow gradient steps in the space of probability measures to be computed through finite-dimensional convex optimization. The practical significance is that an update defined over distributions becomes accessible through a more manageable optimization problem.

The authors specify step sizes that guarantee exponentially fast convergence in the number of iterations under assumptions on the objective functional, which they describe as mild. They also apply the algorithm to several functionals from nonparametric estimation. The result links distribution-level optimization to concrete computations, while its convergence claim remains conditional on the functional satisfying the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: A modified Frank-Wolfe method computes probability-space updates through finite-dimensional convex optimization and achieves exponential iteration convergence under stated assumptions.

title: Modified Frank Wolfe in Probability Space

abstract: Can we leverage high-resolution information without the unsustainable quadratic complexity to input scale? We propose Traversal Network (TNet), a novel multi-scale hard-attention architecture, which traverses image scale-space in a top-down fashion, visiting only the most informative image regions along the way. TNet offers an adjustable trade-off between accuracy and complexity, by changing the number of attended image locations. We compare our model against hard-attention baselines on ImageNet, achieving higher accuracy with less resources (FLOPs, processing time and memory). We further test our model on fMoW dataset, where we process satellite images of size up to $896 \times 896$ px, getting up to $2.5$x faster processing compared to baselines operating on the same resolution, while achieving higher accuracy as well. TNet is modular, meaning that most classification models could be adopted as its backbone for feature extraction, making the reported performance gains orthogonal to benefits offered by existing optimized deep models. Finally, hard-attention guarantees a degree of interpretability to our model's predictions, without any extra cost beyond inference.

paragraphs: High-resolution images contain useful detail, but processing the entire image becomes increasingly expensive as resolution grows. Traversal Network, or TNet, addresses this by selectively examining informative regions at multiple scales. It traverses the image’s scale hierarchy from the top down, using hard attention to choose which locations receive processing.

The number of attended locations provides an adjustable balance between accuracy and computational cost. TNet is also modular: most image classification models could supply its feature-extraction backbone. This means the proposed selective traversal can be combined with benefits from existing optimized classification architectures. Its chosen regions additionally provide a degree of interpretability without an extra inference procedure.

On ImageNet, TNet achieves higher accuracy than the tested hard-attention baselines while using fewer operations, less processing time, and less memory. On fMoW satellite images up to 896 by 896 pixels, it achieves higher accuracy and up to 2.5 times faster processing than baselines using the same resolution. These results support selective access to detail as a useful strategy for scaling image classification.
summary.tldr: TNet selectively visits informative image regions across scales to improve classification accuracy while reducing computation on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Hard-Attention for Scalable Image Classification

abstract: A good visual representation is an inference map from observations (images) to features (vectors) that faithfully reflects the hidden modularized generative factors (semantics). In this paper, we formulate the notion of "good" representation from a group-theoretic view using Higgins' definition of disentangled representation, and show that existing Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) only disentangles simple augmentation features such as rotation and colorization, thus unable to modularize the remaining semantics. To break the limitation, we propose an iterative SSL algorithm: Iterative Partition-based Invariant Risk Minimization (IP-IRM), which successfully grounds the abstract semantics and the group acting on them into concrete contrastive learning. At each iteration, IP-IRM first partitions the training samples into two subsets that correspond to an entangled group element. Then, it minimizes a subset-invariant contrastive loss, where the invariance guarantees to disentangle the group element. We prove that IP-IRM converges to a fully disentangled representation and show its effectiveness on various benchmarks. Codes are available at https://github.com/Wangt-CN/IP-IRM.

In this paper, we formulate the notion of "good" representation from a group-theoretic view using Higgins' definition of disentangled representation, and show that existing Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) only disentangles simple augmentation features such as rotation and colorization, thus unable to modularize the remaining semantics. To break the limitation, we propose an iterative SSL algorithm: Iterative Partition-based Invariant Risk Minimization (IP-IRM), which successfully grounds the abstract semantics and the group acting on them into concrete contrastive learning. At each iteration, IP-IRM first partitions the training samples into two subsets that correspond to an entangled group element. Then, it minimizes a subset-invariant contrastive loss, where the invariance guarantees to disentangle the group element. We prove that IP-IRM converges to a fully disentangled representation and show its effectiveness on various benchmarks. Codes are available at https://github.com/Wangt-CN/IP-IRM.

paragraphs: A useful visual representation should reflect the separate semantic factors that generate an image. This paper formalizes that goal through group theory and a definition of disentangled representation. Within its analysis, existing self-supervised learning disentangles simple augmentation features, such as rotation and colorization, while leaving other semantics entangled.

The proposed method, Iterative Partition-based Invariant Risk Minimization, or IP-IRM, turns this abstract formulation into a contrastive learning procedure. Each iteration partitions training examples into two subsets corresponding to an entangled group element. It then minimizes a contrastive loss that is invariant across the subsets, with that invariance providing the guarantee of disentangling the targeted group element.

Repeating these steps addresses remaining entanglement through successive partitions and invariant learning. The authors prove convergence to a fully disentangled representation in their formulation and demonstrate effectiveness on several benchmarks. The contribution is the link between a mathematical account of semantic structure and a concrete training algorithm. It gives partitioning a specific purpose: expose an entangled factor so that the next learning step can separate it.
summary.tldr: IP-IRM alternates data partitioning and invariant contrastive learning, with a proof of convergence to disentangled representations in its group-theoretic formulation.

title: Self-Supervised Learning Disentangled Group Representation as Feature

abstract: The Configurable Markov Decision Process framework includes two entities: a Reinforcement Learning agent and a configurator that can modify some environmental parameters to improve the agent's performance. This presupposes that the two actors have the same reward functions. What if the configurator does not have the same intentions as the agent? This paper introduces the Non-Cooperative Configurable Markov Decision Process, a setting that allows having two (possibly different) reward functions for the configurator and the agent. Then, we consider an online learning problem, where the configurator has to find the best among a finite set of possible configurations. We propose two learning algorithms to minimize the configurator's expected regret, which exploits the problem's structure, depending on the agent's feedback. While a naive application of the UCB algorithm yields a regret that grows indefinitely over time, we show that our approach suffers only bounded regret. Furthermore, we empirically show the performance of our algorithm in simulated domains.

paragraphs: A configurable Markov decision process contains an agent that learns to act and a configurator that can change some environmental parameters. The usual formulation gives both participants the same reward. This paper introduces a non-cooperative version in which their reward functions may differ, allowing configuration choices to serve objectives distinct from the agent's.

The learning problem belongs to the configurator, which must choose the best option from a finite collection of configurations through online interaction. The authors propose two algorithms that use the structure of this interaction and depend on the feedback available from the agent. Their objective is to minimize the configurator's expected regret.

In the studied setting, a naive application of the UCB algorithm incurs regret that continues growing over time, whereas the proposed approach has bounded regret. This shows why treating configurations as ordinary choices without exploiting the problem's structure can be inadequate. Simulated-domain experiments provide an empirical assessment alongside the theoretical comparison.
summary.tldr: For configurators and agents with potentially different rewards, structured learning algorithms achieve bounded regret over a finite configuration set.

title: Learning in Non-Cooperative Configurable Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Lewis signaling games are a class of simple communication games for simulating the emergence of language. In these games, two agents must agree on a communication protocol in order to solve a cooperative task. Previous work has shown that agents trained to play this game with reinforcement learning tend to develop languages that display undesirable properties from a linguistic point of view (lack of generalization, lack of compositionality, etc). In this paper, we aim to provide better understanding of this phenomenon by analytically studying the learning problem in Lewis games. As a core contribution, we demonstrate that the standard objective in Lewis games can be decomposed in two components: a co-adaptation loss and an information loss. This decomposition enables us to surface two potential sources of overfitting, which we show may undermine the emergence of a structured communication protocol. In particular, when we control for overfitting on the co-adaptation loss, we recover desired properties in the emergent languages: they are more compositional and generalize better.

paragraphs: Lewis signaling games study how two agents develop a communication protocol while cooperating on a task. Earlier reinforcement-learning approaches often produced protocols that generalized poorly or lacked compositional structure. This paper analyzes the learning objective to understand why successful cooperation may still yield these undesirable language properties.

The authors show that the standard objective separates into a co-adaptation loss and an information loss. This decomposition exposes two potential sources of overfitting that can interfere with the emergence of structured communication. It gives a more specific account of the problem than treating the agents' overall task performance as a single measure of learning success.

When the authors control overfitting associated with the co-adaptation component, the resulting languages become more compositional and generalize better. The finding links properties of the learned protocol to how the agents fit their shared training problem. It indicates that controlling a particular source of overfitting can improve communication structure, without asserting that every signaling game will naturally produce a generalizable language.
summary.tldr: Decomposing the Lewis-game objective reveals overfitting sources, and controlling co-adaptation overfitting produces more compositional, better-generalizing communication.

title: Emergent Communication: Generalization and Overfitting in Lewis Games

abstract: We study the complexity of finding the global solution to stochastic nonconvex optimization when the objective function satisfies global Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz (KL) inequality and the queries from stochastic gradient oracles satisfy mild expected smoothness assumption. We first introduce a general framework to analyze Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and its associated nonlinear dynamics under the setting. As a byproduct of our analysis, we obtain a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-(4-\alpha)/\alpha})$ for SGD when the objective satisfies the so called $\alpha$-P{\L} condition, where $\alpha$ is the degree of gradient domination. Furthermore, we show that a modified SGD with variance reduction and restarting (PAGER) achieves an improved sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2/\alpha})$ when the objective satisfies the average smoothness assumption. This leads to the first optimal algorithm for the important case of $\alpha=1$ which appears in applications such as policy optimization in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Nonconvex optimization can be difficult even when only noisy gradient information is available. This paper studies objectives with a global Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality, a structural condition that makes global optimization analysis possible. It also assumes a mild expected-smoothness property for the stochastic gradient queries and develops a framework for analyzing SGD's nonlinear dynamics.

For objectives satisfying the α-PL condition, the analysis gives SGD a sample complexity of order ε^−((4−α)/α), where ε is the target accuracy and α describes gradient domination. For α equal to one, the paper establishes the first optimal algorithm for that case, which occurs in applications including reinforcement-learning policy optimization. The improved rate is therefore tied to the stated objective and smoothness assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under global KL-related conditions, variance reduction and restarting improve stochastic optimization rates and achieve optimality for α=1.

title: Sharp Analysis of Stochastic Optimization under Global Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz Inequality

abstract: Federated Learning allows the training of machine learning models by using the computation and private data resources of many distributed clients. Most existing results on Federated Learning (FL) assume the clients have ground-truth labels. However, in many practical scenarios, clients may be unable to label task-specific data due to a lack of expertise or resource. We propose SemiFL to address the problem of combining communication-efficient FL such as FedAvg with Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL). In SemiFL, clients have completely unlabeled data and can train multiple local epochs to reduce communication costs, while the server has a small amount of labeled data. We provide a theoretical understanding of the success of data augmentation-based SSL methods to illustrate the bottleneck of a vanilla combination of communication-efficient FL with SSL. To address this issue, we propose alternate training to 'fine-tune global model with labeled data' and 'generate pseudo-labels with the global model.' We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the performance of a labeled server with unlabeled clients training with multiple local epochs. Moreover, our method outperforms many existing SSFL baselines and performs competitively with the state-of-the-art FL and SSL results.

paragraphs: Federated learning often assumes that participating clients have labeled data. SemiFL addresses a different arrangement: clients have entirely unlabeled data, while the server holds a small labeled dataset. Clients also need to train for multiple local epochs so that they can reduce communication costs instead of repeatedly contacting the server.

The authors analyze data-augmentation-based semi-supervised learning to explain a bottleneck in simply combining it with communication-efficient federated training. Their solution alternates between fine-tuning the global model using labeled data and generating pseudo-labels using that global model. This gives the server's limited supervision an explicit role in the training process used with unlabeled clients.

Extensive experiments show significant performance improvements in the stated setting with a labeled server and clients performing multiple local epochs. SemiFL outperforms many existing semi-supervised federated learning baselines and is competitive with state-of-the-art federated and semi-supervised results. The contribution is a coordinated training procedure for a specific distribution of labels, designed to make use of unlabeled client data while retaining communication efficiency.
summary.tldr: SemiFL alternates server-side labeled training and global-model pseudo-labeling to learn effectively from entirely unlabeled federated clients.

title: SemiFL: Semi-Supervised Federated Learning for Unlabeled Clients with Alternate Training

abstract: Federated learning (FL) faces challenges of intermittent client availability and computation/communication efficiency. As a result, only a small subset of clients can participate in FL at a given time. It is important to understand how partial client participation affects convergence, but most existing works have either considered idealized participation patterns or obtained results with non-zero optimality error for generic patterns. In this paper, we provide a unified convergence analysis for FL with arbitrary client participation. We first introduce a generalized version of federated averaging (FedAvg) that amplifies parameter updates at an interval of multiple FL rounds. Then, we present a novel analysis that captures the effect of client participation in a single term. By analyzing this term, we obtain convergence upper bounds for a wide range of participation patterns, including both non-stochastic and stochastic cases, which match either the lower bound of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or the state-of-the-art results in specific settings. We also discuss various insights, recommendations, and experimental results.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often proceed with whichever clients are currently available. Limited connectivity and computing resources mean that only a subset contributes in any round. This paper studies how those participation patterns affect convergence, addressing a gap between analyses based on idealized availability and more general analyses that retain a nonzero optimality error.

The authors introduce a generalized version of federated averaging that amplifies parameter updates at intervals spanning multiple rounds. Their analysis gathers the effect of client participation into a single mathematical term. This gives them a common framework for examining different participation patterns instead of treating every availability scenario as an unrelated problem.

Analyzing that term produces convergence upper bounds for a range of stochastic and non-stochastic participation patterns. In specific settings, the bounds match either a stochastic gradient descent lower bound or existing leading results. The contribution is therefore a unified way to connect participation to convergence, accompanied by practical insights and experiments, rather than a claim that every participation pattern performs equally well.
summary.tldr: A generalized federated averaging method and unified analysis connect varied client participation patterns to convergence guarantees.

title: A Unified Analysis of Federated Learning with Arbitrary Client Participation

abstract: Most Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) predict the labels of unseen graphs by learning the correlation between the input graphs and labels. However, by presenting a graph classification investigation on the training graphs with severe bias, surprisingly, we discover that GNNs always tend to explore the spurious correlations to make decision, even if the causal correlation always exists. This implies that existing GNNs trained on such biased datasets will suffer from poor generalization capability. By analyzing this problem in a causal view, we find that disentangling and decorrelating the causal and bias latent variables from the biased graphs are both crucial for debiasing. Inspired by this, we propose a general disentangled GNN framework to learn the causal substructure and bias substructure, respectively. Particularly, we design a parameterized edge mask generator to explicitly split the input graph into causal and bias subgraphs. Then two GNN modules supervised by causal/bias-aware loss functions respectively are trained to encode causal and bias subgraphs into their corresponding representations. With the disentangled representations, we synthesize the counterfactual unbiased training samples to further decorrelate causal and bias variables. Moreover, to better benchmark the severe bias problem, we construct three new graph datasets, which have controllable bias degrees and are easier to visualize and explain. Experimental results well demonstrate that our approach achieves superior generalization performance over existing baselines. Furthermore, owing to the learned edge mask, the proposed model has appealing interpretability and transferability.

paragraphs: Graph classifiers can learn misleading relationships between graph patterns and labels. In an investigation with severely biased training graphs, the authors find that graph neural networks favor these spurious relationships even when causal information is available. Their causal analysis identifies two important steps for addressing this problem: separating causal information from bias and reducing the correlation between them.

The proposed framework learns an edge mask that divides each input graph into causal and bias subgraphs. Separate graph neural networks encode these parts, using losses tailored to their respective roles. The resulting representations also support the synthesis of counterfactual training samples intended to reduce the remaining association between causal and bias variables.

To evaluate severe bias more directly, the authors construct three graph datasets with adjustable bias levels and structures that are easier to visualize and explain. Experiments report better generalization than existing baselines. The learned edge masks also provide interpretability and transferability, connecting the prediction process to explicit graph substructures rather than leaving the separation entirely inside hidden representations.
summary.tldr: The method separates causal and bias subgraphs and generates counterfactual training samples to improve graph-classification generalization under severe bias.

title: Debiasing Graph Neural Networks via Learning Disentangled Causal Substructure

abstract: Capitalizing on large pre-trained models for various downstream tasks of interest have recently emerged with promising performance. Due to the ever-growing model size, the standard full fine-tuning based task adaptation strategy becomes prohibitively costly in terms of model training and storage. This has led to a new research direction in parameter-efficient transfer learning. However, existing attempts typically focus on downstream tasks from the same modality (e.g., image understanding) of the pre-trained model. This creates a limit because in some specific modalities, (e.g., video understanding) such a strong pre-trained model with sufficient knowledge is less or not available. In this work, we investigate such a novel cross-modality transfer learning setting, namely parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer learning. To solve this problem, we propose a new Spatio-Temporal Adapter (ST-Adapter) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning per video task. With a built-in spatio-temporal reasoning capability in a compact design, ST-Adapter enables a pre-trained image model without temporal knowledge to reason about dynamic video content at a small ~8% per-task parameter cost, requiring approximately 20 times fewer updated parameters compared to previous work. Extensive experiments on video action recognition tasks show that our ST-Adapter can match or even outperform the strong full fine-tuning strategy and state-of-the-art video models, whilst enjoying the advantage of parameter efficiency.

This paper studies transferring an image model to video, where understanding how content changes over time is essential.

The approach’s significance lies in adding the capability needed for temporal reasoning while limiting the amount of model capacity that must be adapted for each task.
summary.tldr: ST-Adapter equips pretrained image models for video understanding with compact temporal adaptation and approximately 8% per-task parameter cost.

title: ST-Adapter: Parameter-Efficient Image-to-Video Transfer Learning

abstract: We use the "map of elections" approach of Szufa et al. (AAMAS 2020) to analyze several well-known vote distributions. For each of them, we give an explicit formula or an efficient algorithm for computing its frequency matrix, which captures the probability that a given candidate appears in a given position in a sampled vote. We use these matrices to draw the "skeleton map" of distributions, evaluate its robustness, and analyze its properties. We further develop a general and unified framework for learning the distribution of real-world preferences using the frequency matrices of established vote distributions.

paragraphs: A distribution over votes describes how candidate rankings might be generated. This paper studies several established vote distributions through frequency matrices. Each matrix entry gives the probability that a particular candidate occupies a particular ranking position in a sampled vote, providing a common representation of candidate-position probabilities across distributions.

For each distribution considered, the authors supply either an explicit formula or an efficient algorithm for computing this matrix. They then use the matrices within the map-of-elections approach to construct a skeleton map of the distributions. This turns the matrix representation into a way to study how distributions relate geometrically. The work also examines the map's properties and evaluates its robustness.

The same representation supports a general framework for learning the distribution of real-world preferences using established vote distributions. The contribution therefore connects computation, comparison, and learning: matrices can be calculated systematically, used to organize known distributions, and incorporated into preference modeling. This provides a unified basis for working with multiple voting models.
summary.tldr: Frequency matrices provide a shared representation for computing, mapping, and learning distributions of ranked voting preferences.

title: Expected Frequency Matrices of Elections: Computation, Geometry, and Preference Learning

abstract: We investigate properties of goodness-of-fit tests based on the Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD). We introduce a strategy to construct a test, called KSDAgg, which aggregates multiple tests with different kernels. KSDAgg avoids splitting the data to perform kernel selection (which leads to a loss in test power), and rather maximises the test power over a collection of kernels. We provide theoretical guarantees on the power of KSDAgg: we show it achieves the smallest uniform separation rate of the collection, up to a logarithmic term. For compactly supported densities with bounded score function for the model, we derive the rate for KSDAgg over restricted Sobolev balls; this rate corresponds to the minimax optimal rate over unrestricted Sobolev balls, up to an iterated logarithmic term. KSDAgg can be computed exactly in practice as it relies either on a parametric bootstrap or on a wild bootstrap to estimate the quantiles and the level corrections. In particular, for the crucial choice of bandwidth of a fixed kernel, it avoids resorting to arbitrary heuristics (such as median or standard deviation) or to data splitting. We find on both synthetic and real-world data that KSDAgg outperforms other state-of-the-art quadratic-time adaptive KSD-based goodness-of-fit testing procedures.

paragraphs: A goodness-of-fit test asks whether observed data agree with a proposed probability model. For tests based on Kernel Stein Discrepancy, the choice of kernel can affect the ability to detect disagreement. KSDAgg combines tests using multiple kernels, avoiding the loss of testing power associated with setting aside data to select one kernel.

The authors prove that the aggregated test attains the collection's smallest uniform separation rate up to a logarithmic factor. This rate describes how small a discrepancy the test can reliably detect. Under compact support and a bounded model score function, they also obtain a rate over restricted Sobolev classes matching the unrestricted minimax rate up to an iterated logarithmic factor.

Experiments on synthetic and real data report stronger performance than other leading adaptive, quadratic-time KSD tests, supporting the practical value of this theoretically motivated combination.
summary.tldr: KSDAgg combines kernel-based goodness-of-fit tests to adapt kernel choice without splitting data, with theoretical power guarantees.

title: KSD Aggregated Goodness-of-fit Test

abstract: In this paper, we tackle the important yet under-investigated problem of making long-horizon prediction of event sequences. Existing state-of-the-art models do not perform well at this task due to their autoregressive structure. We propose HYPRO, a hybridly normalized probabilistic model that naturally fits this task: its first part is an autoregressive base model that learns to propose predictions; its second part is an energy function that learns to reweight the proposals such that more realistic predictions end up with higher probabilities. We also propose efficient training and inference algorithms for this model. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed HYPRO model can significantly outperform previous models at making long-horizon predictions of future events. We also conduct a range of ablation studies to investigate the effectiveness of each component of our proposed methods.

We propose HYPRO, a hybridly normalized probabilistic model that naturally fits this task: its first part is an autoregressive base model that learns to propose predictions; its second part is an energy function that learns to reweight the proposals such that more realistic predictions end up with higher probabilities. We also propose efficient training and inference algorithms for this model. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed HYPRO model can significantly outperform previous models at making long-horizon predictions of future events. We also conduct a range of ablation studies to investigate the effectiveness of each component of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: HYPRO addresses prediction of event sequences far into the future. The paper identifies the autoregressive structure of existing models as a source of poor performance on this task. Its approach retains an autoregressive model but gives it a specific role within a larger probabilistic system: proposing candidate future predictions.

A second component, an energy function, learns to reweight those proposals so that more realistic predictions receive higher probability. This separates the task of generating candidates from the task of judging their plausibility. The hybrid model therefore supplements the base predictor with a learned correction to how probability is assigned across its proposed futures.

The authors develop efficient procedures for both training and inference, making the two-component construction usable for prediction. Across multiple real-world datasets, HYPRO significantly outperforms previous models on long-horizon event forecasting. Ablation studies examine the contribution of the individual components. The findings support combining autoregressive proposals with learned reweighting as an effective way to improve predictions over extended future sequences.
summary.tldr: HYPRO improves long-horizon event prediction by using an energy function to reweight futures proposed by an autoregressive model.

title: HYPRO: A Hybridly Normalized Probabilistic Model for Long-Horizon Prediction of Event Sequences

abstract: Multi-modal knowledge graph embeddings (KGE) have caught more and more attention in learning representations of entities and relations for link prediction tasks. Different from previous uni-modal KGE approaches, multi-modal KGE can leverage expressive knowledge from a wealth of modalities (image, text, etc.), leading to more comprehensive representations of real-world entities. However, the critical challenge along this course lies in that the multi-modal embedding spaces are usually heterogeneous. In this sense, direct fusion will destroy the inherent spatial structure of different modal embeddings. To overcome this challenge, we revisit multi-modal KGE from a distributional alignment perspective and propose optimal transport knowledge graph embeddings (OTKGE). Specifically, we model the multi-modal fusion procedure as a transport plan moving different modal embeddings to a unified space by minimizing the Wasserstein distance between multi-modal distributions. Theoretically, we show that by minimizing the Wasserstein distance between the individual modalities and the unified embedding space, the final results are guaranteed to maintain consistency and comprehensiveness. Moreover, experimental results on well-established multi-modal knowledge graph completion benchmarks show that our OTKGE achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Different from previous uni-modal KGE approaches, multi-modal KGE can leverage expressive knowledge from a wealth of modalities (image, text, etc.), leading to more comprehensive representations of real-world entities. However, the critical challenge along this course lies in that the multi-modal embedding spaces are usually heterogeneous. In this sense, direct fusion will destroy the inherent spatial structure of different modal embeddings. To overcome this challenge, we revisit multi-modal KGE from a distributional alignment perspective and propose optimal transport knowledge graph embeddings (OTKGE). Specifically, we model the multi-modal fusion procedure as a transport plan moving different modal embeddings to a unified space by minimizing the Wasserstein distance between multi-modal distributions. Theoretically, we show that by minimizing the Wasserstein distance between the individual modalities and the unified embedding space, the final results are guaranteed to maintain consistency and comprehensiveness. paragraphs: Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations numerically to help predict missing links. Images, text, and other modalities can enrich those representations, but their embedding spaces may have different structures. The paper argues that directly combining these spaces can disrupt the relationships already encoded within each modality, undermining the purpose of adding information.

OTKGE treats combination as a distribution-alignment problem. It constructs a transport plan that moves embeddings from different modalities into a shared space, minimizing the Wasserstein distance between their distributions. This makes the arrangement of representations part of the fusion objective, rather than treating multimodal integration as a direct combination of unrelated coordinates.

The authors provide a theoretical result guaranteeing consistency and comprehensiveness through minimizing the Wasserstein distances between individual modalities and the unified embedding space. They also report state-of-the-art performance on established multimodal knowledge graph completion benchmarks. Together, the theoretical and empirical contributions support optimal transport as a way to integrate heterogeneous information while retaining useful structure for predicting missing graph relationships.
summary.tldr: OTKGE aligns multimodal embedding distributions through optimal transport to improve knowledge graph completion while preserving structured information.

title: OTKGE: Multi-modal Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Optimal Transport

abstract: We study the problem of transfer learning via Multi-Task Representation Learning (MTRL), wherein multiple source tasks are used to learn a good common representation, and a predictor is trained on top of it for the target task. Under standard regularity assumptions on the loss function and task diversity, we provide new statistical rates on the excess risk of the target task, which demonstrate the benefit of representation learning. Importantly, our rates are optimistic, i.e., they interpolate between the standard $O(m^{-1/2})$ rate and the fast $O(m^{-1})$ rate, depending on the difficulty of the learning task, where $m$ is the number of samples for the target task. Besides the main result, we make several new contributions, including giving optimistic rates for excess risk of source tasks (multi-task learning (MTL)), a local Rademacher complexity theorem for MTRL and MTL, as well as a chain rule for local Rademacher complexity for composite predictor classes.

paragraphs: Multi-task representation learning uses several source tasks to learn shared features, then trains a predictor on those features for a target task. This paper asks how accurately the target predictor can learn as its number of training examples grows. The analysis makes the benefit of learning a shared representation explicit through statistical bounds on excess risk.

Under regularity assumptions on the loss and assumptions about task diversity, the authors derive rates that adapt to the difficulty of the learning problem. With m target examples, these rates interpolate between the usual order of one over the square root of m and the faster order of one over m. Calling the rates optimistic means easier problems can receive stronger guarantees.

The paper also derives optimistic excess-risk rates for the source tasks themselves. Supporting contributions include a local Rademacher complexity theorem and a chain rule for composite predictor classes. These tools help analyze the shared representation and the predictor built on top of it, extending the contribution beyond the target-task bound alone.
summary.tldr: Under loss-regularity and task-diversity assumptions, shared representations yield target-task learning rates that improve with problem difficulty.

title: Optimistic Rates for Multi-Task Representation Learning

abstract: While policy optimization algorithms have played an important role in recent empirical success of Reinforcement Learning (RL), the existing theoretical understanding of policy optimization remains rather limited---they are either restricted to tabular MDPs or suffer from highly suboptimal sample complexity, especial in online RL where exploration is necessary. This paper proposes a simple efficient policy optimization framework---Optimistic NPG for online RL. Optimistic NPG can be viewed as simply combining of the classic natural policy gradient (NPG) algorithm [Kakade, 2001] with optimistic policy evaluation subroutines to encourage exploration. For $d$-dimensional linear MDPs, Optimistic NPG is computationally efficient, and learns an $\epsilon$-optimal policy within $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^2/\epsilon^3)$ samples, which is the first computationally efficient algorithm whose sample complexity has the optimal dimension dependence $\tilde{\Theta}(d^2)$. It also improves over state-of-the-art results of policy optimization algorithms [Zanette et al., 2021] by a factor of $d$. For general function approximation that subsumes linear MDPs, Optimistic NPG, to our best knowledge, is also the first policy optimization algorithm that achieves the polynomial sample complexity for learning near-optimal policies.
