paragraphs: Online reinforcement learning requires a policy to improve while also exploring actions whose consequences are uncertain. The paper addresses a gap in theoretical understanding of policy optimization: previous guarantees either focus on tabular environments or require too many samples. Optimistic NPG combines natural policy gradient with optimistic policy evaluation to encourage exploration.

For linear Markov decision processes with dimension d, the framework is computationally efficient and learns an ε-optimal policy using roughly d²/ε³ samples, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its dependence on dimension is optimal up to those factors. The stated sample requirement improves on previous leading policy-optimization results by a factor of d.

The paper also develops a result for a general function-approximation setting that includes linear MDPs. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first policy-optimization algorithm with polynomial sample complexity for learning near-optimal policies in that setting. The contribution ties an established policy-update method to exploration-aware evaluation, yielding stronger guarantees on the experience needed to learn.
summary.tldr: Optimistic NPG combines natural policy gradient with exploration-oriented evaluation to obtain efficient online reinforcement-learning guarantees.

title: Optimistic Natural Policy Gradient: a Simple Efficient Policy Optimization Framework for Online RL

abstract: Large-scale generative models are capable of producing high-quality images from detailed prompts. However, many aspects of an image are difficult or impossible to convey through text. We introduce self-guidance, a method that provides precise control over properties of the generated image by guiding the internal representations of diffusion models. We demonstrate that the size, location, and appearance of objects can be extracted from these representations, and show how to use them to steer the sampling process. Self-guidance operates similarly to standard classifier guidance, but uses signals present in the pretrained model itself, requiring no additional models or training. We demonstrate the flexibility and effectiveness of self-guided generation through a wide range of challenging image manipulations, such as modifying the position or size of a single object (keeping the rest of the image unchanged), merging the appearance of objects in one image with the layout of another, composing objects from multiple images into one, and more. We also propose a new method for reconstruction using self-guidance, which allows extending our approach to editing real images.

paragraphs: Text prompts can describe an image in detail while still leaving object placement, size, or appearance difficult to specify precisely. This paper introduces self-guidance, which controls image generation through representations already present inside a pretrained diffusion model. The authors show that these representations contain extractable information about those object properties.

Self-guidance uses that information to steer the sampling process. Its operation resembles classifier guidance, but the guiding signals come from the diffusion model itself, so the method requires neither an additional model nor additional training. This turns internal representations into practical control signals: a desired change can be expressed through properties of the developing image rather than solely through a rewritten prompt.

Demonstrations include moving or resizing one object while retaining the rest of an image, combining appearance from one image with layout from another, and assembling objects from multiple images. The authors also introduce a reconstruction method that extends self-guidance to real-image editing. These examples establish a range of controls available from a pretrained model’s own internal information.
summary.tldr: Self-guidance uses a diffusion model’s internal representations to control object properties and edit images without extra models or training.

title: Diffusion Self-Guidance for Controllable Image Generation

abstract: Large vision models with billions of parameters and trained on broad data have great potential in numerous downstream applications. However, these models are typically difficult to adapt due to their large parameter size and sometimes lack of accesss to their weights---entities able to develop large vision models often provide APIs only. In this paper, we study how to better utilize large vision models through the lens of in-context learning, a concept that has been well-known in natural language processing but has only been studied very recently in computer vision. In-context learning refers to the ability to perform inference on tasks never seen during training by simply conditioning on in-context examples (i.e., input-output pairs) without updating any internal model parameters. To demystify in-context learning in computer vision, we conduct an extensive research and identify a critical problem: downstream performance is highly sensitivie to the choice of visual in-context examples. To address this problem, we propose a prompt retrieval framework specifically for large vision models, allowing the selection of in-context examples to be fully automated. Concretely, we provide two implementations: (i) an unsupervised prompt retrieval method based on nearest example search using an off-the-shelf model, and (ii) a supervised prompt retrieval method, which trains a neural network to choose examples that directly maximize in-context learning performance. Both methods do not require access to the internal weights of large vision models. Our results demonstrate that our methods can bring non-trivial improvements to visual in-context learning in comparison to the commonly-used random selection. Code and models will be released.

paragraphs: Large vision models can be difficult to adapt because of their size or because users can access only an API. This paper finds that downstream performance depends strongly on which examples are supplied.

The authors propose automatically retrieving examples for the prompt. One implementation is unsupervised: it uses an off-the-shelf model to search for nearby examples. The other is supervised: it trains a neural network to select examples that directly improve in-context task performance. Neither approach requires access to the large vision model's internal weights.

Both retrieval methods produce meaningful improvements over the commonly used strategy of random example selection. The results identify example choice as an important part of using a fixed vision model effectively. They also show that adaptation can involve learning or designing the selection process around the model, even when the model itself remains unchanged and its weights are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Automatically retrieving demonstration examples improves visual in-context learning without requiring access to the vision model's internal weights.

title: What Makes Good Examples for Visual In-Context Learning?

abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to trace students' knowledge states by predicting whether students answer correctly on exercises. Despite the excellent performance of existing Transformer-based KT approaches, they are criticized for the manually selected input features for fusion and the defect of single global context modelling to directly capture students' forgetting behavior in KT, when the related records are distant from the current record in terms of time. To address the issues, this paper first considers adding convolution operations to the Transformer to enhance its local context modelling ability used for students' forgetting behavior, then proposes an evolutionary neural architecture search approach to automate the input feature selection and automatically determine where to apply which operation for achieving the balancing of the local/global context modelling. In the search space, the original global path containing the attention module in Transformer is replaced with the sum of a global path and a local path that could contain different convolutions, and the selection of input features is also considered. To search the best architecture, we employ an effective evolutionary algorithm to explore the search space and also suggest a search space reduction strategy to accelerate the convergence of the algorithm. Experimental results on the two largest and most challenging education datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the architecture found by the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Knowledge tracing predicts whether a student will answer an exercise correctly to track their knowledge over time. Transformer approaches perform well, but their input features are often chosen manually. The paper also identifies a weakness in relying on a single global context mechanism to capture forgetting, particularly when relevant records are temporally distant from the current interaction.

The proposed approach adds convolutional operations to strengthen local context modeling and uses evolutionary architecture search to choose how local and global processing are combined. Within the search space, a Transformer's attention path becomes the sum of a global path and a local path that may use different convolutions. Input-feature selection is part of the same search.

An evolutionary algorithm explores these alternatives, while a search-space reduction strategy aims to accelerate convergence. The resulting architecture is evaluated on two datasets described as the largest and most challenging in education. The reported results support its effectiveness, showing the value of jointly searching feature choices and the balance between local and global context rather than fixing those decisions manually.
summary.tldr: Evolutionary search jointly selects input features and local/global processing operations for Transformer-based knowledge tracing.

title: Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search for Transformer in Knowledge Tracing

abstract: Estimating the generalization performance is practically challenging on out-of-distribution (OOD) data without ground-truth labels. While previous methods emphasize the connection between distribution difference and OOD accuracy, we show that a large domain gap not necessarily leads to a low test accuracy. In this paper, we investigate this problem from the perspective of feature separability empirically and theoretically. Specifically, we propose a dataset-level score based upon feature dispersion to estimate the test accuracy under distribution shift. Our method is inspired by desirable properties of features in representation learning: high inter-class dispersion and high intra-class compactness. Our analysis shows that inter-class dispersion is strongly correlated with the model accuracy, while intra-class compactness does not reflect the generalization performance on OOD data. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method in both prediction performance and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Estimating a model's accuracy on unfamiliar data is difficult when the correct labels are unavailable. Many approaches emphasize how much the new data distribution differs from the training distribution. This paper argues that the size of that gap is insufficient: a large distribution difference does not necessarily imply poor test accuracy.

The authors study the problem through the separability of learned features. They distinguish between different classes being spread apart and examples within each class being tightly grouped. Although both are commonly desirable representation properties, their analysis finds that separation between classes correlates strongly with accuracy, while within-class compactness does not reflect generalization performance on out-of-distribution data.

Building on this distinction, the paper proposes a dataset-level score based on feature dispersion to estimate accuracy under distribution shift. Extensive experiments report advantages in both prediction performance and computational efficiency. The practical implication is that the organization of the model's features can provide useful evidence about its likely accuracy beyond what is captured by a general measure of distribution difference.
summary.tldr: Separation between class features provides a useful basis for estimating accuracy on shifted data without ground-truth labels.

title: On the Importance of Feature Separability in Predicting Out-Of-Distribution Error

abstract: The matrix completion problem involves reconstructing a low-rank matrix by using a given set of revealed (and potentially noisy) entries. Although existing methods address the completion of the entire matrix, the accuracy of the completed entries can vary significantly across the matrix, due to differences in the sampling distribution. For instance, users may rate movies primarily from their country or favorite genres, leading to inaccurate predictions for the majority of completed entries.We propose a novel formulation of the problem as Partial Matrix Completion, where the objective is to complete a substantial subset of the entries with high confidence. Our algorithm efficiently handles the unknown and arbitrarily complex nature of the sampling distribution, ensuring high accuracy for all completed entries and sufficient coverage across the matrix. Additionally, we introduce an online version of the problem and present a low-regret efficient algorithm based on iterative gradient updates. Finally, we conduct a preliminary empirical evaluation of our methods.

paragraphs: Matrix completion predicts missing entries in a low-rank table from the entries that have been observed, potentially with noise. Uneven observation patterns can make prediction quality vary sharply across the table. In movie ratings, for example, users may mainly rate familiar genres or films from their own country, leaving other parts of the matrix poorly supported.

The paper changes the objective to partial matrix completion: accurately fill a substantial subset of entries with high confidence. Its algorithm handles an unknown sampling distribution even when that distribution has arbitrarily complex structure. The stated guarantees combine high accuracy for every completed entry with sufficient coverage, addressing both reliability and how much of the matrix gets completed.

The authors also formulate an online version and provide an efficient algorithm based on iterative gradient updates with low regret. A preliminary empirical evaluation accompanies the methods. The contribution makes the choice of which entries to complete part of the problem itself, explicitly connecting the amount of completion to confidence in the resulting predictions.
summary.tldr: Partial matrix completion seeks a substantial, reliably predicted subset of missing entries despite unknown and complex sampling patterns.

title: Partial Matrix Completion

abstract: Modern policy optimization methods in reinforcement learning, such as TRPO and PPO, owe their success to the use of parameterized policies. However, while theoretical guarantees have been established for this class of algorithms, especially in the tabular setting, the use of general parameterization schemes remains mostly unjustified. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for policy optimization based on mirror descent that naturally accommodates general parameterizations. The policy class induced by our scheme recovers known classes, e.g., softmax, and generates new ones depending on the choice of mirror map. Using our framework, we obtain the first result that guarantees linear convergence for a policy-gradient-based method involving general parameterization. To demonstrate the ability of our framework to accommodate general parameterization schemes, we provide its sample complexity when using shallow neural networks, show that it represents an improvement upon the previous best results, and empirically validate the effectiveness of our theoretical claims on classic control tasks.

paragraphs: Policy optimization improves an agent’s decision rule by adjusting its parameters. Popular methods such as TRPO and PPO rely on parameterized policies, but theoretical understanding has been stronger for tabular representations than for more general ones. This paper introduces a mirror-descent framework designed to accommodate general policy parameterizations and provide convergence guarantees in that setting.

The framework uses the choice of a mirror map to determine the resulting policy class. It can recover familiar classes such as softmax policies, while other mirror maps produce new classes. This links the representation of a policy to the optimization framework used to improve it. Within this framework, the authors establish a linear-convergence guarantee for a policy-gradient-based method involving general parameterization.

The paper also analyzes the number of samples needed when policies use shallow neural networks, reporting an improvement over previous best results. Experiments on classic control tasks support the theoretical claims. Together, these results broaden the theoretical footing for parameterized policy optimization while demonstrating a concrete neural-network application.
summary.tldr: A mirror-descent framework accommodates general policy parameterizations and establishes linear convergence with improved sample-complexity results for shallow networks.

title: A Novel Framework for Policy Mirror Descent with General Parameterization and Linear Convergence

abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) is a task that predicts students' future performance based on their historical learning interactions. With the rapid development of deep learning techniques, existing KT approaches follow a data-driven paradigm that uses massive problem-solving records to model students' learning processes. However, although the educational contexts contain various factors that may have an influence on student learning outcomes, existing public KT datasets mainly consist of anonymized ID-like features, which may hinder the research advances towards this field. Therefore, in this work, we present, \emph{XES3G5M}, a large-scale dataset with rich auxiliary information about questions and their associated knowledge components (KCs)\footnote{\label{ft:kc}A KC is a generalization of everyday terms like concept, principle, fact, or skill.}. The XES3G5M dataset is collected from a real-world online math learning platform, which contains 7,652 questions, and 865 KCs with 5,549,635 interactions from 18,066 students. To the best of our knowledge, the XES3G5M dataset not only has the largest number of KCs in math domain but contains the richest contextual information including tree structured KC relations, question types, textual contents and analysis and student response timestamps. Furthermore, we build a comprehensive benchmark on 19 state-of-the-art deep learning based knowledge tracing (DLKT) models. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging the auxiliary information in our XES3G5M with DLKT models. We hope the proposed dataset can effectively facilitate the KT research work.

summary.tldr: XES3G5M provides millions of math-learning interactions with rich educational context and a benchmark showing the value of that information.

title: XES3G5M: A Knowledge Tracing Benchmark Dataset with Auxiliary Information

abstract: Capturing screen contents by smartphone cameras has become a common way for information sharing. However, these images and videos are often degraded by moiré patterns, which are caused by frequency aliasing between the camera filter array and digital display grids. We observe that the moiré patterns in raw domain is simpler than those in sRGB domain, and the moiré patterns in raw color channels have different properties. Therefore, we propose an image and video demoiréing network tailored for raw inputs. We introduce a color-separated feature branch, and it is fused with the traditional feature-mixed branch via channel and spatial modulations. Specifically, the channel modulation utilizes modulated color-separated features to enhance the color-mixed features. The spatial modulation utilizes the feature with large receptive field to modulate the feature with small receptive field. In addition, we build the first well-aligned raw video demoiréing (RawVDemoiré) dataset and propose an efficient temporal alignment method by inserting alternating patterns. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance for both image and video demoiréing. Our dataset and code will be released after the acceptance of this work.

The authors observe that these artifacts are simpler in raw sensor data than in sRGB images and have different properties across raw color channels. They design a removal network around those observations.

The network combines a branch that keeps color features separate with a conventional branch that mixes them. Channel modulation uses the separated information to improve the mixed features. Spatial modulation lets features with a large receptive field influence features with a smaller receptive field, combining broader spatial information with more local processing.

The work also introduces RawVDemoiré, a well-aligned raw video dataset, and an efficient temporal alignment method based on inserted alternating patterns. Experiments report state-of-the-art results for both image and video moiré removal. The contribution links a raw-input representation, a network that respects color-channel differences, and aligned video data for evaluating the removal task.
summary.tldr: A raw-input network combines color-separated and mixed features through channel and spatial modulation to remove moiré from screen images and videos.

title: Recaptured Raw Screen Image and Video Demoiréing via Channel and Spatial Modulations

abstract: Although pairwise causal relations have been extensively studied in observational longitudinal analyses across many disciplines, incorporating knowledge of causal pairs into deep learning models for temporal event sequences remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing the performance of transformer-based models in multivariate event sequences by injecting pairwise qualitative causal knowledge such as `event Z amplifies future occurrences of event Y'. We establish a new framework for causal inference in temporal event sequences using a transformer architecture, providing a theoretical justification for our approach, and show how to obtain unbiased estimates of the proposed measure. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art models in terms of prediction accuracy by effectively leveraging knowledge about causal pairs. We also consider a unique application where we extract knowledge around sequences of societal events by generating them from a large language model, and demonstrate how a causal knowledge graph can help with event prediction in such sequences. Overall, our framework offers a practical means of improving the performance of transformer-based models in multivariate event sequences by explicitly exploiting pairwise causal information.

This paper studies how to incorporate qualitative causal relationships into transformers for multivariate event sequences. An example is knowing that the occurrence of one event type increases future occurrences of another, even without specifying a precise numerical effect.

The authors propose a transformer-based causal inference framework for temporal event sequences, provide theoretical justification, and show how to obtain unbiased estimates of their proposed measure. The approach explicitly brings pairwise causal knowledge into the model. This connects information about relationships between event types with the task of predicting how a sequence will develop.

The paper also explores societal event sequences generated by a large language model, showing how a causal knowledge graph can support prediction in those sequences. These results support the practical value of incorporating qualitative causal structure into event models, including the particular generated-sequence application studied.
summary.tldr: The framework incorporates qualitative pairwise causal knowledge into transformers to improve prediction of multivariate event sequences.

title: Pairwise Causality Guided Transformers for Event Sequences

abstract: We introduce a technique for tuning the learning rate scale factor of any base optimization algorithm and schedule automatically, which we call Mechanic. Our method provides a practical realization of recent theoretical reductions for accomplishing a similar goal in online convex optimization. We rigorously evaluate Mechanic on a range of large scale deep learning tasks with varying batch sizes, schedules, and base optimization algorithms. These experiments demonstrate that depending on the problem, Mechanic either comes very close to, matches or even improves upon manual tuning of learning rates.

paragraphs: Mechanic automates the choice of a learning-rate scale factor for an existing optimization algorithm and schedule. This factor controls the overall scale of the learning rate used during training. The paper targets a practical tuning decision that otherwise requires manual selection, while allowing the base optimizer and its schedule to remain part of the training setup.

The method turns recent theoretical reductions from online convex optimization into a practical tuning technique. Its stated scope covers any base optimization algorithm and schedule. The core contribution is therefore an automatic mechanism for setting their learning-rate scale, connecting a theoretical approach to the demands of large-scale deep-learning training.

The authors evaluate Mechanic across large-scale tasks with different batch sizes, schedules, and optimization algorithms. Depending on the problem, it comes close to manually tuned learning rates, matches them, or improves on them. This variation is central to interpreting the findings: the experiments support competitive automatic tuning across the tested settings, without claiming that it always exceeds manual tuning.
summary.tldr: Mechanic automatically tunes learning-rate scale and approaches, matches, or improves on manual tuning across evaluated deep-learning tasks.

title: Mechanic: A Learning Rate Tuner

abstract: Recent research in mechanistic interpretability has attempted to reverse-engineer Transformer models by carefully inspecting network weights and activations. However, these approaches require considerable manual effort and still fall short of providing complete, faithful descriptions of the underlying algorithms. In this work, we introduce a procedure for training Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design. We build on RASP [Weiss et al., 2021], a programming language that can be compiled into Transformer weights. Instead of compiling human-written programs into Transformers, we design a modified Transformer that can be trained using gradient-based optimization and then automatically converted into a discrete, human-readable program. We refer to these models as Transformer Programs. To validate our approach, we learn Transformer Programs for a variety of problems, including an in-context learning task, a suite of algorithmic problems (e.g. sorting, recognizing Dyck languages), and NLP tasks including named entity recognition and text classification. The Transformer Programs can automatically find reasonable solutions, performing on par with standard Transformers of comparable size; and, more importantly, they are easy to interpret. To demonstrate these advantages, we convert Transformers into Python programs and use off-the-shelf code analysis tools to debug model errors and identify the “circuits” used to solve different sub-problems. We hope that Transformer Programs open a new path toward the goal of intrinsically interpretable machine learning.

Such analysis can also fall short of a complete, faithful account of its computation. This paper instead designs Transformers so that training can produce models that are automatically convertible into readable programs.

abstract: Modern predictive models are often deployed to environments in which computational budgets are dynamic. Anytime algorithms are well-suited to such environments as, at any point during computation, they can output a prediction whose quality is a function of computation time. Early-exit neural networks have garnered attention in the context of anytime computation due to their capability to provide intermediate predictions at various stages throughout the network. However, we demonstrate that current early-exit networks are not directly applicable to anytime settings, as the quality of predictions for individual data points is not guaranteed to improve with longer computation. To address this shortcoming, we propose an elegant post-hoc modification, based on the Product-of-Experts, that encourages an early-exit network to become gradually confident. This gives our deep models the property of *conditional monotonicity* in the prediction quality---an essential building block towards truly anytime predictive modeling using early-exit architectures. Our empirical results on standard image-classification tasks demonstrate that such behaviors can be achieved while preserving competitive accuracy on average.

paragraphs: An anytime predictor should provide an answer whenever computation stops, with prediction quality related to the time available. Early-exit networks appear suitable because they produce predictions at intermediate stages. This paper shows a mismatch: spending more computation on an individual example does not necessarily improve its prediction, even when the network performs well on average.

The authors propose a post-hoc modification based on a Product-of-Experts combination. It encourages confidence to develop gradually across the network's exits and gives prediction quality a property called conditional monotonicity. This targets the behavior of predictions as computation proceeds, addressing an issue that aggregate accuracy alone does not resolve.

Experiments on standard image-classification tasks show that the desired behavior can be achieved while maintaining competitive average accuracy. The result supports early-exit networks whose intermediate predictions are better suited to variable computational budgets. The authors present conditional monotonicity as a building block toward genuinely anytime prediction, preserving the distinction between this property and an unrestricted promise that every additional computation improves every prediction.
summary.tldr: A Product-of-Experts modification gives early-exit networks conditionally monotonic prediction quality while preserving competitive average image-classification accuracy.

title: Towards Anytime Classification in Early-Exit Architectures by Enforcing Conditional Monotonicity

abstract: As concerns about data privacy continue to grow, differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a fundamental concept that aims to guarantee privacy by ensuring individuals' indistinguishability in data analysis. Local differential privacy (LDP) is a rigorous type of DP that requires individual data to be privatized before being sent to the collector, thus removing the need for a trusted third party to collect data. Among the numerous (L)DP-based approaches, functional DP has gained considerable attention in the DP community because it connects DP to statistical decision-making by formulating it as a hypothesis-testing problem and also exhibits Gaussian-related properties. However, the utility of privatized data is generally lower than that of non-private data, prompting research into optimal mechanisms that maximize the statistical utility for given privacy constraints. In this study, we investigate how functional LDP preserves the statistical utility by analyzing minimax risks of univariate mean estimation as well as nonparametric density estimation. We leverage the contraction property of functional LDP mechanisms and classical information-theoretical bounds to derive private minimax lower bounds. Our theoretical study reveals that it is possible to establish an interpretable, continuous balance between the statistical utility and privacy level, which has not been achieved under the $\epsilon$-LDP framework. Furthermore, we suggest minimax optimal mechanisms based on Gaussian LDP (a type of functional LDP) that achieve the minimax upper bounds and show via a numerical study that they are superior to the counterparts derived under $\epsilon$-LDP. The theoretical and empirical findings of this work suggest that Gaussian LDP should be considered a reliable standard for LDP.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy protects individual data before it reaches a collector, removing the need to trust that collector with raw records. This protection can reduce statistical usefulness. The paper studies that tradeoff through functional local differential privacy, which expresses privacy in terms of a hypothesis-testing problem and has connections to Gaussian distributions.

The analysis covers estimation of a one-dimensional mean and nonparametric density estimation. Using contraction properties of privacy mechanisms and information-theoretic arguments, the authors derive minimax lower bounds: limits on the best worst-case estimation performance permitted by the privacy constraint. They establish an interpretable, continuous relationship between privacy strength and statistical utility.

The authors also propose Gaussian local-privacy mechanisms that attain the corresponding minimax upper bounds. A numerical study finds them superior to counterparts derived under epsilon-local differential privacy. Together, the optimality results and numerical evidence motivate the authors' recommendation to consider Gaussian local privacy a reliable standard. The theoretical conclusions concern the estimation problems analyzed in the paper.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal estimation guarantees under functional local privacy and proposes Gaussian mechanisms with a continuous privacy–utility tradeoff.

title: Minimax Risks and Optimal Procedures for Estimation under Functional Local Differential Privacy

abstract: Methods for training models on graphs distributed across multiple clients have recently grown in popularity, due to the size of these graphs as well as regulations on keeping data where it is generated. However, the cross-client edges naturally exist among clients. Thus, distributed methods for training a model on a single graph incur either significant communication overhead between clients or a loss of available information to the training. We introduce the Federated Graph Convolutional Network (FedGCN) algorithm, which uses federated learning to train GCN models for semi-supervised node classification with fast convergence and little communication. Compared to prior methods that require extra communication among clients at each training round, FedGCN clients only communicate with the central server in one pre-training step, greatly reducing communication costs and allowing the use of homomorphic encryption to further enhance privacy. We theoretically analyze the tradeoff between FedGCN's convergence rate and communication cost under different data distributions. Experimental results show that our FedGCN algorithm achieves better model accuracy with 51.7\% faster convergence on average and at least 100$\times$ less communication compared to prior work.

paragraphs: When a graph is divided among clients, some edges still connect nodes held by different clients. Training a graph model therefore creates a tension: exchanging information across those edges can be expensive, while leaving it out discards useful structure. This paper addresses that tension for semi-supervised node classification with graph convolutional networks.

FedGCN uses federated learning and moves the communication described in the abstract into a single pre-training exchange with a central server. This contrasts with methods requiring extra communication among clients during each training round. Reducing these exchanges lowers communication costs and makes it possible to use homomorphic encryption for additional privacy protection.

The authors theoretically study how communication cost and convergence rate trade off under different data distributions. Their experiments report better accuracy, convergence that is 51.7% faster on average, and at least 100 times less communication than prior work. These findings connect the communication design to both learning speed and predictive performance, showing that reduced communication did not require an accuracy sacrifice in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FedGCN reduces communication in distributed graph learning while reporting better accuracy and faster convergence than prior methods.

title: FedGCN: Convergence-Communication Tradeoffs in Federated Training of Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: The expressive power of transformers over inputs of unbounded size can be studied through their ability to recognize classes of formal languages. In this paper, we establish exact characterizations of transformers with hard attention (in which all attention is focused on exactly one position) and attention masking (in which each position only attends to positions on one side). With strict masking (each position cannot attend to itself) and without position embeddings, these transformers are expressively equivalent to linear temporal logic (LTL), which defines exactly the star-free languages. A key technique is the use of Boolean RASP as a convenient intermediate language between transformers and LTL. We then take numerous results known for LTL and apply them to transformers, showing how position embeddings, strict masking, and depth all increase expressive power.

paragraphs: Formal languages provide a way to study what a transformer can recognize when input length is unbounded. This paper investigates transformers with hard attention, where attention selects exactly one position, and directional masks, where a position can attend only to positions on one side. These architectural constraints define the setting of its theoretical results.

Under strict masking, which excludes attention to the current position, and without position embeddings, the authors prove an exact equivalence with linear temporal logic. That logic characterizes the star-free languages. The equivalence establishes both what these transformers can express and the boundary of that capability under the stated restrictions.

The proof uses Boolean RASP as an intermediate language linking transformers and temporal logic. This connection also lets the authors transfer existing results about the logic to transformer architectures. They use it to show how position embeddings, strict masking, and depth increase expressive power. The contribution is an architectural expressivity characterization, grounded in recognition over inputs of unbounded size.
summary.tldr: Hard-attention transformers with strict directional masking and no position embeddings recognize exactly the star-free languages.

title: Masked Hard-Attention Transformers Recognize Exactly the Star-Free Languages

abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms have achieved great success in solving many challenging tasks while their black-box nature hinders interpretability and real-world applicability, making it difficult for human experts to interpret and understand DRL policies. Existing works on interpretable reinforcement learning have shown promise in extracting decision tree (DT) based policies from DRL policies with most focus on the single-agent settings while prior attempts to introduce DT policies in multi-agent scenarios mainly focus on heuristic designs which do not provide any quantitative guarantees on the expected return.In this paper, we establish an upper bound on the return gap between the oracle expert policy and an optimal decision tree policy. This enables us to recast the DT extraction problem into a novel non-euclidean clustering problem over the local observation and action values space of each agent, with action values as cluster labels and the upper bound on the return gap as clustering loss.Both the algorithm and the upper bound are extended to multi-agent decentralized DT extractions by an iteratively-grow-DT procedure guided by an action-value function conditioned on the current DTs of other agents. Further, we propose the Return-Gap-Minimization Decision Tree (RGMDT) algorithm, which is a surprisingly simple design and is integrated with reinforcement learning through the utilization of a novel Regularized Information Maximization loss. Evaluations on tasks like D4RL show that RGMDT significantly outperforms heuristic DT-based baselines and can achieve nearly optimal returns under given DT complexity constraints (e.g., maximum number of DT nodes).

paragraphs: Decision trees can make reinforcement-learning policies easier for people to inspect, but replacing a neural policy with a tree can sacrifice return. This paper develops a quantitative basis for that replacement by bounding the return gap between an oracle expert policy and an optimal decision-tree policy. The bound gives extraction an explicit performance-oriented objective.

The authors turn tree extraction into a non-Euclidean clustering problem over each agent's local observations and action values. Action values provide cluster labels, while the return-gap bound serves as the clustering loss. They extend both the algorithm and bound to decentralized multi-agent extraction by growing trees iteratively, using action values conditioned on the other agents' current trees.

The resulting RGMDT algorithm incorporates a regularized information-maximization loss. Evaluations on tasks including D4RL show substantial improvements over heuristic tree-based baselines and nearly optimal returns under specified tree-complexity constraints, such as a maximum node count. The work connects policy interpretability to a measurable return objective while explicitly accounting for the limited size of the extracted trees.
summary.tldr: RGMDT uses a return-gap bound to guide interpretable decision-tree extraction for single-agent and decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning.

title: RGMDT: Return-Gap-Minimizing Decision Tree Extraction in Non-Euclidean Metric Space

abstract: Recent advances in immunology and synthetic biology have accelerated the development of deep generative methods for DNA sequence design. Two dominant approaches in this field are AutoRegressive (AR) models and Diffusion Models (DMs). However, genomic sequences are functionally heterogeneous, consisting of multiple connected regions (e.g., Promoter Regions, Exons, and Introns) where elements within each region come from the same probability distribution, but the overall sequence is non-homogeneous. This heterogeneous nature presents challenges for a single model to accurately generate genomic sequences. In this paper, we analyze the properties of AR models and DMs in heterogeneous genomic sequence generation, pointing out crucial limitations in both methods: (i) AR models capture the underlying distribution of data by factorizing and learning the transition probability but fail to capture the global property of DNA sequences. (ii) DMs learn to recover the global distribution but tend to produce errors at the base pair level. To overcome the limitations of both approaches, we propose a post-training sampling method, termed Absorb & Escape (A&E) to perform compositional generation from AR models and DMs. This approach starts with samples generated by DMs and refines the sample quality using an AR model through the alternation of the Absorb and Escape steps. To assess the quality of generated sequences, we conduct extensive experiments on 15 species for conditional and unconditional DNA generation. The experiment results from motif distribution, diversity checks, and genome integration tests unequivocally show that A&E outperforms state-of-the-art AR models and DMs in genomic sequence generation. A&E does not suffer from the slowness of traditional MCMC to sample from composed distributions with Energy-Based Models whilst it obtains higher quality samples than single models. Our research sheds light on the limitations of current single-model approaches in DNA generation and provides a simple but effective solution for heterogeneous sequence generation. Code is available at the [Github Repo](https://github.com/Zehui127/Absorb-Escape).

Its analysis identifies complementary weaknesses: autoregressive models miss global sequence properties, while diffusion models tend to make errors at the base-pair level.

An autoregressive model then helps refine it through alternating Absorb and Escape steps. This arrangement aims to combine the diffusion model's global modeling strength with the autoregressive model's local modeling strength, addressing the heterogeneous structure that challenges either model alone.

Experiments cover conditional and unconditional DNA generation across 15 species. The authors report that the combined method outperforms state-of-the-art individual autoregressive and diffusion models in motif distributions, diversity checks, and genome integration tests. They also report avoiding the slow sampling associated with traditional Markov chain Monte Carlo for composed energy-based distributions. These findings support combining pretrained models to improve sequence quality.
summary.tldr: Absorb & Escape refines diffusion-generated DNA with an autoregressive model, improving sequence quality across experiments involving 15 species.

title: Absorb & Escape: Overcoming Single Model Limitations in Generating Heterogeneous Genomic Sequences

abstract: We propose a new model for dimensionality reduction, the PCA tree, which works like a regular autoencoder, having explicit projection and reconstruction mappings. The projection is effected by a sparse oblique tree, having hard, hyperplane splits using few features and linear leaves. The reconstruction mapping is a set of local linear mappings. Thus, rather than producing a global map as in t-SNE and other methods, which often leads to distortions, it produces a hierarchical set of local PCAs. The use of a sparse oblique tree and PCA makes the overall model interpretable and very fast to project or reconstruct new points. Joint optimization of all the parameters in the tree is a nonconvex nondifferentiable problem. We propose an algorithm that is guaranteed to decrease the error monotonically and which scales to large datasets without any approximation. In experiments, we show PCA trees are able to identify a wealth of low-dimensional and cluster structure in image and document datasets.

The PCA tree instead organizes dimensionality reduction hierarchically, using different local linear representations in different regions. Like an autoencoder, it provides explicit mappings both into the reduced representation and back to the original space.

This combination makes the model interpretable and allows new points to be projected or reconstructed quickly.

Training all tree parameters jointly is nonconvex and nondifferentiable. The authors propose an algorithm guaranteed to decrease error monotonically and report that it scales to large datasets without approximation. Experiments on image and document datasets reveal varied low-dimensional and cluster structure. The approach offers a hierarchy of local views together with reconstruction, while the optimization guarantee concerns decreasing error rather than finding a global optimum.
summary.tldr: PCA trees provide interpretable hierarchical dimensionality reduction through local linear projections and reconstructions, trained with monotonically decreasing error.

title: The tree autoencoder model, with application to hierarchical data visualization

abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data is often collected from diverse contexts involving different populations and EEG devices. This variability can induce distribution shifts in the data $X$ and in the biomedical variables of interest $y$, thus limiting the application of supervised machine learning (ML) algorithms. While domain adaptation (DA) methods have been developed to mitigate the impact of these shifts, such methods struggle when distribution shifts occur simultaneously in $X$ and $y$. As state-of-the-art ML models for EEG represent the data by spatial covariance matrices, which lie on the Riemannian manifold of Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) matrices, it is appealing to study DA techniques operating on the SPD manifold. This paper proposes a novel method termed Geodesic Optimization for Predictive Shift Adaptation (GOPSA) to address test-time multi-source DA for situations in which source domains have distinct $y$ distributions. GOPSA exploits the geodesic structure of the Riemannian manifold to jointly learn a domain-specific re-centering operator representing site-specific intercepts and the regression model. We performed empirical benchmarks on the cross-site generalization of age-prediction models with resting-state EEG data from a large multi-national dataset (HarMNqEEG), which included $14$ recording sites and more than $1500$ human participants. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our results showed that GOPSA achieved significantly higher performance on three regression metrics ($R^2$, MAE, and Spearman's $\rho$) for several source-target site combinations, highlighting its effectiveness in tackling multi-source DA with predictive shifts in EEG data analysis. Our method has the potential to combine the advantages of mixed-effects modeling with machine learning for biomedical applications of EEG, such as multicenter clinical trials.

title: Geodesic Optimization for Predictive Shift Adaptation on EEG data

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely used to train large language models (LLMs). However, it is unclear whether LLMs accurately learn the underlying preferences in human feedback data. We coin the term **Learned Feedback Pattern** (LFP) for patterns in an LLM's activations learned during RLHF that improve its performance on the fine-tuning task. We hypothesize that LLMs with LFPs accurately aligned to the fine-tuning feedback exhibit consistent activation patterns for outputs that would have received similar feedback during RLHF. To test this, we train probes to estimate the feedback signal implicit in the activations of a fine-tuned LLM. We then compare these estimates to the true feedback, measuring how accurate the LFPs are to the fine-tuning feedback. Our probes are trained on a condensed, sparse and interpretable representation of LLM activations, making it easier to correlate features of the input with our probe's predictions. We validate our probes by comparing the neural features they correlate with positive feedback inputs against the features GPT-4 describes and classifies as related to LFPs. Understanding LFPs can help minimize discrepancies between LLM behavior and training objectives, which is essential for the **safety** and **alignment** of LLMs.

paragraphs: Training a language model with human feedback does not by itself reveal whether its internal behavior reflects the preferences in that feedback. The aim is to inspect what feedback the model appears to have learned.

summary.tldr: Interpretable probes estimate feedback signals from language-model activations to investigate how faithfully models internalize fine-tuning preferences.

title: Interpreting Learned Feedback Patterns in Large Language Models

abstract: Inverse protein folding is a fundamental task in computational protein design, which aims to design protein sequences that fold into the desired backbone structures. While the development of machine learning algorithms for this task has seen significant success, the prevailing approaches, which predominantly employ a discriminative formulation, frequently encounter the error accumulation issue and often fail to capture the extensive variety of plausible sequences. To fill these gaps, we propose Bridge-IF, a generative diffusion bridge model for inverse folding, which is designed to learn the probabilistic dependency between the distributions of backbone structures and protein sequences. Specifically, we harness an expressive structure encoder to propose a discrete, informative prior derived from structures, and establish a Markov bridge to connect this prior with native sequences. During the inference stage, Bridge-IF progressively refines the prior sequence, culminating in a more plausible design. Moreover, we introduce a reparameterization perspective on Markov bridge models, from which we derive a simplified loss function that facilitates more effective training. We also modulate protein language models (PLMs) with structural conditions to precisely approximate the Markov bridge process, thereby significantly enhancing generation performance while maintaining parameter-efficient training. Extensive experiments on well-established benchmarks demonstrate that Bridge-IF predominantly surpasses existing baselines in sequence recovery and excels in the design of plausible proteins with high foldability. The code is available at https://github.com/violet-sto/Bridge-IF.

paragraphs: Inverse protein folding seeks amino-acid sequences that will fold into a desired backbone structure. The paper argues that prevailing discriminative approaches can accumulate errors and struggle to represent the many sequences that could plausibly fit a structure. Bridge-IF instead treats sequence design as a generative process linking backbone structures with a distribution of possible protein sequences.

A structure encoder first proposes an informative initial sequence distribution. A Markov bridge connects this structure-derived starting point to native sequences during learning. At inference, the model progressively refines an initial sequence into a more plausible design. Starting from structural information makes the refinement process directly responsive to the backbone that the designed protein should match.

The authors also derive a simpler training loss through a reparameterization of the bridge model. They condition protein language models on structure to approximate the bridge while keeping training parameter-efficient. On established benchmarks, Bridge-IF surpasses existing baselines in most sequence-recovery comparisons and performs strongly at designing plausible, highly foldable proteins. These findings support both recovering native sequence information and generating structurally suitable designs.
summary.tldr: Bridge-IF progressively refines structure-informed protein sequences through a Markov bridge, improving sequence recovery and plausible protein design.

title: Bridge-IF: Learning Inverse Protein Folding with Markov Bridges

abstract: Among the research topics in multi-agent learning, mixed-motive cooperation is one of the most prominent challenges, primarily due to the mismatch between individual and collective goals. The cutting-edge research is focused on incorporating domain knowledge into rewards and introducing additional mechanisms to incentivize cooperation. However, these approaches often face shortcomings such as the effort on manual design and the absence of theoretical groundings. To close this gap, we model the mixed-motive game as a differentiable game for the ease of illuminating the learning dynamics towards cooperation. More detailed, we introduce a novel optimization method named \textbf{\textit{A}}ltruistic \textbf{\textit{G}}radient \textbf{\textit{A}}djustment (\textbf{\textit{AgA}}) that employs gradient adjustments to progressively align individual and collective objectives. Furthermore, we theoretically prove that AgA effectively attracts gradients to stable fixed points of the collective objective while considering individual interests, and we validate these claims with empirical evidence. We evaluate the effectiveness of our algorithm AgA through benchmark environments for testing mixed-motive collaboration with small-scale agents such as the two-player public good game and the sequential social dilemma games, Cleanup and Harvest, as well as our self-developed large-scale environment in the game StarCraft II.

paragraphs: Cooperation becomes difficult when what benefits an individual agent differs from what benefits the group. Existing approaches often encourage cooperation through manually designed rewards or extra mechanisms. This paper instead examines how the learning updates themselves can gradually bring individual and collective objectives into alignment.

The authors represent mixed-motive interaction as a differentiable game, making its learning dynamics accessible to gradient-based analysis. Their method, Altruistic Gradient Adjustment, or AgA, modifies gradients to promote alignment while still considering individual interests. The theoretical result concerns attraction toward stable fixed points of the collective objective, giving the adjustment a mathematical foundation beyond manual reward design.

The paper supplies empirical support using the two-player public good game, the sequential social dilemma environments Cleanup and Harvest, and a larger environment developed in StarCraft II. These settings examine cooperation at different scales. The findings support gradient adjustment as a way to encourage collective behavior; the stated theoretical target is stable collective fixed points, rather than a claim that every interaction reaches a globally best cooperative outcome.
summary.tldr: AgA adjusts learning gradients to align individual and collective objectives, with theoretical and empirical support for more cooperative dynamics.

title: Aligning Individual and Collective Objectives in Multi-Agent Cooperation

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have gained significant attention due to their impressive capabilities in multimodal understanding. However, existing methods rely heavily on extensive modal-specific pretraining and joint-modal tuning, leading to significant computational burdens when expanding to new modalities. In this paper, we propose \textbf{PathWeave}, a flexible and scalable framework with modal-\textbf{path} s\textbf{w}itching and \textbf{e}xp\textbf{a}nsion abilities that enables MLLMs to continually \textbf{ev}olve on modalities for $\mathbb{X}$-modal reasoning. We leverage the concept of Continual Learning and develop an incremental training strategy atop pre-trained MLLMs, enabling their expansion to new modalities using uni-modal data, without executing joint-modal pretraining. In detail, a novel Adapter-in-Adapter (AnA) framework is introduced, in which uni-modal and cross-modal adapters are seamlessly integrated to facilitate efficient modality alignment and collaboration. Additionally, an MoE-based gating module is applied between two types of adapters to further enhance the multimodal interaction. To investigate the proposed method, we establish a challenging benchmark called \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning of \textbf{M}odality (MCL), which consists of high-quality QA data from five distinct modalities: image, video, \textcolor{black}{audio, depth} and point cloud. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed AnA framework on learning plasticity and memory stability during continual learning. Furthermore, PathWeave performs comparably to state-of-the-art MLLMs while concurrently reducing parameter training burdens by 98.73\%. Our code locates at \url{https://github.com/JiazuoYu/PathWeave}.

paragraphs: Adding new input modalities to a multimodal language model can require extensive modality-specific pretraining and joint training across modalities. PathWeave addresses that expansion cost with an incremental strategy built on pretrained models. It learns new modalities using unimodal data, without carrying out joint-modal pretraining for the expansion.

The framework introduces Adapter-in-Adapter, which integrates adapters for individual modalities with adapters for cross-modal interaction. A mixture-of-experts gating module connects the two kinds of adapters to improve their collaboration. Its modality-path switching and expansion mechanisms support the broader goal of extending the model while retaining previously learned capabilities.

The authors introduce a continual-modality-learning benchmark containing question-answering data for images, video, audio, depth, and point clouds. Experiments demonstrate learning plasticity and memory stability, addressing both acquisition of new capabilities and retention of earlier ones. PathWeave performs comparably to state-of-the-art multimodal models while reporting a 98.73% reduction in parameter-training burden. The findings support incremental adaptation as an efficient approach to expanding multimodal reasoning.
summary.tldr: PathWeave incrementally adds modalities through interacting adapters, reporting comparable multimodal performance with a 98.73% reduction in parameter-training burden.

title: LLMs Can Evolve Continually on Modality for $\mathbb{X}$-Modal Reasoning

abstract: Diffusion models have garnered widespread attention in Reinforcement Learning (RL) for their powerful expressiveness and multimodality. It has been verified that utilizing diffusion policies can significantly improve the performance of RL algorithms in continuous control tasks by overcoming the limitations of unimodal policies, such as Gaussian policies. Furthermore, the multimodality of diffusion policies also shows the potential of providing the agent with enhanced exploration capabilities. However, existing works mainly focus on applying diffusion policies in offline RL, while their incorporation into online RL has been less investigated. The diffusion model's training objective, known as the variational lower bound, cannot be applied directly in online RL due to the unavailability of 'good' samples (actions). To harmonize the diffusion model with online RL, we propose a novel model-free diffusion-based online RL algorithm named Q-weighted Variational Policy Optimization (QVPO). Specifically, we introduce the Q-weighted variational loss and its approximate implementation in practice. Notably, this loss is shown to be a tight lower bound of the policy objective. To further enhance the exploration capability of the diffusion policy, we design a special entropy regularization term. Unlike Gaussian policies, the log-likelihood in diffusion policies is inaccessible; thus this entropy term is nontrivial. Moreover, to reduce the large variance of diffusion policies, we also develop an efficient behavior policy through action selection. This can further improve its sample efficiency during online interaction. Consequently, the QVPO algorithm leverages the exploration capabilities and multimodality of diffusion policies, preventing the RL agent from converging to a sub-optimal policy. To verify the effectiveness of QVPO, we conduct comprehensive experiments on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The final results demonstrate that QVPO achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both cumulative reward and sample efficiency.

Bringing them into online reinforcement learning creates a training problem, however: the usual diffusion objective cannot be applied directly when good example actions are unavailable. QVPO develops an objective suited to learning while interacting with an environment.

Its central idea is a Q-weighted variational loss, which connects diffusion training to estimated action values. summary.tldr: QVPO makes diffusion policies usable for online reinforcement learning through value-weighted training, entropy regularization, and action selection.

title: Diffusion-based Reinforcement Learning via Q-weighted Variational Policy Optimization

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically harmless but remain vulnerable to carefully crafted prompts known as ``jailbreaks'', which can bypass protective measures and induce harmful behavior. Recent advancements in LLMs have incorporated moderation guardrails that can filter outputs, which trigger processing errors for certain malicious questions. Existing red-teaming benchmarks often neglect to include questions that trigger moderation guardrails, making it difficult to evaluate jailbreak effectiveness. To address this issue, we introduce JAMBench, a harmful behavior benchmark designed to trigger and evaluate moderation guardrails. JAMBench involves 160 manually crafted instructions covering four major risk categories at multiple severity levels. Furthermore, we propose a jailbreak method, JAM (Jailbreak Against Moderation), designed to attack moderation guardrails using jailbreak prefixes to bypass input-level filters and a fine-tuned shadow model functionally equivalent to the guardrail model to generate cipher characters to bypass output-level filters. Our extensive experiments on four LLMs demonstrate that JAM achieves higher jailbreak success ($\sim$ $\times$ 19.88) and lower filtered-out rates ($\sim$ $\times$ 1/6) than baselines.

paragraphs: The paper examines jailbreak evaluation when an LLM is surrounded by moderation filters. Some harmful questions trigger those filters or processing errors, yet existing red-teaming benchmarks often leave such questions out. This omission makes it difficult to assess attacks against the complete guarded system.

The authors introduce JAMBench, containing 160 manually written instructions across four major risk categories and several severity levels. They also propose JAM, an attack that targets input and output moderation separately. At a high level, it combines input prefixes with cipher-character outputs produced using a fine-tuned shadow model intended to function like the guardrail model.

Experiments on four LLMs report approximately 19.88 times the jailbreak success of baselines and filtered-out rates about one-sixth as large. The research contribution combines a benchmark that explicitly exercises moderation guardrails with evidence that guardrail behavior needs direct evaluation alongside the underlying model's responses.
summary.tldr: JAMBench and JAM evaluate weaknesses in LLM moderation guardrails, reporting substantially higher attack success across four tested models.

title: Jailbreaking Large Language Models Against Moderation Guardrails via Cipher Characters

abstract: In this work we consider Code World Models, world models generated by a Large Language Model (LLM) in the form of Python code for model-based Reinforcement Learning (RL). Calling code instead of LLMs for planning has potential to be more precise, reliable, interpretable, and extremely efficient.However, writing appropriate Code World Models requires the ability to understand complex instructions, to generate exact code with non-trivial logic and to self-debug a long program with feedback from unit tests and environment trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose Generate, Improve and Fix with Monte Carlo Tree Search (GIF-MCTS), a new code generation strategy for LLMs. To test our approach in an offline RL setting, we introduce the Code World Models Benchmark (CWMB), a suite of program synthesis and planning tasks comprised of 18 diverse RL environments paired with corresponding textual descriptions and curated trajectories. GIF-MCTS surpasses all baselines on the CWMB and two other benchmarks, and we show that the Code World Models synthesized with it can be successfully used for planning, resulting in model-based RL agents with greatly improved sample efficiency and inference speed.

paragraphs: A world model lets a reinforcement learning agent reason about an environment when planning. This paper studies models written as Python code by a language model. Once generated, the code can be called during planning, offering the potential for more precise, reliable, interpretable, and efficient computation than repeatedly querying a language model.

Producing suitable code requires understanding the environment, implementing complicated logic correctly, and repairing a long program using feedback. The authors introduce Generate, Improve and Fix with Monte Carlo Tree Search, or GIF-MCTS, to address these demands. They also create the Code World Models Benchmark, containing 18 reinforcement learning environments with textual descriptions and curated trajectories for offline evaluation.

GIF-MCTS outperforms all evaluated baselines on that benchmark and two additional benchmarks. The authors further demonstrate that its generated world models can support planning, producing agents with greatly improved sample efficiency and inference speed. These findings connect code-generation quality to the practical usefulness of the resulting programs within model-based reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: GIF-MCTS guides language models in generating and repairing executable world models that improve reinforcement learning planning.

title: Generating Code World Models with Large Language Models Guided by Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: In this study, we consider multi-class multi-server asymmetric queueing systems consisting of $N$ queues on one side and $K$ servers on the other side, where jobs randomly arrive in queues at each time. The service rate of each job-server assignment is unknown and modeled by a feature-based Multi-nomial Logit (MNL) function. At each time, a scheduler assigns jobs to servers, and each server stochastically serves at most one job based on its preferences over the assigned jobs. The primary goal of the algorithm is to stabilize the queues in the system while learning the service rates of servers. To achieve this goal, we propose algorithms based on UCB and Thompson Sampling, which achieve system stability with an average queue length bound of $O(\min\\{N,K\\}/\epsilon)$ for a large time horizon $T$, where $\epsilon$ is a traffic slackness of the system. Furthermore, the algorithms achieve sublinear regret bounds of $\tilde{O}(\min\\{\sqrt{T}Q_{\max},T^{3/4}\\})$, where $Q_{\max}$ represents the maximum queue length over agents and times. Lastly, we provide experimental results to demonstrate the performance of our algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies scheduling when jobs arrive randomly into multiple queues and servers have unknown service behavior. A scheduler assigns jobs to servers, but each server serves at most one assigned job, chosen stochastically according to its preferences. The service rates follow a feature-based multinomial logit model.

The learning challenge is coupled to queue management. The scheduler must discover which assignments work well while preventing waiting jobs from accumulating without control. The authors propose algorithms based on upper confidence bounds and Thompson sampling, combining learning about service behavior with the objective of stabilizing the system.

For sufficiently long time horizons, the algorithms achieve stability with average queue length bounded in order by the smaller of the queue and server counts divided by traffic slackness. The guarantee thus depends explicitly on the system’s spare capacity. The authors also establish sublinear regret bounds involving the time horizon and maximum queue length, and provide experimental results. Together, the results characterize learning performance and congestion control under the stated preference-based service model.
summary.tldr: Preference-aware bandit schedulers learn unknown service rates while providing queue-stability and sublinear-regret guarantees.

title: Queueing Matching Bandits with Preference Feedback

abstract: Molecular property prediction (MPP) is integral to drug discovery and material science, but often faces the challenge of data scarcity in real-world scenarios. Addressing this, few-shot molecular property prediction (FSMPP) has been developed. Unlike other few-shot tasks, FSMPP typically employs a pre-trained molecular encoder and a context-aware classifier, benefiting from molecular pre-training and molecular context information. Despite these advancements, existing methods struggle with the ineffective fine-tuning of pre-trained encoders. We attribute this issue to the imbalance between the abundance of tunable parameters and the scarcity of labeled molecules, and the lack of contextual perceptiveness in the encoders. To overcome this hurdle, we propose a parameter-efficient in-context tuning method, named Pin-Tuning. Specifically, we propose a lightweight adapter for pre-trained message passing layers (MP-Adapter) and Bayesian weight consolidation for pre-trained atom/bond embedding layers (Emb-BWC), to achieve parameter-efficient tuning while preventing over-fitting and catastrophic forgetting. Additionally, we enhance the MP-Adapters with contextual perceptiveness. This innovation allows for in-context tuning of the pre-trained encoder, thereby improving its adaptability for specific FSMPP tasks. When evaluated on public datasets, our method demonstrates superior tuning with fewer trainable parameters, improving few-shot predictive performance.

paragraphs: Predicting molecular properties with only a few labeled molecules makes adaptation difficult, even when a molecular encoder has already been pretrained. The paper attributes ineffective fine-tuning to too many adjustable parameters relative to the available labels and to encoders that do not adequately use task context. Pin-Tuning addresses both issues.

The method adds lightweight adapters to pretrained message-passing layers and uses Bayesian weight consolidation for atom and bond embedding layers. These components support parameter-efficient adaptation while guarding against overfitting and forgetting pretrained knowledge. The adapters are also made context-aware, allowing the encoder's adaptation to reflect information relevant to the particular few-shot prediction task.

This extends contextual adaptation into the molecular encoder itself, alongside the context-aware classification already used in this setting. Evaluations on public datasets report better tuning and improved few-shot prediction with fewer trainable parameters. The results support combining a restricted adaptation mechanism with task context when labeled molecular examples are scarce and preserving pretrained information is valuable.
summary.tldr: Pin-Tuning combines context-aware adapters and weight consolidation to improve few-shot molecular prediction with fewer trainable parameters.

title: Pin-Tuning: Parameter-Efficient In-Context Tuning for Few-Shot Molecular Property Prediction

abstract: No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment (NR-PCQA) aims to objectively assess the human perceptual quality of point clouds without relying on pristine-quality point clouds for reference. It is becoming increasingly significant with the rapid advancement of immersive media applications such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR). However, current NR-PCQA models attempt to indiscriminately learn point cloud content and distortion representations within a single network, overlooking their distinct contributions to quality information. To address this issue, we propose DisPA, a novel disentangled representation learning framework for NR-PCQA. The framework trains a dual-branch disentanglement network to minimize mutual information (MI) between representations of point cloud content and distortion. Specifically, to fully disentangle representations, the two branches adopt different philosophies: the content-aware encoder is pretrained by a masked auto-encoding strategy, which can allow the encoder to capture semantic information from rendered images of distorted point clouds; the distortion-aware encoder takes a mini-patch map as input, which forces the encoder to focus on low-level distortion patterns. Furthermore, we utilize an MI estimator to estimate the tight upper bound of the actual MI and further minimize it to achieve explicit representation disentanglement. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that DisPA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple PCQA datasets.

paragraphs: Assessing a point cloud's perceptual quality without a pristine reference requires distinguishing what the scene contains from how it has been distorted. The paper argues that existing models mix those two kinds of information in one network, overlooking their different roles. DisPA addresses this through separate representations for content and distortion.

The distortion branch receives a mini-patch map designed to focus attention on local, low-level distortion patterns. These choices encourage the branches to specialize.

DisPA also explicitly minimizes the mutual information between the two representations, using an estimator of a tight upper bound on their actual mutual information. Reducing this objective encourages less shared information between content and distortion. Experiments across multiple point-cloud quality datasets report performance above state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining specialized encoders with an explicit separation objective when predicting human-perceived quality without a clean reference.
summary.tldr: DisPA separates point-cloud content from distortion using specialized encoders and mutual-information minimization to improve reference-free quality assessment.

title: Learning Disentangled Representations for Perceptual Point Cloud Quality Assessment via Mutual Information Minimization

abstract: While the expected calibration error (ECE), which employs binning, is widely adopted to evaluate the calibration performance of machine learning models, theoretical understanding of its estimation bias is limited. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive analysis of the estimation bias in the two common binning strategies, uniform mass and uniform width binning.Our analysis establishes upper bounds on the bias, achieving an improved convergence rate. Moreover, our bounds reveal, for the first time, the optimal number of bins to minimize the estimation bias. We further extend our bias analysis to generalization error analysis based on the information-theoretic approach, deriving upper bounds that enable the numerical evaluation of how small the ECE is for unknown data. Experiments using deep learning models show that our bounds are nonvacuous thanks to this information-theoretic generalization analysis approach.
