paragraphs: Time-series classification often has access to many recordings but relatively few labels. Virtual Adversarial Training helps use unlabeled examples by encouraging predictions to remain stable under challenging perturbations. Straightforward applications can nevertheless perform poorly when those perturbations ignore the temporal organization of the signal.

Functional Virtual Adversarial Training, or f-VAT, incorporates that organization into how perturbations are constructed. The authors establish a theoretical duality between the norm used to measure a perturbation and the model’s sensitivity to changes in the underlying function. They use this relationship to motivate a Sobolev H⁻ˢ norm for generating structured adversarial changes to time-series data.

The choice of norm matters because it determines which disturbances the training procedure asks the classifier to withstand. By reflecting functional structure, f-VAT makes that pressure more appropriate for time-dependent observations. Extensive semi-supervised classification experiments report better performance than recent methods, with improvements reaching approximately 9%. Additional visualizations provide further insight into the method’s behavior and its reported advantages.
summary.tldr: f-VAT improves semi-supervised time-series classification by constructing adversarial perturbations that account for the signal’s functional structure.

title: Functional Virtual Adversarial Training for Semi-Supervised Time Series Classification

abstract: Large language model (LLM) based agentic workflows have become a popular paradigm for coordinating multiple specialized agents to solve complex tasks. To improve serving efficiency, existing LLM systems employ prefix caching to reuse key-value (KV) tensors corresponding to agents' fixed prompts, thereby avoiding redundant computation across repeated invocations. However, current systems typically evict KV caches using a Least Recently Used (LRU) policy, which fails to anticipate future agent usage and often discards KV caches shortly before their reuse. This leads to frequent cache misses and substantial recomputation or swap- ping overhead. We present KVFlow, a workflow-aware KV cache management framework tailored for agentic workloads. KVFlow abstracts the agent execution schedule as an Agent Step Graph and assigns each agent a steps-to-execution value that estimates its temporal proximity to future activation. These values guide a fine-grained eviction policy at the KV node level, allowing KVFlow to preserve entries likely to be reused and efficiently manage shared prefixes in tree-structured caches. Moreover, KVFlow introduces a fully overlapped KV prefetching mecha- nism, which proactively loads required tensors from CPU to GPU in background threads for agents scheduled in the next step, thereby avoiding cache miss stalls during generation. Compared to SGLang with hierarchical radix cache, KVFlow achieves up to 1.83× speedup for single workflows with large prompts, and up to 2.19× speedup for scenarios with many concurrent workflows.

paragraphs: Multi-agent language-model workflows repeatedly invoke agents with fixed prompts. Prefix caching saves the internal key-value tensors for those prompts, avoiding repeated computation. These estimates guide eviction at individual cache nodes, preserving entries likely to be needed soon while accounting for prefixes shared across agents. This finer control also fits tree-structured caches, where several prompts can reuse common initial segments.

Compared with SGLang using a hierarchical radix cache, it reports speedups up to 1.83× for individual workflows with large prompts and 2.19× with many concurrent workflows. The gains demonstrate the value of scheduling knowledge for cache management.
summary.tldr: KVFlow accelerates multi-agent workflows by using upcoming agent executions to guide prefix-cache eviction and prefetching.

title: KVFlow: Efficient Prefix Caching for Accelerating LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows

abstract: Knowledge in modern neural networks is often entangled and structurally opaque, making current transfer methods—typically based on reusing entire parameter sets—inefficient and inflexible. Efforts to improve flexibility by reusing partial parameters frequently depend on handcrafted heuristics or rigid structural assumptions, which constrain generalization. In contrast, biological evolution enables efficient knowledge transfer by encoding only essential information into genes through iterative refinement under environmental pressure. Inspired by this principle, we propose **ECO**, a framework that **E**volves **CO**re knowledge into modular, reusable neural components—termed *learngenes*—through similar evolutionary dynamics. To this end, we redefine learngenes as neural circuits and introduce Genetic Transfer Learning (GTL), a biologically inspired paradigm that establishes a genetic mechanism within neural networks in the context of supervised learning. GTL simulates evolutionary processes by generating diverse network populations, selecting high-performing individuals, and transferring their learngenes to subsequent generations. Through iterative refinement, GTL enables learngenes to accumulate transferable common knowledge. Extensive experiments show that ECO achieves efficient initialization and strong generalization across diverse models and tasks, while significantly reducing computational and memory costs compared to conventional methods.

Selecting smaller portions can require handcrafted rules or rigid assumptions about network structure. ECO proposes learning reusable components through an evolutionary process, with the aim of retaining essential, transferable knowledge more efficiently.

The framework represents these components, called learngenes, as neural circuits. Its Genetic Transfer Learning procedure generates diverse populations of networks, selects high-performing members, and passes their learngenes to later generations. Repeating this process is intended to let common knowledge accumulate within modular circuits through supervised learning and selection.

The resulting components support initialization and transfer across models and tasks. Extensive experiments report strong generalization and efficient initialization, together with substantial reductions in computation and memory relative to conventional approaches. The evolutionary analogy therefore guides a concrete transfer mechanism: reusable circuits are refined through repeated selection, making the unit of transferred knowledge smaller and more modular than a complete network parameter set.
summary.tldr: ECO evolves reusable neural circuits that transfer knowledge across models and tasks while reducing computational and memory costs in experiments.

title: ECO: Evolving Core Knowledge for Efficient Transfer

abstract: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Object Detection (CD-FSOD) aims to generalize to unseen domains by leveraging a few annotated samples of the target domain, requiring models to exhibit both strong generalization and localization capabilities. However, existing well-trained detectors typically have strong localization capabilities but lack generalization, whereas vision foundation models (VFMs) generally exhibit better generalization but lack accurate localization capabilities. In this paper, we propose a novel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) structure that integrates the detector's localization capability and the VFM's generalization by using VFM features to improve detector features. Specifically, we propose Expert-wise Router (ER) that selects the most relevant VFM experts for each backbone layer, and Region-wise Router (RR) that emphasizes foreground and suppress background. To bridge representation gaps, we further propose Shared Expert Projection (SEP) module and Private Expert Projection (PEP) module, which align VFM features to the detector feature space while decoupling shared image feature from private image feature in the VFM feature map. Finally, we propose MoE module to transfer the VFM’s generalization to the detector without altering the detector original architecture. Furthermore, our method extend well-trained detectors for detecting novel classes in unseen domains without re-training on the base classes. Experimental results on multiple cross-domain datasets validate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar object classes in a new domain from a few labeled examples requires both accurate localization and strong generalization. The paper identifies complementary strengths: trained detectors locate objects well, while vision foundation models generalize better but are less precise at localization. Its approach combines their features through a mixture-of-experts structure.

An Expert-wise Router chooses relevant foundation-model experts for each detector backbone layer. A Region-wise Router emphasizes foreground information and suppresses background information. Shared and Private Expert Projection modules bring foundation-model features into the detector’s feature space while separating shared and private image features. Together, these components let foundation-model information improve the detector’s internal representations.

The method transfers this generalization capability without changing the detector’s original architecture. It also extends trained detectors to novel classes in unseen domains without retraining on base classes; that is the specific retraining claim supported here. Experiments on multiple cross-domain datasets validate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a structured way to combine existing models’ complementary capabilities for detection with limited target-domain annotations.
summary.tldr: A mixture-of-experts framework combines detector localization with foundation-model generalization for new domains without retraining on base classes.

title: DON’T NEED RETRAINING: A Mixture of DETR and Vision Foundation Models for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Object Detection

abstract: Diverse decoding of large language models is crucial for applications requiring multiple semantically distinct responses, yet existing methods primarily achieve lexical rather than semantic diversity. This limitation significantly constrains Best-of-N strategies, group-based reinforcement learning, and data synthesis. While temperature sampling and diverse beam search modify token distributions or apply n-gram penalties, they fail to ensure meaningful semantic differentiation. We introduce Semantic-guided Diverse Decoding (SemDiD), operating directly in embedding space that balances quality with diversity through three complementary mechanisms: orthogonal directional guidance, dynamic inter-group repulsion, and position-debiased probability assessment. SemDiD harmonizes these competing objectives using adaptive gain functions and constraint optimization, ensuring both quality thresholds and maximal semantic differentiation. Experiments show SemDiD consistently outperforms existing methods, improving Best-of-N coverage by 1.4-5.2% across diverse tasks and accelerating RLHF training convergence by 15% while increasing accuracy by up to 2.1%.

paragraphs: SemDiD aims to make multiple language-model responses differ in meaning, rather than mainly in wording. This distinction matters when a system selects the best of several answers, learns from groups of responses, or generates synthetic data. The paper argues that changing token probabilities or penalizing repeated word sequences does not ensure meaningful semantic differences.

The method works directly in embedding space. It combines orthogonal directional guidance, dynamic repulsion between groups, and probability assessment that corrects for position bias. Adaptive gain functions and constrained optimization coordinate these mechanisms, balancing response quality against semantic separation. The design explicitly treats quality and diversity as objectives that need to be managed together.

Experiments report consistent improvements over existing methods, including a 1.4–5.2% increase in Best-of-N coverage across tasks. The authors also report 15% faster RLHF training convergence and accuracy improvements of up to 2.1%. These findings indicate that the proposed diversity mechanism can benefit downstream selection and training in the evaluated settings, beyond producing responses that merely look different.
summary.tldr: SemDiD guides decoding in embedding space to produce meaningfully different responses while balancing quality, improving reported selection and RLHF results.

title: Semantic-guided Diverse Decoding for Large Language Model

abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) have made great achievements in Earth vision. However, complex disaster scenes with diverse disaster types, geographic regions, and satellite sensors have posed new challenges for VLM applications. To fill this gap, we curate the first remote sensing vision-language dataset (DisasterM3) for global-scale disaster assessment and response. DisasterM3 includes 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and 123k instruction pairs across 5 continents, with three characteristics: **1) Multi-hazard**: DisasterM3 involves 36 historical disaster events with significant impacts, which are categorized into 10 common natural and man-made disasters. **2) Multi-sensor**: Extreme weather during disasters often hinders optical sensor imaging, making it necessary to combine Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery for post-disaster scenes. **3) Multi-task**: Based on real-world scenarios, DisasterM3 includes 9 disaster-related visual perception and reasoning tasks, harnessing the full potential of VLM's reasoning ability with progressing from disaster-bearing body recognition to structural damage assessment and object relational reasoning, culminating in the generation of long-form disaster reports. We extensively evaluated 14 generic and remote sensing VLMs on our benchmark, revealing that state-of-the-art models struggle with the disaster tasks, largely due to the lack of a disaster-specific corpus, cross-sensor gap, and damage object counting insensitivity. Focusing on these issues, we fine-tune four VLMs using our dataset and achieve stable improvements (up to 10.4\%$\uparrow$QA, 2.1$\uparrow$Report, 40.8\%$\uparrow$Referring Seg.) with robust cross-sensor and cross-disaster generalization capabilities. Project: https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DisasterM3.

paragraphs: DisasterM3 is a remote sensing vision-language dataset designed for disaster assessment and response. It contains 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and about 123,000 instruction pairs spanning five continents. Its 36 historical events cover ten categories of natural and human-made disasters, providing varied scenes for studying how models interpret damage and support reporting.

The dataset combines multiple sensors, including synthetic aperture radar imagery for post-disaster scenes where extreme weather can hinder optical imaging. Its nine tasks range from recognizing affected objects to assessing structural damage, reasoning about object relationships, and producing long reports. This range connects visual perception with the more involved reasoning needed to describe a disaster's consequences.

Evaluation of 14 general and remote sensing vision-language models reveals difficulties associated with limited disaster-specific training material, differences between sensors, and poor sensitivity to damaged-object counts. Fine-tuning four models on DisasterM3 produces consistent improvements, alongside reported generalization across sensors and disaster types. The results position the dataset as both a diagnostic benchmark and training material for improving performance on these demanding tasks.
summary.tldr: DisasterM3 benchmarks satellite-based disaster understanding across hazards, sensors, and tasks, and improves evaluated models through targeted fine-tuning.

title: DisasterM3: A Remote Sensing Vision-Language Dataset for Disaster Damage Assessment and Response

abstract: Given an undirected, weighted $n$-vertex graph $G = (V, E, w)$, a Gomory-Hu tree $T$ is a weighted tree on $V$ that preserves the Min-$s$-$t$-Cut between any pair of vertices $s, t \in V$. Finding cuts in graphs is a key primitive in problems such as bipartite matching, spectral and correlation clustering, and community detection. We design a differentially private (DP) algorithm that computes an approximate Gomory-Hu tree. Our algorithm is $\varepsilon$-DP, runs in polynomial time, and can be used to compute $s$-$t$ cuts that are $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon)$-additive approximations of the Min-$s$-$t$-Cuts in $G$ for all distinct $s, t \in V$ with high probability. Our error bound is essentially optimal, since [Dalirrooyfard, Mitrovic and Nevmyvaka, Neurips 2023] showed that privately outputting a single Min-$s$-$t$-Cut requires $\Omega(n)$ additive error even with $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP and allowing for multiplicative error. Prior to our work, the best additive error bounds for approximate all-pairs Min-$s$-$t$-Cuts were $O(n^{3/2}/\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon$-DP [Gupta, Roth, Ullman, TCC 2009] and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{mn}/ \varepsilon)$ for $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP [Liu, Upadhyay and Zou, SODA 2024], both achieved by DP algorithms that preserve all cuts in the graph. To achieve our result, we develop an $\varepsilon$-DP algorithm for the Minimum Isolating Cuts problem with near-linear error, and introduce a novel privacy composition technique combining elements of both parallel and basic composition to handle `bounded overlap' computational branches in recursive algorithms, which maybe of independent interest.

paragraphs: A Gomory-Hu tree summarizes the minimum cuts between every pair of vertices in an undirected weighted graph. These cuts describe the least costly way to separate two vertices, a primitive used in clustering and other graph problems. The paper develops a differentially private algorithm for producing an approximate version of this compact representation.

The algorithm runs in polynomial time and satisfies epsilon differential privacy. With high probability, it supports cuts for all vertex pairs whose additive error is roughly n divided by epsilon, apart from logarithmic factors, where n is the number of vertices. This improves the stated previous bounds for private all-pairs cuts. The authors characterize the error as essentially optimal in light of an existing lower bound for privately outputting even one cut.

Two technical components enable the result: a private minimum-isolating-cuts algorithm with near-linear error, and a privacy accounting technique for recursive branches with bounded overlap. The latter combines aspects of parallel and basic composition. Together, these contributions improve private graph summarization while supplying a potentially reusable way to analyze privacy in recursive algorithms.
summary.tldr: A private Gomory-Hu tree algorithm approximates all pairwise minimum cuts with essentially optimal additive error.

title: Differentially Private Gomory-Hu Trees

abstract: Point cloud completion, aiming to reconstruct missing part from incomplete point clouds, is a pivotal task in 3D computer vision. Traditional supervised approaches often necessitate complete point clouds for training supervision, which are not readily accessible in real-world applications. Recent studies have attempted to mitigate this dependency by employing self-supervise mechanisms. However, these approaches frequently yield suboptimal results due to the absence of complete structure in the point cloud data during training. To address these issues, in this paper, we propose an effective framework to complete the point cloud under the guidance of self learned complete structure. A key contribution of our work is the development of a novel self-supervised complete structure reconstruction module, which can learn the complete structure explicitly from incomplete point clouds and thus eliminate the reliance on training data from complete point clouds. Additionally, we introduce a contrastive learning approach at both the cluster- and instance-level to extract shape features guided by the complete structure and to capture style features, respectively. This dual-level learning design ensures that the generated point clouds are both shape-completed and detail-preserving. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised methods.

paragraphs: Point cloud completion reconstructs the missing portions of an object represented by a collection of three-dimensional points. Supervised methods commonly need complete objects as training targets, but those targets can be difficult to obtain. Existing self-supervised approaches reduce this dependence, yet their training data may provide too little information about complete shapes.

The proposed framework introduces a self-supervised module that explicitly learns complete structure from incomplete point clouds. That learned structure then guides the completion process, removing the need for training examples containing complete point clouds. This makes structural guidance an internally learned component of the method rather than something supplied through complete training targets.

Two forms of contrastive learning serve complementary purposes. Learning at the cluster level extracts shape features under the guidance of the reconstructed structure, while learning at the individual-instance level captures style features. The design aims to recover overall shape while retaining detail. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report significant improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised methods, supporting the value of combining learned structural guidance with these two feature-learning objectives.
summary.tldr: The framework learns complete-shape guidance from incomplete point clouds and uses two levels of contrastive learning to preserve shape and detail.

title: Complete Structure Guided Point Cloud Completion via Cluster- and Instance-Level Contrastive Learning

abstract: The i.i.d. assumption in machine learning is endemic, but often flawed. Complex data sets exhibit partial correlations between both instances and features. A model specifying both types of correlation can have a number of parameters that scales quadratically with the number of features and data points. We introduce the bigraphical lasso, an estimator for precision matrices of matrix-normals based on the Cartesian product of graphs. A prominent product in spectral graph theory, this structure has appealing properties for regression, enhanced sparsity and interpretability. To deal with the parameter explosion we introduce L1 penalties and fit the model through a flip-flop algorithm that results in a linear number of lasso regressions.

paragraphs: Data arranged in a matrix can contain dependencies both among observations and among features. Treating observations as independent can miss part of this structure, but freely modeling both kinds of relationship creates a large number of parameters. This paper introduces the bigraphical lasso to represent these dependencies more economically.

The estimator learns precision matrices for matrix-normal models using a structure based on the Cartesian product of graphs. That graph construction provides a way to organize the two types of partial correlation together. The authors identify useful properties for regression, sparsity, and interpretation, making the structural assumption part of the model's appeal.

summary.tldr: The bigraphical lasso models dependencies among both observations and features using graph-product structure and sparse estimation.

title: The Bigraphical Lasso

abstract: We study linear control problems with quadratic losses and adversarially chosen tracking targets. We present an efficient algorithm for this problem and show that, under standard conditions on the linear system, its regret with respect to an optimal linear policy grows as O(\log^2 T), where T is the number of rounds of the game. We also study a problem with adversarially chosen transition dynamics; we present an exponentially-weighted average algorithm for this problem, and we give regret bounds that grow as O(\sqrt T).

For adversarial tracking targets, the authors give an efficient algorithm with regret growing as O(log² T). The guarantee holds under standard conditions on the linear system. Its slow growth means the cumulative performance gap to the comparison policy increases only polylogarithmically with the number of rounds, within the stated setting and assumptions.

The paper separately considers adversarially chosen transition dynamics, where the system's evolution itself can vary adversarially. It provides an exponentially weighted averaging algorithm with O(√T) regret bounds for that problem. These results distinguish uncertainty in the target from adversarial variation in the dynamics, and provide different algorithms and guarantees for the two control settings.
summary.tldr: The paper gives low-regret algorithms for linear control with adversarial targets and, separately, adversarial transition dynamics.

title: Tracking Adversarial Targets

abstract: We explore an active top-$K$ ranking problem based on pairwise comparisons that are collected possibly in a sequential manner as per our design choice. We consider two settings: (1) top-$K$ sorting in which the goal is to recover the top-$K$ items in order out of $n$ items; (2) top-$K$ partitioning where only the set of top-$K$ items is desired. Under a fairly general model which subsumes as special cases various models (e.g., Strong Stochastic Transitivity model, BTL model and uniform noise model), we characterize upper bounds on the sample size required for top-$K$ sorting as well as for top-$K$ partitioning. As a consequence, we demonstrate that active ranking can offer significant multiplicative gains in sample complexity over passive ranking. Depending on the underlying stochastic noise model, such gain varies from around $\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ to $\frac{ n^2 \log n }{\log \log n}$. We also present an algorithm that is applicable to both settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best K items when the available evidence consists of noisy comparisons between pairs. It distinguishes two goals: finding those items in the correct order, and simply finding the set of best items. Keeping these goals separate matters because identifying membership and resolving order place different demands on the comparisons collected.

The approach is active: the procedure can choose which comparisons to collect, potentially making those choices sequentially. The authors analyze both goals under a noise model broad enough to include several established comparison models. They give upper bounds on the number of comparisons required and present an algorithm that applies to both sorting and partitioning.

The analysis shows that active selection can substantially reduce the comparison budget relative to passive ranking. The size of this multiplicative advantage depends on the underlying noise model. Thus, the contribution identifies circumstances in which choosing comparisons strategically offers a provable efficiency benefit, rather than promising one fixed improvement across every ranking problem.
summary.tldr: Choosing noisy pairwise comparisons actively can substantially reduce the samples needed to identify or order the top K items.

title: Active Learning for Top-$K$ Rank Aggregation from Noisy Comparisons

abstract: Most of the semi-supervised classification methods developed so far use unlabeled data for regularization purposes under particular distributional assumptions such as the cluster assumption. In contrast, recently developed methods of classification from positive and unlabeled data (PU classification) use unlabeled data for risk evaluation, i.e., label information is directly extracted from unlabeled data. In this paper, we extend PU classification to also incorporate negative data and propose a novel semi-supervised learning approach. We establish generalization error bounds for our novel methods and show that the bounds decrease with respect to the number of unlabeled data without the distributional assumptions that are required in existing semi-supervised learning methods. Through experiments, we demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed methods.

This paper develops a different approach based on positive-and-unlabeled classification. In that framework, unlabeled observations contribute directly to evaluating classification risk.

The authors extend positive-and-unlabeled methods to also incorporate negative labeled examples. This produces semi-supervised methods that combine positive, negative, and unlabeled data within a risk-evaluation approach. The conceptual change concerns what unlabeled data are used for: they help evaluate the learning objective rather than serving only as a source of distribution-based regularization.

The paper establishes generalization-error bounds that decrease as the amount of unlabeled data increases, without requiring the distributional assumptions used by the existing semi-supervised approaches discussed. Experiments also demonstrate the methods' usefulness. The theoretical finding gives a concrete reason additional unlabeled observations can help: their contribution appears in improving error bounds for the proposed methods, rather than depending on the particular cluster-style assumptions motivating earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: Extending positive-and-unlabeled classification yields semi-supervised methods whose error bounds improve with more unlabeled data.

title: Semi-Supervised Classification Based on Classification from Positive and Unlabeled Data

abstract: Inference from complex distributions is a common problem in machine learning needed for many Bayesian methods. We propose an efficient, gradient-free method for learning general GMM approximations of multimodal distributions based on recent insights from stochastic search methods. Our method establishes information-geometric trust regions to ensure efficient exploration of the sampling space and stability of the GMM updates, allowing for efficient estimation of multi-variate Gaussian variational distributions. For GMMs, we apply a variational lower bound to decompose the learning objective into sub-problems given by learning the individual mixture components and the coefficients. The number of mixture components is adapted online in order to allow for arbitrary exact approximations. We demonstrate on several domains that we can learn significantly better approximations than competing variational inference methods and that the quality of samples drawn from our approximations is on par with samples created by state-of-the-art MCMC samplers that require significantly more computational resources.

It draws on stochastic search methods to fit a flexible collection of Gaussian components without relying on gradients.

A variational lower bound divides the mixture-learning objective into subproblems for the individual components and their coefficients. These empirical findings support the combination of controlled distribution updates and adaptable mixtures as an efficient way to approximate multimodal targets.
summary.tldr: A gradient-free method uses trust regions and adaptive Gaussian mixtures to efficiently approximate complex, multimodal distributions.

title: Efficient Gradient-Free Variational Inference using Policy Search

abstract: An interesting approach to analyzing neural networks that has received renewed attention is to examine the equivalent kernel of the neural network. This is based on the fact that a fully connected feedforward network with one hidden layer, a certain weight distribution, an activation function, and an infinite number of neurons can be viewed as a mapping into a Hilbert space. We derive the equivalent kernels of MLPs with ReLU or Leaky ReLU activations for all rotationally-invariant weight distributions, generalizing a previous result that required Gaussian weight distributions. Additionally, the Central Limit Theorem is used to show that for certain activation functions, kernels corresponding to layers with weight distributions having $0$ mean and finite absolute third moment are asymptotically universal, and are well approximated by the kernel corresponding to layers with spherical Gaussian weights. In deep networks, as depth increases the equivalent kernel approaches a pathological fixed point, which can be used to argue why training randomly initialized networks can be difficult. Our results also have implications for weight initialization.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes neural networks through their equivalent kernels, a perspective that describes how network representations relate inputs to one another. For a fully connected network with one hidden layer and infinitely many neurons, the construction depends on the activation function and weight distribution. The authors investigate how sensitive that kernel is to the distributional choice.

summary.tldr: Equivalent-kernel analysis shows when different weight distributions produce similar rectified-network behavior and connects depth to training difficulties.

title: Invariance of Weight Distributions in Rectified MLPs

abstract: This work aims to provide understandings on the remarkable success of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by theoretically analyzing their generalization performance and establishing optimization guarantees for gradient descent based training algorithms. Specifically, for a CNN model consisting of $l$ convolutional layers and one fully connected layer, we prove that its generalization error is bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\theta\widetilde{\varrho}/n})$ where $\theta$ denotes freedom degree of the network parameters and $\widetilde{\varrho}=\mathcal{O}(\log(\prod_{i=1}^{l}b_{i} (k_{i}-s_{i}+1)/p)+\log(b_{l+1}))$ encapsulates architecture parameters including the kernel size $k_{i}$, stride $s_{i}$, pooling size $p$ and parameter magnitude $b_{i}$. To our best knowledge, this is the first generalization bound that only depends on $\mathcal{O}(\log(\prod_{i=1}^{l+1}b_{i}))$, tighter than existing ones that all involve an exponential term like $\mathcal{O}(\prod_{i=1}^{l+1}b_{i})$. Besides, we prove that for an arbitrary gradient descent algorithm, the computed approximate stationary point by minimizing empirical risk is also an approximate stationary point to the population risk. This well explains why gradient descent training algorithms usually perform sufficiently well in practice. Furthermore, we prove the one-to-one correspondence and convergence guarantees for the non-degenerate stationary points between the empirical and population risks. It implies that the computed local minimum for the empirical risk is also close to a local minimum for the population risk, thus ensuring that the optimized CNN model well generalizes to new data.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes why training a convolutional neural network can produce a model that performs well beyond its training data. It studies a network with multiple convolutional layers followed by one fully connected layer, connecting generalization bounds with guarantees about the solutions reached through gradient-based optimization.

Its generalization-error bound scales with the square root of parameter freedom times an architecture-dependent factor divided by sample size. The architecture factor includes kernel sizes, strides, pooling, and parameter magnitudes. A central improvement is logarithmic dependence on the product of parameter-magnitude bounds, compared with the stronger dependence in the existing bounds discussed by the authors.

An approximate stationary point obtained by gradient descent on empirical risk is also approximately stationary for population risk. For non-degenerate stationary points, the paper further establishes correspondence and convergence guarantees. This supports the conclusion that a computed empirical local minimum lies near a population local minimum within the analyzed setting, connecting successful optimization to generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper derives tighter CNN generalization bounds and connects training-risk stationary points with corresponding population-risk behavior.

title: Understanding Generalization and Optimization Performance of Deep CNNs

abstract: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) is a recently proposed particle-based Bayesian inference method, which has attracted a lot of interest due to its remarkable approximation ability and particle efficiency compared to traditional variational inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. However, we observed that particles of SVGD tend to collapse to modes of the target distribution, and this particle degeneracy phenomenon becomes more severe with higher dimensions. Our theoretical analysis finds out that there exists a negative correlation between the dimensionality and the repulsive force of SVGD which should be blamed for this phenomenon. We propose Message Passing SVGD (MP-SVGD) to solve this problem. By leveraging the conditional independence structure of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs), MP-SVGD converts the original high-dimensional global inference problem into a set of local ones over the Markov blanket with lower dimensions. Experimental results show its advantages of preventing vanishing repulsive force in high-dimensional space over SVGD, and its particle efficiency and approximation flexibility over other inference methods on graphical models.

paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent represents a target probability distribution using a collection of particles. Although it can approximate distributions efficiently, the authors observe that its particles tend to gather at modes rather than maintain useful diversity. This degeneracy becomes more pronounced as the number of dimensions increases.

Their theoretical analysis links increasing dimensionality to weakening repulsion between particles. The proposed Message Passing SVGD addresses that mechanism by exploiting conditional independence in probabilistic graphical models. It replaces one high-dimensional global inference problem with local inference problems over Markov blankets, whose lower dimensionality makes the problematic global interaction unnecessary.

Experiments show advantages over ordinary SVGD in preventing repulsive forces from vanishing in high-dimensional spaces. They also demonstrate particle efficiency and flexible approximation relative to other inference methods on graphical models. The central idea is to use the model’s dependence structure to organize inference locally: the same structure that describes which variables directly matter to one another helps preserve a useful collection of particles.
summary.tldr: Message Passing SVGD uses local graphical-model structure to counter weakening particle repulsion in high-dimensional Bayesian inference.

title: Message Passing Stein Variational Gradient Descent

abstract: Batch Bayesian optimization has been shown to be an efficient and successful approach for black-box function optimization, especially when the evaluation of cost function is highly expensive but can be efficiently parallelized. In this paper, we introduce a novel variational framework for batch query optimization, based on the argument that the query batch should be selected to have both high diversity and good worst case performance. This motivates us to introduce a variational objective that combines a quantile-based risk measure (for worst case performance) and entropy regularization (for enforcing diversity). We derive a gradient-based particle-based algorithm for solving our quantile-based variational objective, which generalizes Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD). We evaluate our method on a number of real-world applications and show that it consistently outperforms other recent state-of-the-art batch Bayesian optimization methods. Extensive experimental results indicate that our method achieves better or comparable performance, compared to the existing methods.

paragraphs: Batch Bayesian optimization chooses several queries to an expensive black-box function so that their evaluations can run in parallel. This paper argues that a useful batch should combine diversity with good worst-case performance. Choosing a collection of queries therefore requires considering properties of the batch as a whole.

The authors express those priorities in a variational objective. A quantile-based risk measure addresses worst-case performance, while entropy regularization encourages diversity. They then derive a gradient-based algorithm that represents the solution with particles and generalizes Stein variational gradient descent. The optimization procedure is thus tied directly to the two stated goals for batch selection.

The method is evaluated on several real-world applications. The authors report consistent improvements over recent state-of-the-art batch Bayesian optimization methods in those applications, and describe their broader experimental results as better than or comparable to existing methods. These findings support the combined risk-and-diversity objective empirically, without making worst-case optimization performance a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: A particle-based batch optimization method balances quantile-based risk and diversity, achieving better or comparable performance in reported experiments.

title: Quantile Stein Variational Gradient Descent for Batch Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We study online learning settings in which experts act strategically to maximize their influence on the learning algorithm’s predictions by potentially misreporting their beliefs about a sequence of binary events. Our goal is twofold. First, we want the learning algorithm to be no-regret with respect to the best-fixed expert in hindsight. Second, we want incentive compatibility, a guarantee that each expert’s best strategy is to report his true beliefs about the realization of each event. To achieve this goal, we build on the literature on wagering mechanisms, a type of multi-agent scoring rule. We provide algorithms that achieve no regret and incentive compatibility for myopic experts for both the full and partial information settings. In experiments on datasets from FiveThirtyEight, our algorithms have regret comparable to classic no-regret algorithms, which are not incentive-compatible. Finally, we identify an incentive-compatible algorithm for forward-looking strategic agents that exhibits diminishing regret in practice.

paragraphs: An online learner may combine predictions from experts whose reports are strategic rather than honest. This paper considers experts predicting binary events who want to maximize their influence on the learner. The challenge is to make truthful reporting their best strategy while keeping the learner's regret small relative to the best fixed expert in hindsight.

The authors build algorithms using ideas from wagering mechanisms, which score multiple participants together. For myopic experts, they achieve both incentive compatibility and no regret in full-information and partial-information settings. The qualification about myopic behavior matters: the guarantees address experts focused on immediate incentives rather than strategic effects extending into the future.

Experiments on FiveThirtyEight datasets find regret comparable to classic no-regret algorithms that lack incentive compatibility. The paper also identifies an incentive-compatible algorithm for forward-looking strategic agents, with diminishing regret observed in practice. This latter result is empirical on regret, whereas the myopic setting receives the stated no-regret guarantees. The work connects learning performance with explicit incentives for honest expert reports.
summary.tldr: Wagering-based online algorithms combine truthful-reporting incentives with no-regret guarantees for myopic experts.

title: No-Regret and Incentive-Compatible Online Learning

abstract: Estimation of individual treatment effects is commonly used as the basis for contextual decision making in fields such as healthcare, education, and economics. However, it is often sufficient for the decision maker to have estimates of upper and lower bounds on the potential outcomes of decision alternatives to assess risks and benefits. We show that, in such cases, we can improve sample efficiency by estimating simple functions that bound these outcomes instead of estimating their conditional expectations, which may be complex and hard to estimate. Our analysis highlights a trade-off between the complexity of the learning task and the confidence with which the learned bounds hold. Guided by these findings, we develop an algorithm for learning upper and lower bounds on potential outcomes which optimize an objective function defined by the decision maker, subject to the probability that bounds are violated being small. Using a clinical dataset and a well-known causality benchmark, we demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms baselines, providing tighter, more reliable bounds.

paragraphs: Choosing between interventions often involves estimating the outcomes each alternative might produce. This paper considers decisions for which upper and lower outcome bounds provide enough information to assess risks and benefits. In those cases, learning bounds can be a simpler statistical task than estimating conditional expectations that may have complicated structure.

The authors show that this change in estimation target can improve sample efficiency. Their analysis identifies a trade-off between how complex the learning task is and how confidently the learned bounds hold. Guided by that trade-off, they develop an algorithm that learns upper and lower bounds while optimizing an objective chosen by the decision maker.

The optimization constrains the probability of violating the bounds to remain small. The contribution is therefore a decision-oriented way to allocate estimation effort: when bounds are sufficient, the learner can focus on those bounds and their reliability.
summary.tldr: When outcome bounds suffice for decisions, learning them directly can improve sample efficiency and produce tighter, more reliable bounds.

title: Estimation of Bounds on Potential Outcomes For Decision Making

abstract: We investigate fast and communication-efficient algorithms for the classic problem of minimizing a sum of strongly convex and smooth functions that are distributed among $n$ different nodes, which can communicate using a limited number of bits. Most previous communication-efficient approaches for this problem are limited to first-order optimization, and therefore have \emph{linear} dependence on the condition number in their communication complexity. We show that this dependence is not inherent: communication-efficient methods can in fact have sublinear dependence on the condition number. For this, we design and analyze the first communication-efficient distributed variants of preconditioned gradient descent for Generalized Linear Models, and for Newton’s method. Our results rely on a new technique for quantizing both the preconditioner and the descent direction at each step of the algorithms, while controlling their convergence rate. We also validate our findings experimentally, showing faster convergence and reduced communication relative to previous methods.

This paper considers minimizing a sum of smooth, strongly convex functions held across nodes that communicate with limited bits. They develop communication-efficient distributed versions of preconditioned gradient descent for generalized linear models and of Newton's method. The key technique quantizes both the preconditioner and the descent direction at each iteration while controlling convergence. Experiments also show faster convergence and lower communication costs than previous methods. These results connect the mathematical improvement to observed computational benefits. Their scope is the stated smooth, strongly convex setting and the algorithms analyzed, demonstrating that communication constraints need not force optimization to rely solely on the earlier first-order approaches.
summary.tldr: Quantizing preconditioners and update directions enables distributed optimization with improved condition-number dependence and reduced communication in the studied setting.

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Optimization with Quantized Preconditioners

abstract: Complementary-label learning (CLL) deals with the weak supervision scenario where each training instance is associated with one \emph{complementary} label, which specifies the class label that the instance does \emph{not} belong to. Given the training instance ${\bm x}$, existing CLL approaches aim at modeling the \emph{generative} relationship between the complementary label $\bar y$, i.e. $P(\bar y\mid {\bm x})$, and the ground-truth label $y$, i.e. $P(y\mid {\bm x})$. Nonetheless, as the ground-truth label is not directly accessible for complementarily labeled training instance, strong generative assumptions may not hold for real-world CLL tasks. In this paper, we derive a simple and theoretically-sound \emph{discriminative} model towards $P(\bar y\mid {\bm x})$, which naturally leads to a risk estimator with estimation error bound at $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ convergence rate. Accordingly, a practical CLL approach is proposed by further introducing weighted loss to the empirical risk to maximize the predictive gap between potential ground-truth label and complementary label. Extensive experiments clearly validate the effectiveness of the proposed discriminative complementary-label learning approach.

Previous approaches model a generative relationship between these negative labels and the hidden true labels, but the paper argues that strong assumptions about this relationship may fail in real applications.

The authors instead derive a discriminative model for the probability of observing a complementary label given an input. This leads to a risk estimator with an estimation-error bound that decreases at a rate of O(1/√n), where n is the number of training examples. The bound gives theoretical support for learning through this formulation despite the absence of directly observed correct labels.

This turns the available negative supervision into a discriminative training signal. Extensive experiments support the approach’s effectiveness, linking its theoretical risk formulation to a workable method for learning from excluded classes.
summary.tldr: A discriminative risk estimator and weighted loss enable classification from labels specifying which class an example does not belong to.

title: Discriminative Complementary-Label Learning with Weighted Loss

abstract: Learning curves model a classifier’s test error as a function of the number of training samples. Prior works show that learning curves can be used to select model parameters and extrapolate performance. We investigate how to use learning curves to evaluate design choices, such as pretraining, architecture, and data augmentation. We propose a method to robustly estimate learning curves, abstract their parameters into error and data-reliance, and evaluate the effectiveness of different parameterizations. Our experiments exemplify use of learning curves for analysis and yield several interesting observations.

We propose a method to robustly estimate learning curves, abstract their parameters into error and data-reliance, and evaluate the effectiveness of different parameterizations. Our experiments exemplify use of learning curves for analysis and yield several interesting observations.

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how a classifier’s test error changes as the number of training examples grows. The paper investigates how these curves can help evaluate choices in deep learning, including pretraining, architecture, and data augmentation. This makes performance across training-set sizes the object of analysis, extending earlier uses for parameter selection and performance extrapolation.

The authors propose a method for estimating learning curves robustly. They summarize the curve parameters through two concepts: error and data-reliance. These summaries are intended to make fitted curves useful for assessing model design choices, connecting prediction performance with its dependence on the amount of training data. They also evaluate different ways of parameterizing the curves.

Experiments illustrate how this approach can be used to analyze deep networks. The stated contribution is an analysis method and demonstrations of its use; the abstract does not identify a particular architecture or training technique as the winner. Its practical value is a structured way to examine how design decisions relate to both error and data requirements.
summary.tldr: The paper develops robust learning-curve estimates to analyze how deep-network design choices affect error and reliance on training data.

title: Learning Curves for Analysis of Deep Networks

abstract: Continual learning{—}the ability to learn many tasks in sequence{—}is critical for artificial learning systems. Yet standard training methods for deep networks often suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where learning new tasks erases knowledge of the earlier tasks. While catastrophic forgetting labels the problem, the theoretical reasons for interference between tasks remain unclear. Here, we attempt to narrow this gap between theory and practice by studying continual learning in the teacher-student setup. We extend previous analytical work on two-layer networks in the teacher-student setup to multiple teachers. Using each teacher to represent a different task, we investigate how the relationship between teachers affects the amount of forgetting and transfer exhibited by the student when the task switches. In line with recent work, we find that when tasks depend on similar features, intermediate task similarity leads to greatest forgetting. However, feature similarity is only one way in which tasks may be related. The teacher-student approach allows us to disentangle task similarity at the level of \emph{readouts} (hidden-to-output weights) as well as \emph{features} (input-to-hidden weights). We find a complex interplay between both types of similarity, initial transfer/forgetting rates, maximum transfer/forgetting, and the long-time (post-switch) amount of transfer/forgetting. Together, these results help illuminate the diverse factors contributing to catastrophic forgetting.

summary.tldr: A teacher-student analysis shows how feature and readout similarity jointly shape transfer and forgetting across sequential tasks.

title: Continual Learning in the Teacher-Student Setup: Impact of Task Similarity

abstract: A common workflow in single-cell RNA-seq analysis is to project the data to a latent space, cluster the cells in that space, and identify sets of marker genes that explain the differences among the discovered clusters. A primary drawback to this three-step procedure is that each step is carried out independently, thereby neglecting the effects of the nonlinear embedding and inter-gene dependencies on the selection of marker genes. Here we propose an integrated deep learning framework, Adversarial Clustering Explanation (ACE), that bundles all three steps into a single workflow. The method thus moves away from the notion of "marker genes" to instead identify a panel of explanatory genes. This panel may include genes that are not only enriched but also depleted relative to other cell types, as well as genes that exhibit differences between closely related cell types. Empirically, we demonstrate that ACE is able to identify gene panels that are both highly discriminative and nonredundant, and we demonstrate the applicability of ACE to an image recognition task.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis often compresses gene measurements into a latent representation, groups cells there, and then selects genes to explain the groups. Treating these as separate steps can disconnect the explanation from how the groups were formed. In particular, nonlinear transformations and relationships among genes can affect which genes actually distinguish the resulting clusters.

ACE combines representation learning, clustering, and explanation within one deep learning workflow. Its output is a panel of explanatory genes, broadening the usual emphasis on marker genes. A useful panel can include genes expressed more strongly or less strongly than in other cell types, as well as genes that separate closely related types.

The experiments show that ACE can identify panels that distinguish clusters well without excessive redundancy among their genes. This matters because an explanation should capture complementary differences, rather than repeatedly describe the same distinction. The authors also demonstrate the framework on image recognition, showing an application beyond the gene expression setting that motivates the work.
summary.tldr: ACE jointly learns cell representations, clusters, and explanatory gene panels that empirically distinguish cell types with little redundancy.

title: ACE: Explaining cluster from an adversarial perspective

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient approach for tuning design parameters to optimize expensive-to-evaluate, black-box performance metrics. In many manufacturing processes, the design parameters are subject to random input noise, resulting in a product that is often less performant than expected. Although BO methods have been proposed for optimizing a single objective under input noise, no existing method addresses the practical scenario where there are multiple objectives that are sensitive to input perturbations. In this work, we propose the first multi-objective BO method that is robust to input noise. We formalize our goal as optimizing the multivariate value-at-risk (MVaR), a risk measure of the uncertain objectives. Since directly optimizing MVaR is computationally infeasible in many settings, we propose a scalable, theoretically-grounded approach for optimizing MVaR using random scalarizations. Empirically, we find that our approach significantly outperforms alternative methods and efficiently identifies optimal robust designs that will satisfy specifications across multiple metrics with high probability.

paragraphs: Design optimization often involves expensive evaluations and several competing performance metrics. In manufacturing, the settings selected by an optimizer may also be perturbed by random input noise, reducing realized performance. This paper develops multi-objective Bayesian optimization that explicitly accounts for that uncertainty in the design parameters.

The authors formulate robust design selection using multivariate value-at-risk, a risk measure for uncertain objective values. Directly optimizing this measure is computationally infeasible in many settings. Their scalable approach uses random scalarizations to optimize it, with theoretical grounding connecting this computational strategy to the stated risk-based objective.

Empirically, the method significantly outperforms alternatives and efficiently identifies optimal robust designs that meet specifications across multiple metrics with high probability. The practical aim is therefore reliable performance under perturbed inputs across several objectives at once. The contribution brings together sample-efficient search, multiple performance requirements, and explicit treatment of input uncertainty in a single optimization framework.
summary.tldr: A risk-based Bayesian optimization method searches efficiently for designs that remain reliable across multiple objectives under input noise.

title: Robust Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization Under Input Noise

abstract: This work identifies a common flaw of deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms: a tendency to rely on early interactions and ignore useful evidence encountered later. Because of training on progressively growing datasets, deep RL agents incur a risk of overfitting to earlier experiences, negatively affecting the rest of the learning process. Inspired by cognitive science, we refer to this effect as the primacy bias. Through a series of experiments, we dissect the algorithmic aspects of deep RL that exacerbate this bias. We then propose a simple yet generally-applicable mechanism that tackles the primacy bias by periodically resetting a part of the agent. We apply this mechanism to algorithms in both discrete (Atari 100k) and continuous action (DeepMind Control Suite) domains, consistently improving their performance.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents collect experience as they learn, so early observations can shape how they respond to later evidence. This paper identifies a tendency to over-rely on early interactions and overlook useful information encountered afterward. The authors call this primacy bias and connect it to overfitting earlier experience while training on progressively growing datasets.

Through experiments, the paper examines algorithmic features that worsen the bias. It then proposes a simple mechanism: periodically reset part of the agent. The intervention targets the agent’s continuing dependence on early experience, addressing a learning problem that can persist even as useful new evidence becomes available.

The authors apply partial resetting to algorithms in both discrete-action Atari 100k tasks and continuous-action DeepMind Control Suite tasks, consistently improving performance in those evaluations. The findings identify adaptation to later experience as an important issue in deep reinforcement learning and provide a broadly applicable mechanism to address it. The reported improvements span both action settings, supporting the practical relevance of the diagnosed bias.
summary.tldr: Periodically resetting part of an agent reduces overreliance on early experience and improves performance in the reported reinforcement learning experiments.

title: The Primacy Bias in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider two federated learning algorithms for training partially personalized models, where the shared and personal parameters are updated either simultaneously or alternately on the devices. Both algorithms have been proposed in the literature, but their convergence properties are not fully understood, especially for the alternating variant. We provide convergence analyses of both algorithms in the general nonconvex setting with partial participation and delineate the regime where one dominates the other. Our experiments on real-world image, text, and speech datasets demonstrate that (a) partial personalization can obtain most of the benefits of full model personalization with a small fraction of personal parameters, and, (b) the alternating update algorithm outperforms the simultaneous update algorithm by a small but consistent margin.

paragraphs: Federated learning can combine shared model parameters with parameters tailored to individual devices. This partial personalization offers a middle ground between sharing the entire model and personalizing all of it. The paper studies two existing training approaches for this setting: updating shared and personal parameters simultaneously, or updating them in alternating steps on each device.

Although both approaches were already used, their convergence behavior was incompletely understood, particularly for alternating updates. The authors analyze both in a general nonconvex setting that also allows only some devices to participate. Their theory identifies a regime in which one update strategy has an advantage over the other, giving the comparison a mathematical basis.

Experiments on image, text, and speech datasets show that a small fraction of personal parameters can capture most of the benefits of full personalization. Alternating updates also outperform simultaneous updates by a small but consistent margin in those experiments. Together, these findings support partial personalization as an effective design choice and clarify why the update schedule deserves attention.
summary.tldr: Partial personalization captures much of full personalization's benefit, while analysis and experiments clarify the value of alternating updates.

title: Federated Learning with Partial Model Personalization

abstract: We present unit scaling, a paradigm for designing deep learning models that simplifies the use of low-precision number formats. Training in FP16 or the recently proposed FP8 formats offers substantial efficiency gains, but can lack sufficient range for out-of-the-box training. Unit scaling addresses this by introducing a principled approach to model numerics: seeking unit variance of all weights, activations and gradients at initialisation. Unlike alternative methods, this approach neither requires multiple training runs to find a suitable scale nor has significant computational overhead. We demonstrate the efficacy of unit scaling across a range of models and optimisers. We further show that existing models can be adapted to be unit-scaled, training BERT-Large in FP16 and then FP8 with no degradation in accuracy.

Unit scaling addresses this problem through model design. It seeks to give weights, activations, and gradients unit variance at initialisation, establishing a common numerical scale across these quantities.

The approach makes numerical scaling a principled part of the model rather than requiring repeated training runs to search for an appropriate scale. The authors report that it introduces no significant computational overhead. Its initialisation target is central: the stated design principle concerns the scales present when training begins.

Experiments demonstrate the approach across multiple models and optimisers. The paper also shows that existing architectures can be adapted, with BERT-Large trained in both FP16 and FP8 without loss of accuracy in the reported results. This makes the contribution relevant to adapting established models as well as designing new ones. The findings support unit scaling as a practical way to simplify low-precision training while retaining the efficiency advantages of smaller numerical formats.
summary.tldr: Unit scaling simplifies low-precision training by targeting unit variance at initialisation, with BERT-Large results showing no accuracy degradation in FP16 and FP8.

title: Unit Scaling: Out-of-the-Box Low-Precision Training

abstract: The Schrödinger bridge problem (SBP) is gaining increasing attention in generative modeling and showing promising potential even in comparison with the score-based generative models (SGMs). SBP can be interpreted as an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem, which conducts projections onto every other marginal alternatingly. However, in practice, only approximated projections are accessible and their convergence is not well understood. To fill this gap, we present a first convergence analysis of the Schrödinger bridge algorithm based on approximated projections. As for its practical applications, we apply SBP to probabilistic time series imputation by generating missing values conditioned on observed data. We show that optimizing the transport cost improves the performance and the proposed algorithm achieves the state-of-the-art result in healthcare and environmental data while exhibiting the advantage of exploring both temporal and feature patterns in probabilistic time series imputation.

paragraphs: The Schrödinger bridge problem offers a generative modeling framework based on optimal transport with entropy regularization. Its algorithm alternates projections onto marginal distributions. In practice, these projections are approximations, creating a gap between the ideal procedure and the procedure that can actually be executed.

This paper addresses that gap with a convergence analysis for the Schrödinger bridge algorithm using approximate projections. The distinction matters because understanding an algorithm with exact projections does not by itself explain the behavior of its approximate implementation. The analysis makes approximation part of the convergence question, supporting the use of the framework in practical generative tasks.

The authors apply the method to probabilistic time-series imputation, generating missing values conditional on observed measurements. They show that optimizing the transport cost improves performance and report state-of-the-art results on healthcare and environmental data. The method can exploit patterns across both time and features. These application results complement the convergence contribution by showing how the framework can support conditional generation for incomplete time series.
summary.tldr: A convergence analysis for approximate Schrödinger bridge projections supports a probabilistic time-series imputation method with strong reported results.

title: Provably Convergent Schrödinger Bridge with Applications to Probabilistic Time Series Imputation

abstract: Many state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimization (HPO) algorithms rely on model-based optimizers that learn surrogate models of the target function to guide the search. Gaussian processes are the de facto surrogate model due to their ability to capture uncertainty. However, they make strong assumptions about the observation noise, which might not be warranted in practice. In this work, we propose to leverage conformalized quantile regression which makes minimal assumptions about the observation noise and, as a result, models the target function in a more realistic and robust fashion which translates to quicker HPO convergence on empirical benchmarks. To apply our method in a multi-fidelity setting, we propose a simple, yet effective, technique that aggregates observed results across different resource levels and outperforms conventional methods across many empirical tasks.

Gaussian processes are a common choice, but their assumptions about observation noise may not match practical evaluations. This paper proposes conformalized quantile regression as an alternative surrogate approach.

The method makes minimal assumptions about observation noise, allowing the target function to be modeled more robustly and realistically in the authors' formulation. Its purpose is to improve the information used to choose subsequent evaluations. On empirical benchmarks, the authors report faster hyperparameter-optimization convergence, linking the alternative uncertainty treatment to practical search efficiency.

The paper also extends the approach to multi-fidelity optimization, where evaluations can use different resource levels. A simple aggregation technique combines observations across those levels. The authors report that this technique outperforms conventional methods across many empirical tasks. Together, the contributions address both noisy evaluations and the problem of using results obtained with different computational commitments within one search.
summary.tldr: Conformalized quantile regression guides hyperparameter search with minimal noise assumptions and improves convergence on empirical benchmarks.

title: Optimizing Hyperparameters with Conformal Quantile Regression

abstract: Generative models, especially diffusion models (DMs), have achieved promising results for generating feature-rich geometries and advancing foundational science problems such as molecule design. Inspired by the recent huge success of Stable (latent) Diffusion models, we propose a novel and principled method for 3D molecule generation named Geometric Latent Diffusion Models (GeoLDM). GeoLDM is the first latent DM model for the molecular geometry domain, composed of autoencoders encoding structures into continuous latent codes and DMs operating in the latent space. Our key innovation is that for modeling the 3D molecular geometries, we capture its critical roto-translational equivariance constraints by building a point-structured latent space with both invariant scalars and equivariant tensors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoLDM can consistently achieve better performance on multiple molecule generation benchmarks, with up to 7% improvement for the valid percentage of large biomolecules. Results also demonstrate GeoLDM’s higher capacity for controllable generation thanks to the latent modeling. Code is provided at https://github.com/MinkaiXu/GeoLDM.

paragraphs: Generating three-dimensional molecules requires modeling both molecular features and spatial geometry. GeoLDM brings latent diffusion to this problem: an autoencoder converts molecular structures into continuous codes, and a diffusion model learns to generate within that latent space. The authors present it as the first latent diffusion model for molecular geometry.

The main design challenge is preserving the way geometry behaves under rotations and translations. GeoLDM addresses this with a point-structured latent space containing invariant scalars and equivariant tensors. The scalar components remain unchanged under the relevant transformations, while the tensor components transform consistently with the geometry. This makes spatial symmetry part of the representation used by the generative model.

Across multiple molecule-generation benchmarks, the authors report consistently improved performance, including up to 7% improvement in the valid percentage of large biomolecules. They also report stronger capacity for controllable generation through latent modeling. Together, the results support combining latent-space generation with a representation explicitly designed around the geometric constraints of three-dimensional molecules.
summary.tldr: GeoLDM generates molecules through a geometrically structured latent diffusion model, improving reported validity and controllability.

title: Geometric Latent Diffusion Models for 3D Molecule Generation

abstract: Spatial-temporal graph learning has emerged as the state-of-the-art solution for modeling structured spatial-temporal data in learning region representations for various urban sensing tasks (e.g., crime forecasting, traffic flow prediction). However, most existing models are vulnerable to the quality of the generated region graph due to the inartistic graph-structured information aggregation schema. The ubiquitous spatial-temporal data noise and incompleteness in real-life scenarios bring difficulties to generate high-quality region representations. In this paper, we propose a Spatial-Temporal Adversarial Graph contrastive learning model (STAG) to tackle this challenge for adaptive self-supervised graph augmentation. Specifically, we propose a learnable contrastive learning function that enables the automated distillation of important multi-view self-supervised signals for adaptive spatial-temporal graph augmentation. To enhance the representation discrimination ability and robustness, the designed adversarial contrastive learning mechanism empowers STAG to adaptively identify hard samples for better self-supervision. Finally, a cross-view contrastive learning paradigm is introduced to model the inter-dependencies across view-specific region representations and preserve the underlying relation heterogeneity. We verify the superiority of our STAG method in various spatial-temporal prediction tasks on several benchmark datasets.

Noise and incomplete observations make it difficult to construct reliable region representations, motivating a method that adapts its own self-supervised training signals.

Its adversarial contrastive mechanism identifies hard samples to strengthen self-supervision. These components aim to improve both the ability to distinguish representations and their robustness to imperfect input information.

STAG also compares region representations across views, modeling their dependencies while preserving differences among relationship types. This allows the learning process to use shared information across views without discarding their distinct relational structure. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show superior performance across multiple spatial-temporal prediction tasks. The findings support adapting augmentation and sample difficulty to the data as useful components of graph-based urban representation learning.
summary.tldr: STAG adapts graph augmentation and hard-sample selection through adversarial contrastive learning to improve spatial-temporal prediction.

title: Spatial-Temporal Graph Learning with Adversarial Contrastive Adaptation

abstract: The generalization analysis of deep kernel learning (DKL) is a crucial and open problem of kernel methods for deep learning. The implicit nonlinear mapping in DKL makes existing methods of capacity-based generalization analysis for deep learning invalid. In an attempt to overcome this challenge and make up for the gap in the generalization theory of DKL, we develop an analysis method based on the composite relationship of function classes and derive capacity-based bounds with mild dependence on the depth, which generalizes learning theory bounds to deep kernels and serves as theoretical guarantees for the generalization of DKL. In this paper, we prove novel and nearly-tight generalization bounds based on the uniform covering number and the Rademacher chaos complexity for deep (multiple) kernel machines. In addition, for some common classes, we estimate their uniform covering numbers and Rademacher chaos complexities by bounding their pseudo-dimensions and kernel pseudo-dimensions, respectively. The mild bounds without strong assumptions partially explain the good generalization ability of deep learning combined with kernel methods.

The paper explains that this mapping prevents existing capacity-based analyses for deep learning from applying directly. It develops a different analysis to address that gap in the theory.

The approach uses the way function classes compose to derive bounds on the capacity of deep kernel models. Its main results are nearly tight generalization bounds based on uniform covering numbers and Rademacher chaos complexity. These are mathematical tools for characterizing the richness of the functions a model can represent, and the resulting bounds have only mild dependence on depth.
