The claim is a partial theoretical explanation, rather than a complete account of empirical performance.
summary.tldr: The paper derives nearly tight generalization bounds for deep kernel models with mild dependence on network depth.

title: Nearly-tight Bounds for Deep Kernel Learning

abstract: In an effort to reduce the computational load of Transformers, research on linear attention has gained significant momentum. However, the improvement strategies for attention mechanisms typically necessitate extensive retraining, which is impractical for large language models with a vast array of parameters. In this paper, we present DiJiang, a novel Frequency Domain Kernelization approach that enables the transformation of a pre-trained vanilla Transformer into a linear complexity model with little training costs. By employing a weighted Quasi-Monte Carlo method for sampling, the proposed approach theoretically offers superior approximation efficiency. To further reduce the training computational complexity, our kernelization is based on Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) operations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to the original Transformer, but with significantly reduced training costs and much faster inference speeds. Our DiJiang-7B achieves comparable performance with LLaMA2-7B on various benchmark while requires only about 1/50 training cost. Code is available at https://github.com/YuchuanTian/DiJiang.

paragraphs: Linear attention offers a route to reducing Transformer computation, but changing the attention mechanism can require extensive retraining. That cost is especially consequential for large pretrained language models. DiJiang addresses the conversion problem: adapting an existing standard Transformer into a model with linear complexity while keeping the required training cost low.

The method uses frequency-domain kernelization to approximate the attention computation. Its weighted Quasi-Monte Carlo sampling method comes with a theoretical claim of improved approximation efficiency. Discrete Cosine Transform operations provide the basis for the kernelization, further reducing the computational burden of training. These components connect the quality of the approximation with the cost of obtaining it.

Experiments report performance comparable to the original Transformer alongside substantially lower training costs and faster inference. In particular, DiJiang-7B achieves comparable results to LLaMA2-7B across various benchmarks at about one-fiftieth of the training cost. The reported result supports converting pretrained models efficiently while retaining benchmark performance, rather than requiring the attention redesign to begin with extensive training.
summary.tldr: DiJiang converts pretrained Transformers to linear-complexity models using frequency-domain kernelization, with comparable reported performance and much lower training costs.

title: DiJiang: Efficient Large Language Models through Compact Kernelization

abstract: In response to everyday queries, humans explicitly signal uncertainty and offer alternative answers when they are unsure. Machine learning models that output calibrated prediction sets through conformal prediction mimic this human behaviour; larger sets signal greater uncertainty while providing alternatives. In this work, we study the usefulness of conformal prediction sets as an aid for human decision making by conducting a pre-registered randomized controlled trial with conformal prediction sets provided to human subjects. With statistical significance, we find that when humans are given conformal prediction sets their accuracy on tasks improves compared to fixed-size prediction sets with the same coverage guarantee. The results show that quantifying model uncertainty with conformal prediction is helpful for human-in-the-loop decision making and human-AI teams.

paragraphs: When a model is uncertain, presenting several possible answers can give a person more useful guidance than presenting a single prediction. Conformal prediction produces calibrated sets of possible answers, with larger sets communicating greater uncertainty. This paper tests whether that form of uncertainty communication actually helps people make more accurate decisions.

The authors conduct a pre-registered randomized controlled trial in which human participants receive prediction sets. The comparison is between conformal sets and fixed-size sets with the same coverage guarantee. Matching coverage makes the comparison particularly informative: both forms of assistance provide the same stated guarantee about including the correct answer, while differing in how the alternatives communicate uncertainty.

Participants given conformal prediction sets achieve statistically significantly higher task accuracy. The result supports using calibrated, variable-size answer sets as an aid in human-AI decision making. Its significance is that an uncertainty representation can improve the human’s eventual choice, beyond simply providing a technically meaningful guarantee about the model’s output.
summary.tldr: A randomized trial finds that conformal prediction sets improve human accuracy compared with fixed-size sets offering the same coverage guarantee.

title: Conformal Prediction Sets Improve Human Decision Making

abstract: Offline optimization is an important task in numerous material engineering domains where online experimentation to collect data is too expensive and needs to be replaced by an in silico maximization of a surrogate of the black-box function. Although such a surrogate can be learned from offline data, its prediction might not be reliable outside the offline data regime, which happens when the surrogate has narrow prediction margin and is (therefore) sensitive to small perturbations of its parameterization. This raises the following questions: (1) how to regulate the sensitivity of a surrogate model; and (2) whether conditioning an offline optimizer with such less sensitive surrogate will lead to better optimization performance. To address these questions, we develop an optimizable sensitivity measurement for the surrogate model, which then inspires a sensitivity-informed regularizer that is applicable to a wide range of offline optimizers. This development is both orthogonal and synergistic to prior research on offline optimization, which is demonstrated in our extensive experiment benchmark.

paragraphs: Offline optimization searches for promising designs using an existing dataset, often because new physical experiments are expensive. A learned surrogate predicts the value of candidate designs and guides the search. The difficulty is that optimization can move beyond the region covered by the data, where those predictions may become unreliable.

This paper focuses on sensitivity to small changes in the surrogate's parameters. The authors connect a narrow prediction margin with this sensitivity and ask whether making the surrogate less sensitive can improve optimization. They develop a sensitivity measure that can itself be optimized, then use it to construct a regularizer for guiding surrogate learning.

The regularizer can be applied to a wide range of offline optimizers, making it a component that can complement existing approaches. Extensive benchmark experiments demonstrate that the sensitivity-based development works synergistically with prior methods. Its significance is to make surrogate sensitivity an explicit optimization concern, alongside the broader problem of finding high-value candidates from a fixed body of observations.
summary.tldr: A sensitivity-based regularizer improves offline optimization by helping control how surrogate predictions respond to parameter perturbations.

title: Boosting Offline Optimizers with Surrogate Sensitivity

abstract: While self-supervised learning (SSL) in speech has greatly reduced the reliance of speech processing systems on annotated corpora, the success of SSL still hinges on the availability of a large-scale unannotated corpus, which is still often impractical for many low-resource languages or under privacy concerns. Some existing work seeks to alleviate the problem by data augmentation, but most works are confined to introducing perturbations to real speech and do not introduce new variations in speech prosody, speakers, and speech content, which are important for SSL. Motivated by the recent finding that diffusion models have superior capabilities for modeling data distributions, we propose DiffS4L, a pretraining scheme that augments the limited unannotated data with synthetic data with different levels of variations, generated by a diffusion model trained on the limited unannotated data. Finally, an SSL model is pre-trained on the real and the synthetic speech. Our experiments show that DiffS4L can significantly improve the performance of SSL models, such as reducing the WER of the HuBERT pretrained model by 6.26 percentage points in the English ASR task. Notably, we find that the synthetic speech with all levels of variations, i.e. new prosody, new speakers, and even new content (despite the new content being mostly babble), accounts for significant performance improvement. The code is available at github.com/Hertin/DiffS4L.

Such data can be difficult to obtain for low-resource languages or under privacy concerns. Conventional augmentation often perturbs existing recordings without adding new speakers, prosody, or content, leaving important kinds of variation unexplored.

DiffS4L trains a diffusion model on the limited available unlabeled speech, then uses it to generate synthetic audio with different levels of variation. A speech model is subsequently pretrained on both the original recordings and the generated examples. The approach uses synthesis to broaden the material available for self-supervised learning.

Experiments report significant gains, including a 6.26-percentage-point reduction in word error rate for a HuBERT-pretrained model on an English speech-recognition task. The authors also find that synthetic audio varying prosody, speakers, and content contributes substantially to improvement, even though the new content is mostly babble. This suggests that useful pretraining variation can extend beyond recordings containing coherent new linguistic content.
summary.tldr: DiffS4L improves speech self-supervised learning by supplementing limited recordings with diffusion-generated audio containing new acoustic and content variation.

title: Speech Self-Supervised Learning Using Diffusion Model Synthetic Data

abstract: Modern deep learning models are usually highly over-parameterized so that they can overfit the training data. Surprisingly, such overfitting neural networks can usually still achieve high prediction accuracy. To study this “benign overfitting” phenomenon, a line of recent works has theoretically studied the learning of linear models and two-layer neural networks. However, most of these analyses are still limited to the very simple learning problems where the Bayes-optimal classifier is linear. In this work, we investigate a class of XOR-type classification tasks with label-flipping noises. We show that, under a certain condition on the sample complexity and signal-to-noise ratio, an over-parameterized ReLU CNN trained by gradient descent can achieve near Bayes-optimal accuracy. Moreover, we also establish a matching lower bound result showing that when the previous condition is not satisfied, the prediction accuracy of the obtained CNN is an absolute constant away from the Bayes-optimal rate. Our result demonstrates that CNNs have a remarkable capacity to efficiently learn XOR problems, even in the presence of highly correlated features.

paragraphs: A neural network can fit its training examples extremely closely and still predict new examples accurately. This phenomenon, called benign overfitting, challenges the idea that fitting training data too well necessarily harms generalization. The paper studies it in XOR-type classification problems with randomly flipped labels, moving beyond earlier analyses centered on problems whose best possible classifier is linear.

The authors analyze an overparameterized, two-layer ReLU convolutional neural network trained with gradient descent. They establish a condition involving the number of training examples and the signal-to-noise ratio under which the network approaches Bayes-optimal accuracy: the best accuracy permitted by the underlying data distribution. The result therefore connects successful learning to both the amount and quality of available information.

A matching lower bound establishes the other side of this condition. When it fails, the trained network remains a fixed positive amount below Bayes-optimal accuracy. Together, the results characterize a boundary between successful and unsuccessful learning in the studied setting, including XOR problems with strongly correlated features.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies when an overparameterized ReLU CNN can learn noisy XOR data nearly optimally, and proves a matching failure boundary.

title: Benign Overfitting in Two-Layer ReLU Convolutional Neural Networks for XOR Data

abstract: Temporal distances lie at the heart of many algorithms for planning, control, and reinforcement learning that involve reaching goals, allowing one to estimate the transit time between two states. However, prior attempts to define such temporal distances in stochastic settings have been stymied by an important limitation: these prior approaches do not satisfy the triangle inequality. This is not merely a definitional concern, but translates to an inability to generalize and find shortest paths. In this paper, we build on prior work in contrastive learning and quasimetrics to show how successor features learned by contrastive learning (after a change of variables) form a temporal distance that does satisfy the triangle inequality, even in stochastic settings. Importantly, this temporal distance is computationally efficient to estimate, even in high-dimensional and stochastic settings. Experiments in controlled settings and benchmark suites demonstrate that an RL algorithm based on these new temporal distances exhibits combinatorial generalization (i.e., "stitching") and can sometimes learn more quickly than prior methods, including those based on quasimetrics.

paragraphs: Goal-directed planning depends on estimating how long it takes to travel between states. In stochastic environments, earlier definitions of temporal distance can violate the triangle inequality. That property relates a direct distance to the distance of a route through an intermediate state, making its absence relevant to shortest-path reasoning and generalization.

The paper shows that successor features learned through contrastive learning can define a temporal distance satisfying the triangle inequality after a change of variables. The result holds even in stochastic settings. The resulting distance is also computationally efficient to estimate in high-dimensional environments, connecting a useful mathematical property with a learnable representation.

Experiments in controlled settings and benchmark suites evaluate a reinforcement learning algorithm built around these distances. It demonstrates combinatorial generalization, described as stitching together behavior, and sometimes learns faster than earlier methods, including methods based on quasimetrics. The findings support the usefulness of the distance construction without asserting a universal learning-speed advantage.
summary.tldr: Contrastively learned successor features yield an efficient temporal distance satisfying the triangle inequality, supporting demonstrated behavioral stitching.

title: Learning Temporal Distances: Contrastive Successor Features Can Provide a Metric Structure for Decision-Making

abstract: We study how to make decisions that minimize Bayesian regret in offline linear bandits. Prior work suggests that one must take actions with maximum lower confidence bound (LCB) on their reward. We argue that reliance on LCB is inherently flawed in this setting and propose a new algorithm that directly minimizes upper-bounds on the Bayesian regret using efficient conic optimization solvers. Our bounds build heavily on new connections to monetary risk measures. Proving a matching lower-bound, we show that our upper-bounds are tight, and by minimizing them we are guaranteed to outperform the LCB approach. Our numerical results on synthetic domains confirm that our approach is superior to maximizing LCB.

paragraphs: This paper studies choosing actions in offline linear bandits, where decisions must be made using already available information. Its objective is Bayesian regret: the expected loss from choosing an action instead of the best one, accounting for uncertainty. The authors question a common prescription that selects whichever action has the largest lower confidence bound on reward.

They propose optimizing a quantity directly tied to the desired objective. Their algorithm minimizes upper bounds on Bayesian regret using efficient conic optimization solvers. The derivation connects these regret bounds to monetary risk measures, bringing tools for reasoning about uncertain financial outcomes into the analysis of uncertain action rewards.

A matching lower bound establishes tightness of the proposed upper bounds. The authors use this result to guarantee an advantage over the lower-confidence-bound approach in their setting. Numerical experiments on synthetic domains also favor the proposed method. Together, the theoretical and numerical findings support targeting Bayesian regret directly when choosing actions in this offline problem.
summary.tldr: Directly optimizing tight Bayesian regret bounds provides a theoretically supported alternative to lower-confidence-bound action selection in offline linear bandits.

title: Bayesian Regret Minimization in Offline Bandits

abstract: Distributed LLM serving is costly and often underutilizes hardware accelerators due to three key challenges: bubbles in pipeline-parallel deployments caused by the bimodal latency of prompt and token processing, GPU memory overprovisioning, and long recovery times in case of failures. DéjàVu addresses all these challenges using a versatile and efficient KV cache streaming library (DéjàVuLib). Using DéjàVuLib, we propose and implement efficient prompt-token disaggregation to reduce pipeline bubbles, microbatch swapping for efficient GPU memory management, and state replication for fault-tolerance. We highlight the efficacy of these solutions on a range of large models across cloud deployments.

paragraphs: Serving large language models across multiple devices can leave expensive accelerators underused. The paper identifies three sources of inefficiency: prompt processing and token generation have different latency patterns, GPU memory is overprovisioned, and failures can require lengthy recovery. In pipeline-parallel deployments, the processing mismatch creates idle gaps that reduce useful hardware work.

DéjàVu addresses these problems through DéjàVuLib, a library for efficiently streaming the model’s key-value cache. The cache holds state used during generation, making its movement relevant to both execution and recovery. The system uses the library to separate prompt processing from token processing, swap microbatches for memory management, and replicate state for fault tolerance.

Each mechanism targets a different operational cost. Separating processing stages reduces pipeline gaps, swapping helps manage GPU memory efficiently, and replication supports recovery after failures. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of these solutions across a range of large models in cloud deployments. The unifying contribution is a reusable cache-streaming facility that supports several improvements to distributed serving within the same system.
summary.tldr: DéjàVu uses KV-cache streaming to improve distributed LLM utilization, memory management, and recovery from failures.

title: DéjàVu: KV-cache Streaming for Fast, Fault-tolerant Generative LLM Serving

abstract: Distributed execution of deep learning training involves a dynamic interplay between hardware accelerator architecture and device placement strategy. This is the first work to explore the co-optimization of determining the optimal architecture and device placement strategy through novel algorithms, improving the balance of computational resources, memory usage, and data distribution. Our architecture search leverages tensor and vector units, determining their quantity and dimensionality, and on-chip and off-chip memory configurations. It also determines the microbatch size and decides whether to recompute or stash activations, balancing the memory footprint of training and storage size. For each explored architecture configuration, we use an Integer Linear Program (ILP) to find the optimal schedule for executing operators on the accelerator. The ILP results then integrate with a dynamic programming solution to identify the most effective device placement strategy, combining data, pipeline, and tensor model parallelism across multiple accelerators. Our approach achieves higher throughput on large language models compared to the state-of-the-art TPUv4 and the Spotlight accelerator search framework. The entire source code of PHAZE is available at https://github.com/msr-fiddle/phaze.

These choices interact because computational capacity, memory, and data distribution all affect execution. The paper treats hardware architecture and placement as a combined optimization problem, allowing decisions on one side to inform the other.

The hardware search varies the number and dimensions of tensor and vector units, along with on-chip and off-chip memory. It also chooses microbatch size and whether activations should be stored or recomputed. This connects individual-accelerator execution to the organization of training across multiple accelerators. The authors report higher throughput on large language models than TPUv4 and the Spotlight accelerator-search framework, supporting the value of coordinating architecture design with distributed execution choices.
summary.tldr: PHAZE co-optimizes accelerator architecture, execution scheduling, and device placement to improve distributed language-model training throughput.

title: Integrated Hardware Architecture and Device Placement Search

abstract: Minimax optimization is fundamental and important for enormous machine learning applications such as generative adversarial network, adversarial training, and robust optimization. Recently, a variety of minimax algorithms with theoretical guarantees based on Lipschitz smoothness have been proposed. However, these algorithms could fail to converge in practice because the requisite Lipschitz smooth condition may not hold even in some classic minimax problems. We will present some counterexamples to reveal this divergence issue. Thus, to fill this gap, we are motivated to delve into the convergence analysis of minimax algorithms under a relaxed Lipschitz smoothness condition, i.e., generalized smoothness. We prove that variants of basic minimax optimization algorithms GDA, SGDA, GDmax and SGDmax can still converge in generalized smooth problems, and hence their theoretical guarantees can be extended to a wider range of applications. We also conduct a numerical experiment to validate the performance of our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves objectives in which one side minimizes while another maximizes. It appears in adversarial training, generative adversarial networks, and robust optimization. Many convergence guarantees for its algorithms assume Lipschitz smoothness, a restriction on how sharply gradients can change. This paper examines what happens when that restriction does not hold.

The authors provide counterexamples showing that existing algorithms can diverge when their smoothness requirement fails, even in some classic minimax problems. They then analyze a relaxed condition called generalized smoothness. Under this setting, they prove convergence for variants of GDA, SGDA, GDmax, and SGDmax, extending the reach of guarantees associated with these basic optimization approaches.

A numerical experiment also evaluates the proposed algorithms. The main contribution is theoretical: it connects convergence analysis to a broader class of objectives than the usual smoothness assumption permits. The result concerns the analyzed algorithm variants in generalized-smooth problems, so it does not imply that arbitrary minimax procedures converge without structural conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves convergence for variants of basic minimax algorithms under generalized smoothness, beyond the usual Lipschitz-smooth setting.

title: Delving into the Convergence of Generalized Smooth Minimax Optimization

abstract: Recent text-to-image generative models have demonstrated remarkable abilities in generating realistic images. Despite their great success, these models struggle to generate high-fidelity images with prompts oriented toward human-object interaction (HOI). The difficulty in HOI generation arises from two aspects. Firstly, the complexity and diversity of human poses challenge plausible human generation. Furthermore, untrustworthy generation of interaction boundary regions may lead to deficiency in HOI semantics. To tackle the problems, we propose a Semantic-Aware HOI generation framework SA-HOI . It utilizes human pose quality and interaction boundary region information as guidance for denoising process, thereby encouraging refinement in these regions to produce more reasonable HOI images. Based on it, we establish an iterative inversion and image refinement pipeline to continually enhance generation quality. Further, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for HOI generation, which comprises a dataset involving diverse and fine-grained HOI categories, along with multiple custom-tailored evaluation metrics for HOI generation. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves generation quality under both HOI-specific and conventional image evaluation metrics. The code is available at https://github.com/XZPKU/SA-HOI.git

Despite their great success, these models struggle to generate high-fidelity images with prompts oriented toward human-object interaction (HOI). The difficulty in HOI generation arises from two aspects. Firstly, the complexity and diversity of human poses challenge plausible human generation. Furthermore, untrustworthy generation of interaction boundary regions may lead to deficiency in HOI semantics. To tackle the problems, we propose a Semantic-Aware HOI generation framework SA-HOI . It utilizes human pose quality and interaction boundary region information as guidance for denoising process, thereby encouraging refinement in these regions to produce more reasonable HOI images. Based on it, we establish an iterative inversion and image refinement pipeline to continually enhance generation quality. Further, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for HOI generation, which comprises a dataset involving diverse and fine-grained HOI categories, along with multiple custom-tailored evaluation metrics for HOI generation. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves generation quality under both HOI-specific and conventional image evaluation metrics. The code is available at https://github.com/XZPKU/SA-HOI.git

paragraphs: An image can look realistic overall while depicting an implausible interaction between a person and an object. This paper identifies two particular difficulties for text-to-image models: generating complex human poses and correctly rendering the boundary regions where people and objects interact. Errors in those regions can undermine the intended meaning of the scene.

SA-HOI guides the denoising process using information about human-pose quality and interaction boundaries. This encourages refinement in the areas most relevant to a plausible interaction. The authors also build an iterative inversion and image-refinement pipeline, allowing the generated image to be revisited and improved through successive processing.

To evaluate the task, the paper introduces a benchmark containing diverse, fine-grained interaction categories and evaluation metrics designed specifically for human-object interaction generation. Experiments show significant improvements under both these specialized metrics and conventional image-quality metrics. The findings support targeting interaction structure during generation and evaluating whether a scene expresses the requested action, alongside assessing its general visual quality.
summary.tldr: SA-HOI guides image refinement with pose and interaction-boundary information, improving human-object interaction generation under specialized and conventional metrics.

title: Semantic-Aware Human Object Interaction Image Generation

abstract: There is a growing interest in the ability of neural networks to execute algorithmic tasks (e.g., arithmetic, summary statistics, and sorting). The goal of this work is to better understand the role of attention in Transformers for algorithmic execution. Its importance for algorithmic execution has been studied theoretically and empirically using parallel computational models. Notably, many parallel algorithms communicate between processors solely using positional information. Inspired by this observation, we investigate how Transformers can execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings. We prove that Transformers with positional attention (positional Transformers) maintain the same expressivity of parallel computational models, incurring a logarithmic depth cost relative to the input length. We analyze their in-distribution learnability and explore how parameter norms in positional attention affect sample complexity. Our results show that positional Transformers introduce a learning trade-off: while they exhibit better theoretical dependence on parameter norms, certain tasks may require more layers, which can, in turn, increase sample complexity. Finally, we empirically explore the out-of-distribution performance of positional Transformers and find that they perform well in tasks where their underlying algorithmic solution relies on positional information.

paragraphs: Transformers can be studied as systems that execute algorithms such as sorting or arithmetic. This paper examines attention whose weights depend entirely on position encodings. The motivation comes from parallel algorithms in which processors decide where to communicate using positional information, without basing that communication on the contents being processed.

The authors prove that positional Transformers retain the expressivity of the parallel computational models considered, with a depth overhead logarithmic in input length. They also analyze learning within the training distribution, focusing on how attention parameter norms affect sample complexity. Positional attention gives better theoretical dependence on those norms, but some tasks require additional layers.

Those extra layers can increase sample complexity, creating a trade-off between the benefits of positional attention and the depth needed to express an algorithm. The results tie the usefulness of this attention design to algorithm structure, rather than establishing a universal learning advantage.

title: Positional Attention: Expressivity and Learnability of Algorithmic Computation

abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to share graph knowledge across diverse domains and tasks to boost graph machine learning. However, existing GFMs rely on hand-designed and fixed graph neural network (GNN) architectures, failing to utilize optimal architectures w.r.t. specific domains and tasks, inevitably leading to suboptimal performance in diverse graph domains and tasks. In this paper, we explore graph neural architecture search (GNAS) for GFMs for the first time, which suffers from the problem of architecture inconsistency, i.e., the optimal architectures for different tasks and domains vary. We tackle this problem by discovering an invariant graph-architecture relationship across domains and tasks, which imposes three challenges: i) how to capture invariant and variant patterns; ii) how to customize architectures to adapt to diverse domains and tasks; iii) how to mitigate the data domination phenomenon during the architecture search process. To address these challenges, we propose Automated Graph Foundation Model with Adaptive Architecture Customization (AutoGFM), providing a theoretical analysis to demonstrate the limitations of existing GNAS. Specifically, we first propose a disentangled contrastive graph encoder to learn invariant and variant patterns. Then, we design an invariant-guided architecture customization strategy to customize architectures for data from diverse domains and tasks. Finally, we propose a curriculum architecture customization mechanism to mitigate the phenomenon of particular data dominating the search process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AutoGFM outperforms baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

AutoGFM addresses the possibility that different tasks and domains need different architectures. This creates an architecture search problem: a design that works well for one setting may not be the best choice elsewhere.

The method seeks a relationship between graphs and architectures that remains useful across settings. A disentangled contrastive encoder learns both patterns that persist across domains and patterns that vary. An architecture customization strategy then uses the invariant information to guide adaptation. A curriculum mechanism also reduces the tendency for particular data to dominate the search.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of limitations in existing graph architecture search and reports that AutoGFM outperforms baselines, reaching state-of-the-art performance in its experiments. Its contribution is to make architecture selection part of transferring graph knowledge. Instead of depending entirely on a single fixed design, the framework learns information that guides architecture customization across diverse tasks and domains.
summary.tldr: AutoGFM adapts graph foundation model architectures across domains and tasks using learned graph patterns and curriculum-guided search.

title: AutoGFM: Automated Graph Foundation Model with Adaptive Architecture Customization

abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models have led to impressive progress in caption generation for images and short video clips. However, these models remain constrained by their limited temporal receptive fields, making it difficult to produce coherent and comprehensive captions for long videos. While several methods have been proposed to aggregate information across video segments, they often rely on supervised fine-tuning or incur significant computational overhead. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework for long video captioning based on graph consolidation. Our approach first generates segment-level captions, corresponding to individual frames or short video intervals, using off-the-shelf visual captioning models. These captions are then parsed into individual scene graphs, which are subsequently consolidated into a unified graph representation that preserves both holistic context and fine-grained details throughout the video. A lightweight graph-to-text decoder then produces the final video-level caption. This framework effectively extends the temporal understanding capabilities of existing models without requiring any additional fine-tuning on long video datasets. Experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms existing LLM-based consolidation approaches, achieving strong zero-shot performance while substantially reducing computational costs.

paragraphs: Models that caption images and short clips can struggle to describe long videos coherently because they observe only limited spans of time. This paper addresses the problem by combining descriptions from short segments into a structured representation of the whole video. The aim is to retain both the broad context and details that could be lost during aggregation.

The pipeline first uses existing visual captioning models to describe individual frames or short intervals. It converts those descriptions into scene graphs, then consolidates the graphs into one unified representation. A lightweight graph-to-text decoder produces the final caption from that representation. The graph serves as the intermediate structure connecting local observations with a video-level description.

The framework requires no additional fine-tuning on long-video datasets, extending the usefulness of existing captioning models. Experiments report significantly better results than existing LLM-based consolidation approaches, strong zero-shot performance, and substantially lower computational costs. These findings support structured graph consolidation as an effective way to assemble detailed long-video captions from shorter observations.
summary.tldr: Consolidating short-segment scene graphs produces detailed long-video captions without additional long-video fine-tuning and with lower reported computational costs.

title: Fine-Grained Captioning of Long Videos through Scene Graph Consolidation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable advancements in enabling language agents to tackle simple tasks. However, applying them for complex, multi-step, long-horizon tasks remains a challenge. Recent work have found success by separating high-level planning from low-level execution, which enables the model to effectively balance high-level planning objectives and low-level execution details. However, generating accurate plans remains difficult since LLMs are not inherently trained for this task. To address this, we propose Plan-and-Act, a novel framework that incorporates explicit planning into LLM-based agents and introduces a scalable method to enhance plan generation through a novel synthetic data generation method. Plan-and-Act consists of a Planner model which generates structured, high-level plans to achieve user goals, and an Executor model that translates these plans into environment-specific actions. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce a synthetic data generation method that annotates ground-truth trajectories with feasible plans, augmented with diverse and extensive examples to enhance generalization. We evaluate Plan-and-Act using web navigation as a representative long-horizon planning environment, demonstrating a state-of-the-art 57.58% success rate on the WebArena-Lite benchmark as well as a text-only state-of-the-art 81.36% success rate on WebVoyager.

paragraphs: Language agents can struggle with tasks that require many coordinated steps. Separating high-level planning from detailed execution helps organize that work, but a language model still needs to learn how to produce useful plans. Plan-and-Act addresses both the division of responsibilities and the training data needed to improve planning.

summary.tldr: Plan-and-Act trains a dedicated planner with synthetic plan annotations and pairs it with an executor to improve long-horizon web navigation.

title: Plan-and-Act: Improving Planning of Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks

abstract: Training large language models to predict beyond their training context lengths has drawn much attention in recent years, yet the principles driving such behavior of length generalization remain underexplored. We propose a new theoretical framework to study length generalization for the next-token prediction task, as performed by decoder-only transformers. Conceptually, we show that length generalization occurs as long as each predicted token depends on a small (fixed) number of previous tokens. We formalize such tasks via a notion we call k-sparse planted correlation distributions, and show that an idealized model of transformers which generalize attention heads successfully length-generalize on such tasks. As a bonus, our theoretical model allows us to provide justifications for techniques to modify positional embeddings which have been introduced to improve length generalization, such as position coupling. We support our theoretical results with experiments on synthetic tasks and natural language, which confirm that a key factor driving length generalization is indeed a “sparse” dependency structure of each token on the previous ones. Further, inspired by our theory, we introduce Predictive Position Coupling, a generalization of position coupling which trains the transformer to predict the position IDs used in a positional coupling approach. Predictive Position Coupling thereby allows us to broaden the array of tasks to which Position Coupling can successfully be applied to achieve length generalization.

paragraphs: Length generalization means predicting successfully beyond the context lengths encountered during training. This paper studies that behavior for next-token prediction in decoder-only transformers. Its central theoretical insight is a sufficient condition: generalization can occur when each predicted token depends on only a small, fixed number of earlier tokens.

The authors formalize this structure using k-sparse planted correlation distributions. They show that an idealized transformer model with generalized attention heads length-generalizes on such tasks. The framework also supplies theoretical justification for positional-embedding modifications such as position coupling. Experiments on synthetic tasks and natural language support sparse token dependencies as a key factor in length generalization.

This trains the transformer to predict the position identifiers used by a position-coupling approach, broadening the set of tasks where that technique can successfully support longer contexts. The contribution connects a structured theoretical condition with an empirical finding and a practical modification to positional information, without making sparsity a necessary condition for every form of length generalization.
summary.tldr: Sparse token dependencies provide a theoretical route to length generalization and motivate a learned extension of position coupling.

title: The Role of Sparsity for Length Generalization in LLMs

abstract: Recent advancements have significantly enhanced the performance of large language models (LLMs) in tackling complex reasoning tasks, achieving notable success in domains like mathematical and logical reasoning. However, these methods encounter challenges with complex planning tasks, primarily due to extended reasoning steps, diverse constraints, and the challenge of handling multiple distinct sub-tasks. To address these challenges, we propose HyperTree Planning (HTP), a novel reasoning paradigm that constructs hypertree-structured planning outlines for effective planning. The hypertree structure enables LLMs to engage in hierarchical thinking by flexibly employing the divide-and-conquer strategy, effectively breaking down intricate reasoning steps, accommodating diverse constraints, and managing multiple distinct sub-tasks in a well-organized manner. We further introduce an autonomous planning framework that completes the planning process by iteratively refining and expanding the hypertree-structured planning outlines. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of HTP, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the TravelPlanner benchmark with Gemini-1.5-Pro, resulting in a 3.6$\times$ performance improvement over o1-preview.

paragraphs: Complex planning requires a language model to manage long reasoning sequences, multiple constraints, and distinct subtasks. Success in mathematical or logical reasoning does not automatically resolve those organizational demands. HyperTree Planning addresses them by giving the planning process an explicit hierarchical outline.

The outline uses a hypertree structure to support flexible divide-and-conquer reasoning. Complicated steps can be broken into smaller parts while constraints and different subtasks remain organized within the overall plan. The authors also introduce an autonomous framework that repeatedly refines and expands these outlines, making the hierarchy an evolving part of planning rather than a single preliminary sketch.

On TravelPlanner, the framework paired with Gemini-1.5-Pro achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and a reported 3.6-fold performance improvement over o1-preview. This result supports the usefulness of hierarchical organization for the evaluated planning task. The contribution links an explicit representation of the plan with an iterative process for developing it, helping the model manage several planning requirements within a coordinated structure.
summary.tldr: HyperTree Planning iteratively develops hierarchical outlines, achieving a reported 3.6-fold improvement over o1-preview on TravelPlanner with Gemini-1.5-Pro.

title: HyperTree Planning: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Hierarchical Thinking

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated exceptional performances in various fields of generative modeling, but suffer from slow sampling speed due to their iterative nature. While this issue is being addressed in continuous domains, discrete diffusion models face unique challenges, particularly in capturing dependencies between elements (e.g., pixel relationships in image, sequential dependencies in language) mainly due to the computational cost of processing high-dimensional joint distributions. In this paper, (i) we propose "mixture" models for discrete diffusion that are capable of treating dimensional correlations while remaining scalable, and (ii) we provide a set of loss functions for distilling the iterations of existing models. Two primary theoretical insights underpin our approach: First, conventional models with element-wise independence can well approximate the data distribution, but essentially require many sampling steps. Second, our loss functions enable the mixture models to distill such many-step conventional models into just a few steps by learning the dimensional correlations. Our experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method in distilling pretrained discrete diffusion models across image and language domains. The code used in the paper is available at https://github.com/sony/di4c.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models generate data through repeated sampling steps, which makes generation slow. Speeding them up requires handling relationships among discrete elements, such as image pixels or positions in a language sequence. Modeling those relationships directly through a high-dimensional joint distribution is computationally costly, creating a challenge for reducing the number of steps.

The paper proposes scalable mixture models that capture correlations across dimensions, together with loss functions for distilling existing diffusion models. Its theoretical analysis explains why conventional models that treat elements independently can still approximate the data distribution well, but essentially need many sampling steps. The proposed losses let mixture models learn the correlations needed to compress that longer process into a few steps.

Experiments demonstrate the approach on pretrained discrete diffusion models for both images and language. The findings connect faster sampling to the model’s ability to represent dependencies between elements. Learning these dependencies gives the distilled model a way to carry out in fewer iterations what the conventional model achieves through a longer sequence.
summary.tldr: Scalable mixture models learn correlations between discrete elements to distill many-step diffusion models into few-step generators.

title: Distillation of Discrete Diffusion through Dimensional Correlations

abstract: Adaptive moment estimation (Adam) is a cornerstone optimization algorithm in deep learning, widely recognized for its flexibility with adaptive learning rates and efficiency in handling large-scale data. However, despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of Adam’s convergence has been constrained by stringent assumptions, such as almost surely bounded stochastic gradients or uniformly bounded gradients, which are more restrictive than those typically required for analyzing stochastic gradient descent (SGD). In this paper, we introduce a novel and comprehensive framework for analyzing the convergence properties of Adam. This framework offers a versatile approach to establishing Adam’s convergence. Specifically, we prove that Adam achieves asymptotic (last iterate sense) convergence in both the almost sure sense and the $L_1$ sense under the relaxed assumptions typically used for SGD, namely $L$-smoothness and the ABC inequality. Meanwhile, under the same assumptions, we show that Adam attains non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds similar to those of SGD.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used to train neural networks, but its theoretical guarantees have often required stronger assumptions than those used for stochastic gradient descent, or SGD. This paper develops a framework for analyzing Adam under less restrictive conditions, narrowing the gap between the optimizer’s practical importance and what convergence theory can establish.

The analysis uses L-smoothness and the ABC inequality, assumptions commonly used in studying SGD. Under these conditions, the authors prove asymptotic convergence for Adam’s last iterate: the guarantee concerns the evolving endpoint of optimization. They establish convergence both almost surely and in the L1 sense, providing two mathematical ways of characterizing the limiting behavior.

The framework also provides non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds similar to SGD’s under the same assumptions. These bounds address progress with finite samples, complementing the results about eventual convergence. The contribution is therefore a broader theoretical foundation for Adam, rather than an empirical claim that it always trains faster or produces better models than SGD.
summary.tldr: A new analysis establishes Adam’s convergence and SGD-like sample complexity under assumptions typically used for SGD.

title: A Comprehensive Framework for Analyzing the Convergence of Adam: Bridging the Gap with SGD

abstract: The effectiveness of scaling up training data in robotic manipulation is still limited. A primary challenge in manipulation is the tasks are diverse, and the trained policy would be confused if the task targets are not specified clearly. Existing works primarily rely on text instruction to describe targets. However, we reveal that current robotic data cannot train policies to understand text instruction effectively, and vision is much more comprehensible. Therefore, we introduce utilizing vision instruction to specify targets. A straightforward implementation is training a policy to predict the intermediate actions linking the current observation and a future image. Nevertheless, a single future image does not describe the task target in insufficient detail. To handle this problem, we propose to use sparse point flows to provide more detailed information. Extensive tasks are designed based on real and simulated environments to evaluate the effectiveness of our vision instructed pre-training (VIP) method. The results indicate VIP improves the performance on diverse tasks significantly, and the derived policy can complete competitive tasks like “opening the lid of a tightly sealed bottle”.

This paper finds that the robotic data studied is insufficient for learning effective understanding of text instructions, while visual instructions are more comprehensible to the policy.

Vision Instructed Pre-training, or VIP, uses visual information to specify task targets. A straightforward version would predict the actions connecting a current observation to a future image. The authors identify insufficient target detail in a single future image and instead use sparse point flows to supply richer information about the desired progression.

The method is evaluated across tasks in both simulated and real environments. The results show significant performance improvements across diverse tasks, and the resulting policy can perform challenging manipulation such as opening a tightly sealed bottle lid. The contribution emphasizes target specification as an important part of making varied robotic training data useful.
summary.tldr: VIP uses visual instructions enriched with sparse point flows to clarify manipulation targets and improve performance across diverse robotic tasks.

title: VIP: Vision Instructed Pre-training for Robotic Manipulation

abstract: The in-context learning paradigm with LLMs has been instrumental in advancing a wide range of natural language processing tasks. The selection of few-shot examples (exemplars / demonstration samples) is essential for constructing effective prompts under context-length budget constraints. In this paper, we formulate the exemplar selection task as a top-m best arms identification problem. A key challenge in this setup is the exponentially large number of arms that need to be evaluated to identify the m-best arms. We propose CASE (Challenger Arm Sampling for Exemplar selection), a novel sample-efficient selective exploration strategy that maintains a shortlist of “challenger” arms, which are current candidates for the top-m arms. In each iteration, only one of the arms from this shortlist or the current top-m set is pulled, thereby reducing sample complexity and, consequently, the number of LLM evaluations. Furthermore, we model the scores of exemplar subsets (arms) using a parameterized linear scoring function, leading to stochastic linear bandits setting. CASE achieves remarkable efficiency gains of up to 7$\times$ speedup in runtime while requiring 7$\times$ fewer LLM calls (87% reduction) without sacrificing performance compared to state-of-the-art exemplar selection methods. We release our code and data (https://github.com/kiranpurohit/CASE).

Furthermore, we model the scores of exemplar subsets (arms) using a parameterized linear scoring function, leading to stochastic linear bandits setting. CASE achieves remarkable efficiency gains of up to 7$\times$ speedup in runtime while requiring 7$\times$ fewer LLM calls (87% reduction) without sacrificing performance compared to state-of-the-art exemplar selection methods. We release our code and data (https://github.com/kiranpurohit/CASE).

paragraphs: Choosing examples for a language-model prompt matters because the context budget permits only a limited selection. Searching over example subsets is expensive: the number of possible subsets grows exponentially, and evaluating candidates requires model calls. This paper formulates the task as identifying the best m arms in a bandit problem, with example subsets serving as arms.

The proposed CASE algorithm keeps a shortlist of challengers that could enter the current top-m set. At each iteration, it evaluates just one candidate from that shortlist or the current leading set. This selective exploration concentrates evaluations on relevant contenders. A parameterized linear scoring function models subset scores, placing the approach in a stochastic linear bandit setting.

The authors report up to sevenfold runtime speedups and sevenfold fewer language-model calls, described as an 87% reduction, without sacrificing performance relative to state-of-the-art selection methods. The result concerns the cost of finding effective demonstrations, making prompt construction itself more efficient. CASE’s contribution is to organize that search around a changing pool of plausible winners instead of broadly evaluating the enormous candidate space.
summary.tldr: CASE selectively evaluates promising demonstration subsets, achieving up to sevenfold faster selection with sevenfold fewer language-model calls.

title: Sample Efficient Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning

abstract: We introduce Flat Hilbert Bayesian Inference (FHBI), an algorithm designed to enhance generalization in Bayesian inference. Our approach involves an iterative two-step procedure with an adversarial functional perturbation step and a functional descent step within the reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This methodology is supported by a theoretical analysis that extends previous findings on generalization ability from finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to infinite-dimensional functional spaces. To evaluate the effectiveness of FHBI, we conduct comprehensive comparisons against nine baseline methods on the VTAB-1K benchmark, which encompasses 19 diverse datasets across various domains with diverse semantics. Empirical results demonstrate that FHBI consistently outperforms the baselines by notable margins, highlighting its practical efficacy.

The paper develops the method in a space of functions called a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This makes functional changes, rather than only changes to a finite list of numerical parameters, central to its formulation.

The algorithm repeatedly performs two steps: an adversarial functional perturbation followed by functional descent. The perturbation step considers an adverse change to the function, and the descent step updates it. The authors support this procedure with theory extending earlier generalization results from finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to infinite-dimensional function spaces.

The authors report consistent improvements over those baselines by notable margins. The contribution therefore combines an extension of generalization analysis with an implementable inference algorithm whose practical effectiveness is demonstrated across the stated benchmark.
summary.tldr: FHBI combines adversarial functional perturbations and descent to improve Bayesian generalization, supported by theory and VTAB-1K experiments.

title: Improving Generalization with Flat Hilbert Bayesian Inference

abstract: Self-supervised learning has garnered increasing attention in time series analysis for benefiting various downstream tasks and reducing reliance on labeled data. Despite its effectiveness, existing methods often struggle to comprehensively capture both long-term dynamic evolution and subtle local patterns in a unified manner. In this work, we propose TimeDART, a novel self-supervised time series pre-training framework that unifies two powerful generative paradigms to learn more transferable representations. Specifically, we first employ a causal Transformer encoder, accompanied by a patch-based embedding strategy, to model the evolving trends from left to right. Building on this global modeling, we further introduce a denoising diffusion process to capture fine-grained local patterns through forward diffusion and reverse denoising. Finally, we optimize the model in an autoregressive manner. As a result, TimeDART effectively accounts for both global and local sequence features in a coherent way.We conduct extensive experiments on public datasets for time series forecasting and classification. The experimental results demonstrate that TimeDART consistently outperforms previous compared methods, validating the effectiveness of our approach.Our code is available at https://github.com/Melmaphother/TimeDART.

The paper focuses on a difficulty in existing approaches: capturing both the long-term evolution of a sequence and its subtle local patterns within one framework. Representations that account for both can be more useful across subsequent analysis tasks.

The method first divides the sequence into patches and uses a causal Transformer encoder to model trends from left to right. It then introduces a diffusion process, with forward diffusion and reverse denoising, to capture finer local structure. Autoregressive optimization brings these components together, combining the sequence-level modeling of the Transformer with the local modeling supplied by denoising.

Experiments on public datasets evaluate the learned representations for forecasting and classification. TimeDART consistently outperforms the previous methods included in those comparisons. The results support unifying the two generative approaches for time-series pre-training: the framework is designed to learn evolving trends and fine detail together, and its usefulness is demonstrated across both future prediction and sequence categorization.
summary.tldr: TimeDART combines autoregressive Transformers and diffusion denoising to learn time-series representations that capture global trends and local detail.

title: TimeDART: A Diffusion Autoregressive Transformer for Self-Supervised Time Series Representation

abstract: Integer-order calculus fails to capture the long-range dependence (LRD) and memory effects found in many complex systems. Fractional calculus addresses these gaps through fractional-order integrals and derivatives, but fractional-order dynamical systems pose substantial challenges in system identification and optimal control tasks. In this paper, we theoretically derive the optimal control via linear quadratic regulator (LQR) for fractional-order linear time-invariant (FOLTI) systems and develop an end-to-end deep learning framework based on this theoretical foundation. Our approach establishes a rigorous mathematical model, derives analytical solutions, and incorporates deep learning to achieve data-driven optimal control of FOLTI systems. Our key contributions include: (i) proposing a novel method for system identification and optimal control strategy in FOLTI systems, (ii) developing the first end-to-end data-driven learning framework, Fractional-Order Learning for Optimal Control (FOLOC), that learns control policies from observed trajectories, and (iii) deriving theoretical bounds on the sample complexity for learning accurate control policies under fractional-order dynamics. Experimental results indicate that our method accurately approximates fractional-order system behaviors without relying on Gaussian noise assumptions, pointing to promising avenues for advanced optimal control.

Fractional calculus provides a way to represent these effects, but identifying such systems and choosing optimal controls remains challenging. This paper focuses on fractional-order linear time-invariant systems, a specific mathematical setting for studying dynamics with memory.

Experiments show that the method accurately approximates fractional-order behavior without relying on Gaussian noise assumptions. These findings support its potential for control problems involving memory, with the stated theory centered on the fractional-order linear time-invariant setting.
summary.tldr: FOLOC combines fractional-order control theory and deep learning to learn control policies from trajectories of systems with memory.

title: End-to-End Learning Framework for Solving Non-Markovian Optimal Control

abstract: Sampling-based search, a simple paradigm for utilizing test-time compute, involves generating multiple candidate responses and selecting the best one—typically by verifying each response for correctness. In this paper, we study the scaling trends governing sampling-based search. Among our findings is that simply scaling up a minimalist implementation that uses only random sampling and direct self-verification results in sustained performance improvements that, for example, elevate the Gemini v1.5 Pro model’s reasoning capabilities past that of o1-Preview on popular benchmarks. We partially attribute the scalability of sampling-based search to a phenomenon of implicit scaling, where sampling a larger pool of responses in turn improves verification accuracy. We further identify two useful principles for improving self-verification capabilities with test-time compute: (1) comparing across responses provides helpful signals about the locations of errors and hallucinations, and (2) different model output styles are useful for different contexts—chains of thought are useful for reasoning but harder to verify. We also find that, though accurate verification can be elicited, frontier models demonstrate remarkably weak out-of-box verification capabilities and introduce a benchmark to measure progress on these deficiencies.

summary.tldr: Scaling simple sampling and self-verification improves reasoning, partly because larger candidate pools provide better signals for checking answers.

title: Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: Effective Inference-Time Search by Scaling Verification

abstract: We consider supervised learning with $n$ labels and show that layerwise SGD on residual networks can efficiently learn a class of hierarchical models. This model class assumes the existence of an (unknown) label hierarchy $L_1 \subseteq L_2 \subseteq …\subseteq L_r = [n]$, where labels in $L_1$ are simple functions of the input, while for $i > 1$, labels in $L_i$ are simple functions of simpler labels. Our class surpasses models that were previously shown to be learnable by deep learning algorithms, in the sense that it reaches the depth limit of efficient learnability. That is, there are models in this class that require polynomial depth to express, whereas previous models can be computed by log-depth circuits. Furthermore, we suggest that learnability of such hierarchical models might eventually form a basis for understanding deep learning. Beyond their natural fit for domains where deep learning excels, we argue that the mere existence of human “teachers“ supports the hypothesis that hierarchical structures are inherently available. By providing granular labels, teachers effectively reveal “hints“ or “snippets“ of the internal algorithms used by the brain. We formalize this intuition, showing that in a simplified model where a teacher is partially aware of their internal logic, a hierarchical structure emerges that facilitates efficient learnability.

Labels at the simplest level are simple functions of the input; labels at later levels are simple functions of labels already available at earlier levels. The hierarchy therefore exposes a sequence of intermediate learning targets.

The authors show that residual networks trained with layerwise stochastic gradient descent can efficiently learn this model class. The class includes models that require polynomial depth to express, extending beyond previously established learnable classes computable by logarithmic-depth circuits. This is a result about learning genuinely deep hierarchical computations under the stated label structure.

In a simplified model where teachers have partial awareness of their internal logic, the authors formalize how a learnable hierarchy emerges. They suggest this could eventually help explain deep learning’s success; that broader explanatory role is presented as a possibility rather than an established general account.
summary.tldr: Layerwise training of residual networks can efficiently learn a class of label hierarchies containing computations that require polynomial depth.

title: Deep Networks Learn Deep Hierarchical Models

abstract: Handling missing node features is a key challenge for deploying Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in real-world domains such as healthcare and sensor networks. Existing studies mostly address relatively benign scenarios, namely benchmark datasets with (a) high-dimensional but sparse node features and (b) incomplete data generated under Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) mechanisms. For (a), we theoretically prove that high sparsity substantially limits the information loss caused by missingness, making all models appear robust and preventing a meaningful comparison of their performance. To overcome this limitation, we introduce one synthetic and three real-world datasets with dense, semantically meaningful features. For (b), we move beyond MCAR and design evaluation protocols with more realistic missingness mechanisms. Moreover, we provide a theoretical background to state explicit assumptions on the missingness process and analyze their implications for different methods. Building on this analysis, we show that a simple baseline adapted to the graph domain is competitive with respect to specialized architectures across diverse datasets and missingness regimes.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks deployed on incomplete data need evaluations that reveal meaningful differences in robustness. This paper argues that common missing-feature tests are often too benign. They frequently use sparse, high-dimensional features and remove values completely at random, conditions that can hide the difficulties encountered with more informative features and structured missingness.

The authors prove that high feature sparsity substantially limits the information lost through missingness. Consequently, many models can appear robust, making comparisons less informative. To address this, they introduce one synthetic and three real-world datasets with dense, semantically meaningful features. They also design protocols that extend beyond completely random removal.

A theoretical treatment makes assumptions about the missingness process explicit and examines their consequences for different methods. Guided by that analysis, a simple baseline adapted to graphs performs competitively with specialized architectures across diverse datasets and missingness regimes. The contribution therefore combines a critique of existing evidence, more demanding evaluations, and a practical baseline whose strength becomes visible under broader testing.
summary.tldr: More realistic missing-feature evaluations expose weaknesses in common graph benchmarks and show a simple adapted baseline competing with specialized methods.

title: Rethinking GNNs and Missing Features: Challenges, Evaluation and a Robust Solution

abstract: Discrete flow matching, a recent framework for modeling categorical data, has shown competitive performance with autoregressive models. However, unlike continuous flow matching, the rectification strategy cannot be applied due to the stochasticity of discrete paths, necessitating alternative methods to minimize state transitions. We propose a dynamic-optimal-transport-like minimization objective and derive its Kantorovich formulation for discrete flows with convex interpolants, where transport cost depends solely on inter-state dissimilarity and can be optimized via minibatch strategies. We show that such methods can reduce the number of transitions up to 32 times (1024 to 32) to reach the same generative perplexity without compromising diversity. Additionally, path nondeterminism in discrete flows precludes an instantaneous change-of-variables analogue, preventing precise probability estimation available to continuous flows. We therefore propose two upper bounds on perplexity, enabling principled training, evaluation and model comparison. Finally, we introduce Multimask Flows which outperform masked flows in generative perplexity without compromising diversity, particularly when utilizing minibatch Optimal Transport.

paragraphs: Discrete flow matching generates categorical data through stochastic sequences of state changes. That randomness prevents direct use of the rectification strategy available in continuous flow matching and also complicates exact probability estimation. This paper tackles both issues: reducing the number of transitions needed for generation and providing principled ways to assess model probabilities.

Its cost depends only on dissimilarities between states, allowing optimization with minibatches. summary.tldr: Minibatch transport reduces discrete-flow generation steps, while new perplexity bounds and Multimask Flows improve evaluation and reported generation quality.

title: Minibatch Optimal Transport and Perplexity Bound Estimation in Discrete Flow Matching

abstract: The Rapid Response (RR) framework (Peng et al., 2024), deployed in production systems including Anthropic’s ASL-3 safeguards (Anthropic, 2025), dynamically adapts jailbreak detection classifiers by generating synthetic training data from emerging attacks. We reveal that prompt injection can infiltrate this pipeline to deliver poisoned samples into the classifier’s training set, enabling two attack objectives: (I) targeted poisoning attacks that create false positives on harmless samples by categorizing them as a jailbreak, with a specific desired feature (e.g., certain formatting, subject, or keyword), (II) concept-based backdoor attacks that induce false negatives on jailbreak inputs, generalizing even to jailbreaks from attack strategies the defender explicitly trained against, when the backdoor trigger is present. Importantly, our threat model restricts adversaries to modify- ing only jailbreak samples (not benign data or labels), a constraint unexplored by prior work that makes the second objective particularly challeng- ing. We address this with Omission Attack, which exploits a new phenomenon: when training on concept-absent unsafe samples, the classifier mis- associates that concept’s presence with the safe label. Both attacks flip nearly all target labels with only 1% poisoning rate. Code: https://github.com/DH-davidhuang/rapid-poison

paragraphs: Rapid Response updates jailbreak detectors by generating synthetic training data from newly encountered attacks. This paper shows that prompt injection can contaminate that adaptation pipeline, causing poisoned examples to enter classifier training. The weakness concerns how incoming attacks influence future defensive behavior through the data-generation process.

The authors study two outcomes: harmless inputs with a chosen feature being incorrectly flagged, and jailbreak inputs being incorrectly accepted when a concept-based trigger is present. Their threat model allows changes only to jailbreak samples, without access to benign examples or labels. The proposed Omission Attack exploits a learned misassociation in which a concept’s absence from unsafe training samples makes its presence appear associated with safety.

In the reported experiments, both attack types flip nearly all targeted labels at a 1% poisoning rate. The backdoor also generalizes to jailbreaks from strategies the defender explicitly trained against. These findings expose a weakness in adaptive defense: learning from emerging threats can introduce misleading associations when the synthetic training pipeline is itself influenced by adversarial input.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that poisoning attack-derived synthetic data can make adaptive jailbreak detectors reject harmless inputs or accept triggered jailbreaks.

title: Rapid Poison: Practical Poisoning Attacks Against the Rapid Response Framework

abstract: Antibodies originate from germline templates and are diversified by somatic hypermutation, producing sequences in which conserved germline residues scaffold structure while rare non-germline (NGL) substitutions refine antigen binding. Current antibody language models (ALMs) treat all residues equivalently and inherit a germline bias that systematically down-weights functionally critical NGL mutations as statistical noise. We introduce PRISM, a germline-aware ALM that explicitly represents germline and non-germline residues as distinct token types over a factorized 53-token vocabulary. PRISM achieves state-of-the-art pseudo-perplexity in hypervariable CDRs and is uniquely positively correlated with experimental binding affinity across three deep mutational scanning landscapes on which all compared ALMs anti-correlate. The dual-vocabulary further enables property-specific controllable generation previously unattainable with entangled ALMs. NGL-directed sampling improves physics-based binding scores while GL-directed sampling preserves stability and solubility. These results establish disentangled germline/non-germline representation as a substantive advance in antibody language modeling.

paragraphs: Antibody sequences combine inherited germline structure with mutations that can refine antigen binding. The paper argues that treating all residues identically causes antibody language models to favor common germline patterns and discount rare but functionally important substitutions. PRISM explicitly separates these two kinds of sequence information.

Its factorized 53-token vocabulary represents germline and non-germline residues as distinct token types. This gives the model a direct way to distinguish conserved structure from diversification. PRISM reports state-of-the-art pseudo-perplexity in hypervariable CDR regions. Together, the findings support representing antibody origin explicitly as a useful basis for both sequence modeling and controllable generation.
summary.tldr: PRISM separates germline and mutated antibody residues, improving sequence modeling, affinity correlation, and property-directed generation.

title: Explicit representation of germline and non-germline residues improves antibody language modeling

abstract: We study the fine-grainded uniform convergence behavior of halfspaces beyond worst-case VC bounds. For inhomogeneous halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $d\ge 2$, we show that standard first-order VC bounds are essentially tight: even consistent hypotheses can incur population error $\Theta(d\log(n/d)/n)$, and in the agnostic setting the deviation scales as $\sqrt{\tau\log(1/\tau)}$ at true error $\tau$. In contrast, homogeneous halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^2$ exhibit a markedly different behavior. In the realizable case, every hypothesis consistent with the sample has error $O(1/n)$. In the agnostic case, we prove a bandwise, log-free deviation bound on each dyadic risk band via a critical-wedge localization argument. Unioning over bands incurs only a $\log\log n$ overhead, and we establish a matching lower bound showing this overhead is unavoidable. Together, these results give a fine-grained and nearly complete picture of uniform convergence for halfspaces, revealing sharp dimensional and structural thresholds.
