paragraphs: Uniform convergence asks how reliably performance on a finite sample represents performance across the underlying population, simultaneously for a family of predictors. This paper examines that question for halfspaces: classifiers that separate inputs with a linear boundary. Its central finding is that the answer depends sharply on the boundary’s structure and the dimension.

For boundaries that can shift away from the origin in two or more dimensions, the authors show that standard first-order VC bounds are essentially tight. Even classifiers that fit every training example can have population error of order d log(n/d)/n. In the agnostic setting, where perfect classification need not be possible, they also establish a corresponding error-dependent deviation scale.

Boundaries constrained to pass through the origin behave differently in two dimensions. In the realizable setting, every sample-consistent classifier has error O(1/n). For agnostic learning, the authors obtain bounds without logarithmic factors within individual risk bands. Combining the bands introduces only a log log n overhead, which a matching lower bound shows is unavoidable. The results identify precisely where familiar worst-case bounds can be improved.
summary.tldr: Uniform convergence for halfspaces changes sharply with geometry: origin-constrained boundaries in two dimensions admit stronger guarantees than general shifted boundaries.

title: A Fine-Grained Understanding of Uniform Convergence for Halfspaces

abstract: Transformer-based large language models exhibit in-context learning, enabling adaptation to downstream tasks via few-shot prompting with demonstrations. In practice, such models are often fine-tuned to improve zero-shot performance on downstream tasks, allowing them to solve tasks without examples and thereby reducing inference costs. However, fine-tuning can degrade in-context learning, limiting the performance of fine-tuned models on tasks not seen during fine-tuning. Using linear attention models, we provide a theoretical analysis that characterizes how fine-tuning objectives modify attention parameters and identifies conditions under which this leads to degraded few-shot performance. We show that fine-tuning all attention parameters can harm in-context learning, whereas restricting updates to the value matrix improves zero-shot performance while preserving in-context learning. We further show that incorporating an auxiliary few-shot loss enhances in-context learning primarily on the target task, at the expense of degraded in-context learning ability on tasks not seen during fine-tuning. We provide empirical evidence from synthetic and real-world datasets consistent with the qualitative predictions of our theory.

This paper studies that tension theoretically using linear attention models, tracing how training objectives change attention parameters.

The analysis identifies conditions under which parameter changes degrade few-shot performance. Updating all attention parameters can damage in-context learning, whereas restricting updates to the value matrix improves zero-shot performance while preserving in-context learning in the analyzed setting. summary.tldr: Linear-attention theory shows how value-only fine-tuning can improve zero-shot performance while preserving in-context learning.

title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

abstract: Learning fluid PDE dynamics has increasingly benefited from neural operators and Transformer-based models, but their latent states often remain opaque, and sample-wise attention can be costly at high resolutions. We propose the Gaussian Particle Operator (GPO), a basis-to-basis neural operator that represents fields with a learned Gaussian basis. Each atom carries explicit geometric parameters, including centers, anisotropic scales, and weights, yielding a compact, mesh-agnostic, and directly visualizable intermediate representation. GPO operates in modal space: learned Gaussian modal windows perform Petrov–Galerkin measurements, and a PG Gaussian Attention module couples the resulting modes globally before scattering them back to the spatial domain. This design is resolution-agnostic, scales near-linearly with the number of samples for a fixed modal budget, and naturally applies to irregular geometries and 3D domains. We separately evaluate Gaussian-basis reconstruction and operator prediction. Across standard PDE benchmarks and real reanalysis datasets, GPO achieves competitive accuracy against neural-operator and Transformer baselines, ranking best on most tasks and close to the best on the remainder. The learned particles and modal couplings further provide representation-level interpretability, positioning GPO as a useful intermediate representation rather than a one-to-one decomposition of physical structures. The code is available at https://github.com/lizhihao2022/GPO.

title: From Basis to Basis: Gaussian Particle Representation for Interpretable PDE Operators

abstract: Learning meaningful representations from medical time series (MedTS), such as ECG or EEG signals, is a critical challenge. These signals are often high-dimensional, variable-length, and rife with noise. Existing self-supervised approaches, such as Masked Autoencoders (MAEs), are highly effective for pre-training general-purpose encoders. However, they do not explicitly learn compact, fixed-size, or semantically interpretable latent representations, typically relying on heuristic aggregation strategies such as global average pooling or a designated [CLS] token. We propose a novel framework that compresses a variable-length MedTS into a fixed-size set of $k$ latent Fingerprint Tokens. Our architecture employs a cross-attention bottleneck to generate these tokens and is trained with a dual-objective function. The first objective is a reconstruction loss, which ensures the tokens are sufficient statistics for the original data. The second, a diversity penalty based on the Total Coding Rate (TCR), explicitly minimizes the redundancy between tokens, encouraging them to become statistically disentangled representations. We present the theoretical justification for our method, framing it as a novel Disentangled Rate-Distortion problem. This approach produces a low-dimensional, interpretable, and sample-efficient representation, where each token is encouraged to capture an independent factor of variation, paving the way for more robust digital biomarkers.

This paper introduces a representation that compresses each recording into a fixed number of learned Fingerprint Tokens.

The proposed representation is presented as groundwork for more robust digital biomarkers.
summary.tldr: A reconstruction-and-diversity objective compresses variable-length medical signals into compact Fingerprint Tokens encouraged to capture distinct factors.

title: Learning Fingerprints for Medical Time Series with Redundancy-Constrained Information Maximization

abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. Existing training methods inherit the Block Training paradigm from LLM pre-training, which introduces destructive gradient noise in instruct models due to attention leakage from unrelated contexts. Using GSNR analysis, we theoretically characterize this issue and propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a sequential training paradigm specifically designed for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns SAE training with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, substantially improving both reconstruction fidelity and feature interpretability. Experimental results show that $\textit{FAST}$ achieves higher GSNR, a significantly lower log-scaled MSE of 0.6468 compared to the baseline’s 5.1985, and a near-zero Delta Loss (-0.51% to 0.37%). Moreover, on Llama-3.2-3B-it, $\textit{FAST}$ produces 21.1% high-quality features, substantially outperforming baseline methods that achieve 7.0% and 10.2%. We further find that intervening on special token activations through SAEs can improve generation quality, revealing new opportunities for fine-grained control. Our codes are available as open source at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

The paper identifies a problem with training these tools on instruction-following models: conventional block training allows attention to leak between unrelated contexts. This introduces destructive noise into the gradients used to learn the autoencoder.

The authors analyze the problem through gradient signal-to-noise ratio, or GSNR, and introduce FAST, a sequential training method aligned with instruction-tuned models. Preserving continuity better matches the data distribution and activation patterns of those models. The intended benefit is twofold: reconstruct internal activity more faithfully and extract features that are easier to interpret.

The authors also find that SAE interventions on special-token activations can improve generation quality, suggesting opportunities for finer control over model behavior.
summary.tldr: FAST preserves data continuity during sparse-autoencoder training, improving reconstruction and feature interpretability for instruction-following models.

title: Breaking the Block: Preserving Data Continuity to Train Superior SAEs for Instruct Models

abstract: Gaussian Splatting has achieved significant improvements by incorporating warping-based techniques. However, such methods suffer from pixel-level inaccuracies due to uncertain geometry. This uncertainty leads to spatial misalignments in the warped images, which disrupt residual learning used in warping-based methods and fundamentally limit the gains of correction, particularly on thin structures and high-frequency details. Driven by our insight that useful visual cues are not lost but locally preserved under slight displacement, we propose Geometry-Aware Deformable Aggregation (GADA). This method introduces an iterative refinement module with deformable offsets to actively correct spatial misalignments and recover these displaced cues. Furthermore, to address the limitations of standard pipelines where visibility checks (i.e., thresholding) often discard valid pixels and multi-view warped image fusion relies on naive mean aggregation, our module is coupled with an implicit confidence weighting mechanism that selectively suppresses unreliable evidence. Consequently, our approach outperforms prior warping-based Gaussian Splatting, preserving high-frequency quality while achieving 2.13 times faster FPS.

paragraphs: Image warping helps Gaussian Splatting reuse information from different views, but uncertain geometry can place that information at the wrong pixels. Such misalignment interferes with correction steps, especially around thin structures and fine visual details. GADA builds on the observation that slightly displaced cues can remain available nearby, even when their initial alignment is inaccurate.

The method introduces iterative refinement with deformable offsets that adjust where visual evidence is gathered. This lets the model recover useful information from neighboring positions. It also learns confidence weights for combining evidence, addressing two weaknesses of standard pipelines: visibility thresholds can discard valid pixels, and simple averaging can mix reliable and unreliable warped views.

The authors report better performance than prior warping-based Gaussian Splatting methods, preservation of high-frequency image quality, and a 2.13-fold improvement in frame rate. The approach matters because it treats local displacement as a recoverable alignment problem. Its refinement and confidence weighting work together to improve how existing visual evidence contributes to the final result.
summary.tldr: GADA corrects displaced visual evidence and weights its reliability to improve Gaussian Splatting quality and rendering speed.

title: GADA: Geometry-Aware Deformable Aggregation for Image-Based Gaussian Splatting

abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to interact with external tools, but this extensibility introduces significant supply chain vulnerabilities that enable covert privacy exfiltration. Prior studies have revealed privacy leakage in MCP-enabled agents via indirect prompt injection; however, existing attacks are typically misaligned with the agent’s tool-usage context and rely on rigid templates, resulting in recognizable patterns that are readily flagged by existing defenses. In this work, we exploit the observation that privacy exposure is inherently scenario-dependent, to associate certain privacy items with specific tools. We introduce SOPE, a Scenario-aware and zerO-click Privacy Exfiltration framework that transforms any benign MCP server into its privacy-exfiltrating variants. SOPE (1) identifies privacy items that are appropriate to the tool usage, (2) embeds privacy-probing instructions into tool-invocation prompts, and (3) achieves zero-click data transmission via code-level modifications. We evaluate SOPE across 27,216 test cases, where 324 SOPE-transformed real-world servers attacking four benchmark and three commercial agents with nine state-of-the-art defenses. Results demonstrate that SOPE remains highly effective and robust, highlighting critical protocol-level safety gaps in the agent ecosystem.

paragraphs: MCP connects language-model agents to external tools, creating a supply-chain surface through which tool providers can influence agent behavior. This paper studies privacy leakage through that connection. It argues that earlier attacks are easier to detect when their requests do not fit the tool's purpose or follow recognizable, rigid templates.

SOPE makes privacy-exfiltration attempts sensitive to the tool-use scenario. At a conceptual level, it associates private information with relevant tools, places probing instructions in tool-invocation prompts, and modifies server code to transmit information without an additional user click. The study examines how contextually plausible malicious behavior can exploit an otherwise useful integration mechanism.

The evaluation covers 27,216 test cases involving 324 transformed real-world servers, four benchmark agents, three commercial agents, and nine defenses. The authors report high effectiveness and robustness across this evaluation. These findings highlight protocol-level safety gaps: the observed risk involves both how agents interpret tool-related instructions and how modified servers handle data, rather than prompt wording alone.
summary.tldr: SOPE shows that context-sensitive malicious MCP servers can expose private data despite a range of evaluated agent defenses.

title: SOPE: Situation-Aware and Statistically Indistinguishable Privacy Exfiltration for MCP-enabled Agents

abstract: Preference optimization for diffusion models relies on reward functions that are both discriminative and computationally efficient. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have emerged as powerful reward providers. However, their computation and memory cost can be substantial, and optimizing a latent diffusion generator through a pixel-space reward introduces a domain mismatch that complicates alignment. In this paper, we propose DiNa-LRM, a diffusion-native latent reward model that formulates preference learning directly on noisy diffusion states. Our method introduces a noise-calibrated Thurstone likelihood with diffusion-noise-dependent uncertainty. DiNa-LRM leverages a pretrained latent diffusion backbone with a timestep-conditioned reward head, and supports inference-time noise ensembling, providing a diffusion-native mechanism for test-time scaling and robust rewarding. Across image alignment benchmarks, DiNa-LRM substantially outperforms existing diffusion-based reward baselines and achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art VLMs while maintaining a substantially lower computational cost. In preference optimization, we demonstrate that DiNa-LRM improves preference optimization dynamics, enabling faster and more resource-efficient model alignment.

paragraphs: DiNa-LRM learns preference rewards directly from the noisy internal states of a diffusion model. The paper motivates this choice with two issues in using vision-language models as reward providers: their computational expense and the mismatch between a generator working in latent space and a reward evaluated on pixels.

The method reuses a pretrained latent diffusion backbone and adds a reward head conditioned on the diffusion timestep. Its preference likelihood explicitly accounts for uncertainty that changes with diffusion noise. This lets the reward model treat different noise levels as part of the scoring problem. At inference time, noise ensembling combines reward evidence across noisy evaluations, providing a way to spend additional computation on more robust scoring.

On image alignment benchmarks, the approach substantially outperforms existing diffusion-based reward methods and performs competitively with leading vision-language models at substantially lower computational cost. The paper also reports faster, more resource-efficient preference optimization. Together, these findings support matching the reward model’s representation to the generator’s own diffusion process as a useful route to efficient alignment.
summary.tldr: DiNa-LRM scores preferences within noisy diffusion latents, offering competitive image rewards and more efficient model alignment.

title: Beyond VLM-Based Rewards: Diffusion-Native Latent Reward Modeling

abstract: Visual tracking aims to estimate target states in video sequences, with applications spanning diverse computational requirements. Recent methods optimize trackers using manually pruned image tokens with a fixed budget to reduce computational costs. However, these trackers, once trained, are constrained to perform tracking under a fixed computational budget, limiting their adaptability to real-world computational diversity. To address the above limitation, we provide the first exploration of the elastic token budget training framework (ETBTrack), enabling trackers to perform robust tracking under varying computational budgets. It enjoys several merits. First, we present a novel result-driven importance criteria, in which we optimize a policy network guided by the localization precision of the tracker to estimate token importance, thereby aligning the objectives of importance estimation and tracking precision. Second, we develop a new budget-collaborative optimization strategy, in which we collaboratively optimize the tracker across varying budgets, thereby enabling the tracker to be compatible with diverse budgets. Two optimization processes are performed alternately to enhance the capability of elastic inference. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Visual trackers estimate a target’s state across video frames, but the computational resources available for tracking can vary. Existing token-pruning approaches train with a fixed number of image tokens, leaving the resulting tracker tied to that budget. ETBTrack trains a tracker to operate across multiple token budgets.

The framework learns which tokens matter through a policy network guided by the tracker’s localization precision. This ties token importance directly to the tracking result: the importance estimator is optimized toward the same practical objective as the tracker. A budget-collaborative strategy also optimizes the tracker across different budgets, helping one trained system accommodate different computational allocations.

These two optimization processes alternate to develop elastic inference capability. Large-scale benchmark experiments support the method’s effectiveness. The approach matters because selecting useful tokens and tolerating different token counts are related training problems: useful selection alone does not establish flexibility across budgets. ETBTrack addresses both within the training framework, aiming to maintain robust tracking when the amount of computation available at inference changes.
summary.tldr: ETBTrack jointly learns token importance and tracking across multiple budgets to support flexible computation at inference.

title: Learning Generalized Trackers with Elastic Token Budgets

abstract: We focus on the problem of Answer-Level Fine-Tuning (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a Distributional Alignment Game. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. This variational perspective transforms the intractable marginalization problem into a tractable projection problem. We demonstrate that this framework unifies recent approaches to diversity and self-improvement (coherence) and provide efficient algorithms compatible with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), such as Coherence-GRPO, yielding significant complexity gains in mathematical reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Answer-level fine-tuning rewards a language model for the correctness or properties of its final answer, without requiring one particular reasoning trace. The computational obstacle is that many different reasoning paths can produce the same answer. Direct optimization requires accounting for this enormous hidden space, making the original formulation intractable.

The paper recasts the problem as a game between two distributions. One player is the policy that generates outputs; the other is an auxiliary target distribution. The authors prove that the game’s Nash equilibrium corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level objective. This reformulation replaces difficult marginalization over reasoning paths with a tractable projection problem.

The framework also brings existing ideas about diversity and coherent self-improvement under one mathematical description. The authors develop efficient algorithms compatible with Group Relative Policy Optimization, including Coherence-GRPO, and report significant complexity gains on mathematical reasoning tasks. The equilibrium result supplies the conceptual justification for the reformulation, while the algorithms show how it can support practical training without explicitly enumerating the possible reasoning routes.
summary.tldr: A two-player distributional game makes answer-level fine-tuning tractable while preserving the original objective at equilibrium.

title: Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning

abstract: Recent work has demonstrated the curse of depth in large language models (LLMs), where later layers contribute less to learning and representation than earlier layers. Such under-utilization is linked to the accumulated growth of variance in Pre-Layer Normalization, which can push deep blocks toward near-identity behavior. In this paper, we provide evidence that sparsity-like mechanisms can dampen variance propagation and are associated with improved depth utilization Our investigation covers two sources of sparsity: (i) implicit sparsity, which emerges from training and data conditions, including weight sparsity induced by weight decay and attention sparsity induced by long-context inputs; and (ii) explicit sparsity, which is enforced by architectural design, including key/value-sharing in Grouped-Query Attention and expert-activation sparsity in Mixture-of-Experts. Our claim is thoroughly supported by controlled depth-scaling experiments and targeted layer effectiveness interventions. Across settings, we observe a consistent relationship: mechanisms with reduced effective interaction density tend to exhibit lower output variance and better layer differentiation. We eventually distill our findings into a practical rule-of-thumb recipe for training depth-effective LLMs, yielding a notable 4.6 accuracy improvement on downstream tasks. Our results suggest that sparsity-like design choices are an important and previously underemphasized factor in effective depth scaling for LLMs. Code is available at https://github. com/pUmpKin-Co/SparsityAndCoD.

paragraphs: The curse of depth describes language models whose later layers contribute less than earlier ones. The paper connects this underuse to accumulated variance growth in pre-layer-normalized models, which can push deep blocks toward behavior that barely changes their inputs. It investigates whether mechanisms resembling sparsity can dampen that growth and improve layer utilization.

The study covers sparsity emerging through training and inputs, including weight decay and long-context attention, as well as architectural mechanisms such as shared keys and values in grouped-query attention and selective expert activation. Controlled depth-scaling experiments and targeted interventions on layer effectiveness examine how these choices relate to variance and layer differentiation.

Across the studied settings, reduced effective interaction density tends to accompany lower output variance and more differentiated layers. The authors turn these observations into a practical training recipe that yields a reported 4.6 accuracy improvement on downstream tasks. The evidence suggests that sparsity-related choices deserve attention in depth scaling, while the central relationship remains empirically qualified rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Experiments link sparsity-like mechanisms to lower variance growth and better use of deep LLM layers, informing an effective training recipe.

title: When Does Sparsity Mitigate the Curse of Depth in LLMs

abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models has catalyzed a surge in scientific idea production, yet this leap has not been accompanied by a matching advance in idea evaluation. The fundamental nature of scientific evaluation needs knowledgeable grounding, collective deliberation, and multi-criteria decision-making. However, existing idea evaluation methods often suffer from narrow knowledge horizons, flattened evaluation dimensions, and the inherent bias in LLM-as-a-Judge. To address these, we regard idea evaluation as a knowledge-grounded, multi-perspective reasoning problem and introduce InnoEval, a deep innovation evaluation framework designed to emulate human-level idea assessment. We apply a heterogeneous deep knowledge search engine that retrieves and grounds dynamic evidence from diverse online sources. We further achieve review consensus with an innovation review board containing reviewers with distinct academic backgrounds, enabling a multi-dimensional decoupled evaluation across multiple metrics. We construct comprehensive datasets derived from authoritative peer-reviewed submissions to benchmark InnoEval. Experiments demonstrate that InnoEval can consistently outperform baselines in point-wise, pair-wise, and group-wise evaluation tasks, exhibiting judgment patterns and consensus highly aligned with human experts.

The paper argues that existing automated evaluators often have narrow knowledge, collapse distinct dimensions of quality together, and inherit biases from using a language model as the judge.

InnoEval treats evaluation as evidence-grounded reasoning across several perspectives. A search engine gathers current evidence from diverse online sources to inform assessments. A review board with distinct academic backgrounds then evaluates multiple dimensions separately and works toward consensus. This design gives knowledge gathering and collective judgment explicit roles in the evaluation process.

The authors build evaluation datasets from authoritative peer-reviewed submissions and test individual scoring, pairwise comparisons, and evaluations involving groups of ideas. InnoEval consistently outperforms the tested baselines, with judgment patterns and consensus closely aligned with human experts. These findings support combining diverse evidence with differentiated reviewer perspectives for research assessment. Although the framework is designed to emulate human-level assessment, the stated evidence is its comparative performance and alignment with expert judgments.
summary.tldr: InnoEval combines evidence retrieval and reviewers with different academic perspectives to assess research ideas more closely in line with human experts.

title: InnoEval: On Research Idea Evaluation as a Knowledge-Grounded, Multi-Perspective Reasoning Problem

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently advanced in reasoning when optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) under verifiable rewards. Existing methods primarily rely on outcome-based supervision to strengthen internal LLM reasoning, often leading to inefficient exploration and sparse rewards. To mitigate this issue, we propose Expert-Assisted Policy Optimization (EAPO), a novel RL framework that enhances exploration by incorporating multi-turn interactions with external experts during training. Unlike prior methods, where policies reason in isolation, EAPO incentivizes the policy to adaptively determine when and how to consult experts, yielding richer reward signals and more reliable reasoning trajectories. External assistance ultimately internalizes expert knowledge into the policy model, amplifying the model’s inherent reasoning capabilities. During evaluation, the policy model has been well-optimized to solve questions independently, producing improved reasoning paths and more accurate solutions. On AIME 2024/2025 and AIMO 2025, EAPO consistently outperforms expert-assisted, expert-distilled, and RL baselines, averaging a 5-point gain over self-exploration RL, and also generalizes to non-math benchmarks, including HumanEval, HLE, GPQA, MMLU, EvalPlus, HotpotQA, and SimpleQA.

paragraphs: EAPO improves reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning by allowing expert consultation during training. When supervision mainly rewards a correct final answer, useful feedback can be sparse and exploration inefficient. The framework introduces multi-turn interaction with external experts to help the policy discover more reliable reasoning trajectories.

The policy learns when to ask for help and how to formulate its requests. This makes assistance part of the exploration process and provides richer reward signals. The intended result is to absorb expert knowledge into the policy’s own capabilities. At evaluation time, the trained model answers independently, so the reported improvement reflects reasoning learned during assisted training.

On AIME 2024/2025 and AIMO 2025, EAPO consistently surpasses the evaluated expert-assisted, expert-distilled, and reinforcement-learning baselines, averaging a five-point gain over self-exploration RL. The paper also reports generalization to non-mathematical benchmarks covering coding, knowledge, and question answering. These findings indicate that learning to seek assistance during training can improve subsequent unaided problem solving.
summary.tldr: EAPO trains reasoning models to consult experts adaptively, improving their later ability to solve problems independently.

title: EAPO: Enhancing Policy Optimization with On-Demand Expert Assistance

abstract: Autonomous computer use agents that powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are emerging as capable assistants for completing complex digital workflows. However, real-world execution environments are far from ideal: pop-ups, resolution changes, and competing applications frequently interfere with agent perception and control. We introduce AgentHijack, a benchmark designed to evaluate the robustness of computer-use agents under common corruptions, where the uncertainties in dynamic environment disrupt the execution flow without direct adversarial intent. Specifically, AgentHijack introduces 9 configurable common corruptions to replicate realistic imperfect scenarios. We evaluate a variety of desktop tasks that utilize MLLM-based agents and discover that even minor instances of corruption can result in substantial performance degradation, which emphasizes the fragility of agents and underscores the necessity of robustness evaluation. Afterward, we propose AgentHijack-Agent, a framework that integrates an action generator with enhanced grounding capabilities and an onlooker responsible for behavior summarization and environment checking. Extensive experiments validate its effectiveness. Our code, environment, baseline models and data are publicly available at: https://AgentHijack.github.io.

paragraphs: AgentHijack examines whether computer-use agents can keep completing tasks when ordinary desktop conditions change. Pop-ups, altered screen resolution, and competing applications can disrupt what an agent sees or how its actions behave. The benchmark focuses on these everyday disruptions without assuming that someone is deliberately attacking the agent.

The authors introduce nine configurable environmental corruptions and evaluate multimodal language-model agents across desktop tasks. They find that even relatively minor disruptions can substantially reduce performance. This makes environmental robustness a distinct evaluation concern: success in an orderly interface does not establish that an agent will maintain its execution flow when the interface changes.

The paper also proposes AgentHijack-Agent, which combines an action generator with enhanced grounding and an onlooker that summarizes behavior and checks the environment. These components connect action selection with monitoring of the surrounding desktop. Experiments support the framework’s effectiveness, while the benchmark supplies a common way to study the fragility revealed by the initial evaluations.
summary.tldr: AgentHijack tests computer-use agents under everyday desktop disruptions and introduces a monitoring framework that improves robustness.

title: AgentHijack: Benchmarking Computer Use Agent Robustness to Common Environment Corruptions

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly powerful and promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract sparse, interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently from autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs provide useful signals for DLM decoding order, and that SAE features remain stable during DLM post-training. Overall, our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and highlights the potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

paragraphs: DLM-Scope adapts sparse autoencoders to interpreting diffusion language models. These tools extract a relatively small collection of interpretable features from model activations, giving researchers a way to inspect internal representations and intervene on behavior. The paper demonstrates that trained Top-K sparse autoencoders can faithfully extract such features from diffusion models, extending a technique already widely used with autoregressive language models.

A notable finding is that inserting these autoencoders has different effects across the two model families. In autoregressive models, insertion typically increases loss. In the studied diffusion models, insertion into early layers can instead reduce cross-entropy loss, with this effect absent or much weaker in autoregressive models. Feature-based interventions during diffusion also often outperform steering in autoregressive models.

The authors further find that the extracted features provide useful signals for deciding decoding order and remain stable during diffusion-model post-training. These observations give the framework a role beyond explaining individual behaviors: its features may also inform generation algorithms. The results establish useful interpretability capabilities while showing that conclusions drawn from autoregressive models do not automatically describe diffusion models.
summary.tldr: DLM-Scope extracts interpretable diffusion-language-model features that support steering, decoding analysis, and sometimes lower early-layer loss.

title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to low-resource domains remains challenging due to the scarcity of domain-specific data. While in-domain data is limited, there exists a vast amount of general-domain data that shares similar question–answer formats and reasoning patterns with domain tasks. This observation raises an important question: can useful general-domain data be mined to improve low-resource domain adaptation? Our initial findings show that general-domain chain-of-thought data contains useful auxiliary signals for domain adaptation, even without careful selection. This observation motivates a new paradigm for domain adaptation beyond exclusive reliance on domain-specific data. To systematically identify the most beneficial general-domain samples, we propose NTK-Selector, motivated by the Neural Tangent Kernel’s ability to capture alignment in training dynamics. Since directly applying NTK to pretrained LLMs is impractical, we introduce a Jacobian-free NTK approximation and empirically demonstrate stable NTK-like behavior during fine-tuning. Extensive experiments across medical, financial, legal, and psychological domains demonstrate that NTK-Selector consistently outperforms domain-only fine-tuning and existing data selection baselines. In particular, NTK-Selector achieves gains of +8.7 and +5.1 points on Llama3-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, respectively, compared to only +0.8 and +0.9 points from domain-only fine-tuning.

This paper investigates whether general-domain reasoning examples can help because they share question-answer structures and reasoning patterns with specialized tasks. Initial experiments find useful auxiliary signals even in general chain-of-thought data that has not been carefully selected.

Because direct application to pretrained language models is impractical, the authors introduce a Jacobian-free approximation and empirically observe stable NTK-like behavior during fine-tuning. Selection is therefore motivated by how examples relate through learning dynamics.

Across medical, financial, legal, and psychological domains, NTK-Selector consistently outperforms domain-only fine-tuning and existing selection baselines. Reported gains are 8.7 points for Llama3-8B-Instruct and 5.1 for Qwen3-8B, compared with 0.8 and 0.9 from domain-only fine-tuning. summary.tldr: NTK-Selector mines general reasoning examples that improve specialized-domain adaptation when domain-specific training data is scarce.

title: Mining Useful General Data for Low-Resource Domain Adaptation

abstract: Medical Large Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) suffer from severe hallucinations, posing critical safety risks in clinical deployment. Editing LVLM activations has shown promise for mitigating hallucination with minimal cost. However, due to the requirements of medical domain expertise, existing methods struggle to capture imaging manifestations and diagnostic principles that are critical for clinical interpretation, thereby limiting their effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose the first MEDical-oriented Activation Editing (MEDA) method by integrating Query-decisive Manifestation Steering (QMS) and Principle-driven Diagnosis Induction (PDI) to promote Med-LVLM’s expertise elicitation. Specifically, QMS retrieves positive query-decisive imaging manifestations as trusted guidance for activation steering, while PDI constructs positive principle-embedded diagnostic prompts to induce expert-like clinical reasoning. Extensive experiments across six benchmarks and six LVLMs demonstrate that MEDA efficiently improves the response factuality with up to a 10.2% gain on IU-Xray, while exhibiting strong generalization and few-shot robustness.

paragraphs: Medical vision-language models can produce unsupported statements when interpreting images. Editing their internal activations offers a relatively inexpensive way to reduce these hallucinations, but generic editing methods can miss the imaging findings and diagnostic principles needed for medical interpretation. MEDA introduces medical guidance into this activation-editing approach.

The method combines two components. Query-decisive Manifestation Steering retrieves positive imaging manifestations relevant to the question and uses them as trusted guidance for steering activations. Principle-driven Diagnosis Induction constructs positive diagnostic prompts that incorporate medical principles to encourage expert-like reasoning. Together, they aim to elicit relevant model expertise through both image-related evidence and diagnostic guidance.

The authors evaluate MEDA across six benchmarks and six vision-language models. They report improved response factuality, including gains of up to 10.2% on IU-Xray, alongside strong generalization and robustness with few examples. These findings support tailoring activation editing to the evidence and reasoning demands of the medical domain in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MEDA uses question-relevant imaging findings and diagnostic principles to guide activation editing and improve medical vision-language response factuality.

title: MEDA: Medical-Oriented Activation Editing for Hallucination Mitigation in Medical Large Vision-Language Model

abstract: Multimodal latent-space reasoning replaces explicit “thinking with images” with reasoning in a compact latent space. Current methods mainly reshape low-level image features under visual supervision. Their latents capture appearance but carry limited high-level abstract semantics. We introduce Semantic-Enriched Latent Visual Reasoning (SLVR), a two-stage framework with a semantic attribute extraction head. In the first stage, this head converts region evidence into attribute-level semantic latents. These latents complement low-level visual features and support richer reasoning. In the second stage, Multi-query Group Relative Policy Optimization (M-GRPO) jointly optimizes multiple queries grounded in the same region. It builds on the invariance of intrinsic region attributes across different questions. M-GRPO constrains the degree of attribute variation across queries while preserving answer correctness. We construct SLV-Set, with approximately 400K region-level attribute annotations and 800K multi-query question answering samples, and introduce SV-QA for evaluation under semantic variation. Experiments show that SLVR improves the robustness and semantic consistency of latent visual reasoning. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/tinnel123666888/slvr.

paragraphs: Reasoning in a compact visual latent space can avoid explicitly generating intermediate images, but existing representations often emphasize appearance over abstract meaning. Semantic-Enriched Latent Visual Reasoning, or SLVR, adds attribute-level information so that the internal representation carries more of the semantics needed to answer questions about an image region.

The first training stage uses a semantic attribute extraction head to convert regional visual evidence into semantic latents that complement low-level features. The second stage applies Multi-query Group Relative Policy Optimization to several questions about the same region. It uses the premise that intrinsic region attributes should stay consistent across questions, constraining attribute variation while preserving answer correctness.

The authors construct SLV-Set with approximately 400,000 region-level attribute annotations and 800,000 multi-query question-answering samples. They also introduce SV-QA to evaluate reasoning under semantic variation. Experiments report improved robustness and semantic consistency. The approach ties richer representations to a training objective that encourages the same visual region to retain coherent attributes across different queries.
summary.tldr: SLVR adds semantic attributes to visual latents and trains across related questions to improve reasoning robustness and consistency.

title: Semantic-Enriched Latent Visual Reasoning

abstract: Stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) provides temporally precise intracranial recordings but is inherently constrained by sparse and irregular spatial sampling due to clinical limitations on electrode implantation. Signal reconstruction under this setting aims to infer neural activity at unmonitored locations, potentially expanding the coverage of neural recordings without increasing the number of implanted electrodes. However, most existing sEEG reconstruction methods underutilize the spatial information of electrode contacts in both encoding and modeling, and rely on deterministic objectives that favor average patterns, leading to over-smoothed reconstructions. We propose EpiTwin, a conditional spatial graph transformer for sEEG signal reconstruction, comprising three key components. Hybrid Spatial Positional Encoding (HSPE) constructs explicit spatial identities from electrode coordinates, graph topology, and anatomical priors. Geometry–Functional Biased Attention (GFBA) incorporates geometric distance and data-driven functional similarity biases into attention computation. The adversarial refinement training employs a multi-scale discriminator to counter reconstruction over-smoothing. Experiments on real-world clinical sEEG data demonstrate that EpiTwin consistently achieves lower reconstruction error under electrode series-level masking, outperforming recent foundation models such as LaBraM with a 16.8% relative reduction in RMSE. Furthermore, EpiTwin effectively mitigates spectral over-smoothing and improves reconstruction fidelity.

EpiTwin reconstructs signals at unmonitored locations, potentially extending recording coverage without more implants. The paper targets two weaknesses in existing reconstruction methods: incomplete use of spatial information and predictions that smooth away meaningful signal variation.

Its spatial graph transformer combines three mechanisms. A positional encoding gives electrode contacts identities based on coordinates, graph connections, and anatomical information. Attention incorporates both physical distance and functional similarity inferred from data. It also reports less spectral over-smoothing and improved fidelity, indicating gains in preserving signal characteristics alongside reductions in aggregate reconstruction error.
summary.tldr: EpiTwin uses spatial, anatomical, and functional relationships to reconstruct missing sEEG signals with lower error and less over-smoothing.

title: EpiTwin: Spatiotemporal Graph Transformers for Epileptic sEEG Signal Reconstruction

abstract: For low-dimensional problems ($d\leq3$), spectral methods can achieve exceptionally high accuracy. For middle-dimensional problems ($4 \leq d \lesssim 10$), spectral methods remain feasible through specific techniques such as sparse grids or hyperbolic cross. However, for high-dimensional problems ($d\gg 10$), spectral methods suffer frome the curse of dimensionality. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising approach to overcome this challenge, offering scalability to high dimensions, but often suffer from limited accuracy and efficiency. Recently proposed spectral-informed neural networks (SINNs) combine spectral methods with PINNs, operating directly in the spectral domain to avoid spatial derivative computations and to reduce memory consumption. In this work, we introduce Modified SINNs, which integrate coefficient decay scaling and basis embeddings motivated by harmonic analysis to enhance accuracy in high-dimensional problems and enable accurate approximation of unknown spectral coefficients. Numerical experiments on steady and time-dependent partial differential equations demonstrate that Modified SINNs outperform sparse grid spectral methods on middle-dimensional problems with incomplete spectral information and achieve superior accuracy compared to PINNs on high-dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Spectral methods can solve low-dimensional partial differential equations very accurately, but their computational burden grows sharply with dimension. Sparse-grid and related techniques extend their usefulness into moderate dimensions. Physics-informed neural networks offer a route to higher dimensions, although accuracy and efficiency can remain problematic.

Spectral-informed neural networks combine these approaches by working directly with spectral representations. This avoids spatial derivative computations and reduces memory consumption. The paper introduces Modified SINNs, adding coefficient-decay scaling and basis embeddings motivated by harmonic analysis. These changes are designed to improve high-dimensional accuracy and help approximate spectral coefficients that are unknown.

Numerical experiments include both steady and time-dependent equations. Modified SINNs outperform sparse-grid spectral methods on middle-dimensional problems when spectral information is incomplete, and outperform PINNs in accuracy on high-dimensional problems. Those are distinct comparisons under stated settings. The contribution is a refined spectral-domain learning method that makes use of spectral structure while addressing situations where conventional spectral computation or neural PDE solvers face difficulties.
summary.tldr: Modified SINNs improve spectral-domain PDE learning, outperforming sparse-grid methods with incomplete spectral information and PINNs on high-dimensional accuracy.

title: Spectral-Informed Neural Networks Outperform Spectral methods in High-dimensional PDEs

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity while preserving computational efficiency through sparse expert activation. However, training high-quality MoEs from scratch is prohibitively expensive. An alternative is to convert pretrained dense models into sparse MoEs. Existing dense-to-MoE methods fall into two categories: dynamic structural pruning that converts dense models into MoEs with moderate sparsity to balance performance and efficiency, and downcycling approaches that use pretrained dense models to initialize highly sparse MoEs. However, existing methods break the intrinsic activation patterns within dense models, leading to suboptimal expert construction. In this work, we argue that the Gated Linear Unit (GLU) provides a natural blueprint for dense-to-MoE conversion. We show that the fine-grained neuron-wise activation patterns of GLU reveal a coarse-grained structure, uncovering an inherent MoE architecture composed of consistently activated universal neurons and dynamically activated specialized neurons. Leveraging this discovery, we introduce ExpertWeaver, a training-free framework that partitions neurons according to their activation patterns and constructs shared experts and specialized routed experts with layer-adaptive configurations. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertWeaver outperforms existing methods, both as a training-free dynamic structural pruning technique and as a downcycling strategy for MoE initialization.
originalAbstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity while preserving computational efficiency through sparse expert activation. However, training high-quality MoEs from scratch is prohibitively expensive. An alternative is to convert pretrained dense models into sparse MoEs. Existing dense-to-MoE methods fall into two categories: dynamic structural pruning that converts dense models into MoEs with moderate sparsity to balance performance and efficiency, and downcycling approaches that use pretrained dense models to initialize highly sparse MoEs. However, existing methods break the intrinsic activation patterns within dense models, leading to suboptimal expert construction. In this work, we argue that the Gated Linear Unit (GLU) provides a natural blueprint for dense-to-MoE conversion. We show that the fine-grained neuron-wise activation patterns of GLU reveal a coarse-grained structure, uncovering an inherent MoE architecture composed of consistently activated universal neurons and dynamically activated specialized neurons. Leveraging this discovery, we introduce ExpertWeaver, a training-free framework that partitions neurons according to their activation patterns and constructs shared experts and specialized routed experts with layer-adaptive configurations. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertWeaver outperforms existing methods, both as a training-free dynamic structural pruning technique and as a downcycling strategy for MoE initialization.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models reduce computation by activating only selected expert components. Converting an existing dense language model into this form can avoid the expense of training an expert model from scratch. This paper argues that existing conversion methods disrupt useful activation patterns already present in dense models, weakening how they construct experts.

The authors examine Gated Linear Units and find a larger-scale organization within their neuron-level activity. Some neurons activate consistently across inputs, while others activate selectively. ExpertWeaver uses these patterns to divide neurons into shared experts and specialized experts chosen by routing, with configurations adapted to individual layers. The conversion framework itself requires no training.

Experiments show that ExpertWeaver outperforms existing methods in two roles: training-free dynamic structural pruning and initialization of highly sparse expert models through downcycling. The finding suggests that dense networks already contain useful clues about how to allocate shared and specialized computation. Preserving those clues gives conversion a structure grounded in the model's observed behavior.
summary.tldr: ExpertWeaver converts dense language models into sparse expert structures by preserving universal and specialized neuron activation patterns.

title: ExpertWeaver: Unlocking the Inherent MoE in Dense LLMs with GLU Activation Patterns

abstract: AI applications have shifted from single, mono-lithic foundation models (FM) to compound agentic systems. Yet today’s stacks remain fragmented: even as protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) ease tool/agent connectivity, each framework embeds an implicit runtime for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails, making behavior non-portable and governance brittle. It mirrors computing before operating systems, when every program re-implemented basic services. This position paper argues that the field now needs a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS): a system layer that virtualizes FM interactions analogous to how virtual machines abstract physical hardware, giving applications the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities. Internally, the FMOS orchestrates knowledge across memory tiers, model selection and resource allocation, and verification and policy enforcement. Like the human brain switching between fast intuition and slow deliberation, the FMOS learns when to intervene and when to let inference proceed directly and continuously adapting its policies based on operational experience.

Current frameworks each handle state, memory, resource budgets, and guardrails in their own ways. The proposal’s description of effectively unbounded capability concerns this abstraction presented to applications.

The paper presents this as an architectural direction: common services and adaptive control would move into a shared layer, addressing fragmentation across application frameworks.
summary.tldr: A proposed foundation-model operating system would unify memory, resources, verification, and policy enforcement behind an adaptive shared interface.

title: Position: It is Time to Virtualize Foundation Models with a Self-evolving Operating System Layer

abstract: LLMs excel at predictive tasks and complex reasoning tasks, but many high-value deployments rely on decisions under uncertainty, for example, which tool to call, which expert to consult, or how many resources to invest. While the usefulness and feasibility of Bayesian approaches remain unclear for LLM inference, this position paper argues that the control layer of an agentic AI system (that orchestrates LLMs and tools) is a clear case where Bayesian principles should shine. Bayesian decision theory provides a framework for agentic systems that can help to maintain beliefs over task-relevant latent quantities, to update these beliefs from observed agentic and human-AI interactions, and to choose actions. Making LLMs themselves explicitly Bayesian belief-updating engines remains computationally intensive and conceptually nontrivial as a general modeling target. In contrast, this paper argues that coherent decision-making requires Bayesian principles at the orchestration level of the agentic system, not necessarily the LLM agent parameters. This paper articulates practical properties for Bayesian control that fit modern agentic AI systems and human-AI collaboration, and provides concrete examples and design patterns to illustrate how calibrated beliefs and utility-aware policies can improve agentic AI orchestration.

paragraphs: An agentic system must decide which tool to use, which expert to consult, and how much effort to spend. These choices involve uncertainty even when its language model is good at prediction or reasoning. This paper argues that Bayesian decision principles belong in the control layer responsible for coordinating those choices.

The proposed approach maintains beliefs about relevant quantities that the system cannot directly observe. It updates those beliefs using evidence from agent activity and human interactions, then chooses actions according to their expected usefulness. The authors describe practical properties and design patterns for this kind of control, connecting calibrated uncertainty with policies that account for what different outcomes are worth.

A central distinction concerns where Bayesian reasoning is implemented. Making a language model itself an explicit Bayesian belief updater remains computationally demanding and conceptually difficult, and its general usefulness is unsettled. The paper argues that orchestration offers a clearer application: a controller can use coherent beliefs and decision rules without requiring the language model’s parameters to serve as a Bayesian engine. The examples illustrate how this could improve coordination.
summary.tldr: Agent controllers should update uncertainty coherently and choose actions by expected utility, without necessarily making the underlying LLM Bayesian.

title: Position: Agentic AI Orchestration Should Be Bayes-Consistent

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as the de facto standard for privacy-preserving machine learning, largely due to Secure Aggregation (SecAgg) protocols rendering individual user contributions cryptographically invisible to the server; we contend that this pursuit of unconditional blind aggregation has produced a systemic vulnerability, the Privacy-Auditability Paradox. By making individual updates indistinguishable in the aggregate, default SecAgg creates a Sanitization Gap in which input-level poisoning is undetectable, and a Regulatory Dead Zone in which compliance with the EU AI Act’s robustness and traceability mandates are structurally undermined. In this position paper, we argue that the community must transition from blind secure aggregation to Controllable Secure Aggregation (CSA), in which privacy is not a binary state of secrecy but a programmable spectrum of cryptographic access. CSA replaces binary secrecy with fine-grained, policy-based governance built on a complementary stack of functional encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and threshold cryptography, yielding Verified Blindness: the server remains blind by default but admits a consensus-bound, cryptographically regulated break-glass channel for auditing specific inputs. Adopting CSA is not merely a technical upgrade but a necessary condition for transforming FL from an unregulated academic prototype into a robust, compliant, and trustworthy privacy infrastructure.

paragraphs: This position paper examines a tension in federated learning: hiding individual contributions can also prevent scrutiny of harmful inputs. Secure aggregation makes individual updates cryptographically invisible to the server. The authors argue that unconditional hiding creates a gap in detecting input-level poisoning and undermines the robustness and traceability needed for regulatory compliance.

They propose Controllable Secure Aggregation, which treats access as something governed by fine-grained cryptographic policies. Its proposed stack combines functional encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and threshold cryptography. The intended result preserves server blindness during ordinary operation while allowing a restricted auditing channel for particular inputs when the required consensus is reached.

The authors call this arrangement verified blindness. Its central distinction is that privacy and auditing are built into the same access design: exceptional inspection must follow cryptographically enforced rules rather than unrestricted server discretion. The paper argues that this shift is necessary for robust and trustworthy federated-learning infrastructure. Its contribution is a governance-oriented technical direction for reconciling protected participation with accountable inspection.
summary.tldr: The authors propose secure aggregation that hides updates by default but permits narrowly governed, consensus-bound audits of specific inputs.

title: Position: The Privacy-Auditability Paradox in Federated Learning: Why We Need Controllable Secure Aggregation
Controlling Search for the Consequences of New Information During Knowledge Integration
Toward Automated Rational Reconstruction: A Case Study

abstract: A standard method for approximating averages in probabilistic models is to construct a Markov chain in the product space of the random variables with the desired equilibrium distribution. Since the number of configurations in this space grows exponentially with the number of random variables we often need to represent the distribution with samples. In this paper we show that if one is interested in averages over single variables only, an alternative Markov chain defined on the much smaller ``union space'', which can be evolved exactly, becomes feasible. The transition kernel of this Markov chain is based on conditional distributions for pairs of variables and we present ways to approximate them using approximate inference algorithms such as mean field, factorized neighbors and belief propagation. Robustness to these approximations and error bounds on the estimates follow from stability analysis for Markov chains. We also present ideas on a new class of algorithms that iterate between increasingly accurate estimates for conditional and marginal distributions. Experiments validate the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference often estimates averages by running a Markov chain over complete configurations of all variables. That space grows exponentially as variables are added, making samples a practical substitute for representing the whole distribution. This paper considers a narrower goal: computing averages involving individual variables rather than arbitrary combinations of them.

For that goal, the authors construct a chain on a much smaller union space that can be evolved exactly. Its transitions depend on conditional distributions involving pairs of variables. Those distributions can themselves be approximated using mean field, factorized neighbors, or belief propagation. Exact evolution of the smaller chain therefore remains distinct from exact inference in the original probabilistic model.

The paper uses Markov-chain stability analysis to establish robustness and error bounds when those conditional distributions are approximate. It also proposes ideas for iteratively improving conditional and marginal estimates together. Experiments validate the proposed methods, supporting the usefulness of matching the inference representation to the particular averages being requested.
summary.tldr: For single-variable averages, a smaller Markov chain enables exact chain evolution with analyzed errors from approximate conditional distributions.

title: Approximate inference by Markov chains on union spaces

abstract: A general framework is proposed for gradient boosting in supervised learning problems where the loss function is defined using a kernel over the output space. It extends boosting in a principled way to complex output spaces (images, text, graphs etc.) and can be applied to a general class of base learners working in kernelized output spaces. Empirical results are provided on three problems: a regression problem, an image completion task and a graph prediction problem. In these experiments, the framework is combined with tree-based base learners, which have interesting algorithmic properties. The results show that gradient boosting significantly improves these base learners and provides competitive results with other tree-based ensemble methods based on randomization.

paragraphs: Supervised prediction can involve outputs such as images, text, or graphs, whose structure is more complicated than a single number. This paper proposes a gradient-boosting framework for problems where the loss is defined through a kernel over outputs. The kernel provides a way to formulate prediction error in these more complex spaces.

The framework extends boosting to a general class of base learners that operate in kernelized output spaces. This separates the overall boosting construction from a single choice of prediction model. In the experiments, the authors use tree-based base learners and examine the resulting method on regression, image completion, and graph prediction.

Across those experiments, gradient boosting significantly improves the underlying learners. It also produces competitive results against other tree-based ensembles built using randomization. These findings support the usefulness of the framework for the evaluated output types without establishing superiority over every ensemble approach. The broader contribution is a principled route for applying gradient boosting when output similarity and loss are expressed through a kernel.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based output formulation extends gradient boosting to complex predictions and improves tree learners in three evaluated problems.

title: Gradient boosting for kernelized output spaces

abstract: We address the problem of detecting batches of emails that have been created according to the same template. This problem is motivated by the desire to filter spam more effectively by exploiting collective information about entire batches of jointly generated messages. The application matches the problem setting of supervised clustering, because examples of correct clusterings can be collected. Known decoding procedures for supervised clustering are cubic in the number of instances. When decisions cannot be reconsidered once they have been made – owing to the streaming nature of the data – then the decoding problem can be solved in linear time. We devise a sequential decoding procedure and derive the corresponding optimization problem of supervised clustering. We study the impact of collective attributes of email batches on the effectiveness of recognizing spam emails.

paragraphs: Messages generated from the same template can form recognizable batches. This paper studies detecting those batches so that spam recognition can use information about related messages collectively. Because examples of correct groupings can be collected, the task is formulated as supervised clustering.

The computational focus is decoding: turning a learned clustering model into decisions about which messages belong together. Existing decoding procedures are cubic in the number of instances. The authors show that decoding can instead be performed in linear time when the streaming setting requires decisions to be final once made. That restriction is central to the efficiency result.

The paper develops a sequential decoding procedure and derives the corresponding supervised-clustering optimization problem. It also studies how attributes of whole email batches affect spam recognition. The contribution therefore connects a learning formulation with the operational demands of arriving messages. Its efficiency claim applies to irreversible sequential decisions, while the application examines how identifying shared message structure can supply collective information for recognizing spam.
summary.tldr: Supervised email-batch clustering admits linear-time decoding when streaming decisions are irreversible, enabling study of collective information for spam recognition.

title: Supervised clustering of streaming data for email batch detection

abstract: In this paper, we survey the current state-ofart models for structured learning problems, including Hidden Markov Model (HMM), Conditional Random Fields (CRF), Averaged Perceptron (AP), Structured SVMs (SV M struct ), Max Margin Markov Networks (M3 N), and an integration of search and learning algorithm (SEARN). With all due tuning efforts of various parameters of each model, on the data sets we have applied the models to, we found that SVMstruct enjoys better performance compared with the others. In addition, we also propose a new method which we call the Structured Learning Ensemble (SLE) to combine these structured learning models. Empirical results show that our SLE algorithm provides more accurate solutions compared with the best results of the individual models.

With all due tuning efforts of various parameters of each model, on the data sets we have applied the models to, we found that SVMstruct enjoys better performance compared with the others. In addition, we also propose a new method which we call the Structured Learning Ensemble (SLE) to combine these structured learning models. Empirical results show that our SLE algorithm provides more accurate solutions compared with the best results of the individual models.

paragraphs: The paper compares several approaches to structured learning, including sequence labeling. These problems require predicting related outputs together, so the choice of model concerns how an entire output structure is learned. The comparison includes hidden Markov models, conditional random fields, averaged perceptrons, structured support vector machines, max-margin Markov networks, and SEARN.

The authors make parameter-tuning efforts for each model before comparing results. On the datasets they evaluate, structured support vector machines perform better than the other individual methods. This is a result about the tested datasets and tuning process; its value is a comparative assessment across several prominent approaches under that evaluation.

The paper also introduces a Structured Learning Ensemble that combines the structured learning models. Empirically, this ensemble provides more accurate solutions than the best individual model results. The two contributions therefore answer related questions: which individual method performs best in the study, and whether combining methods can improve on choosing that single winner.
summary.tldr: Structured SVMs lead the evaluated individual models, while a proposed ensemble achieves still higher accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Comparisons of sequence labeling algorithms and extensions

abstract: In supervised learning, we commonly assume that training and test data are sampled from the same distribution. However, this assumption can be violated in practice and then standard machine learning techniques perform poorly. This paper focuses on revealing and improving the performance of Bayesian estimation when the training and test distributions are different. We formally analyze the asymptotic Bayesian generalization error and establish its upper bound under a very general setting. Our important finding is that lower order terms—which can be ignored in the absence of the distribution change— play an important role under the distribution change. We also propose a novel variant of stochastic complexity which can be used for choosing an appropriate model and hyper-parameters under a particular distribution change.

paragraphs: Supervised learning often assumes that training examples and future test examples come from the same distribution. This paper examines Bayesian estimation when that assumption fails. Its goal is to understand how a distribution change affects predictive performance and to use that understanding when selecting a model and its hyperparameters.

The authors analyze Bayesian generalization error asymptotically, meaning they study its behavior as the amount of training data grows. They establish an upper bound in a setting described as very general. A central finding concerns lower-order terms in the error analysis: terms that can be ignored without distribution change can become important when training and testing differ.

This finding matters because an approximation appropriate for matching distributions may omit contributions that matter under a shift. The paper also proposes a modified form of stochastic complexity for model and hyperparameter selection under a particular distribution change. The analysis addresses a broad theoretical setting, while the proposed selection criterion has the more specific scope stated for that change.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds Bayesian prediction error under distribution change and shows that otherwise negligible terms can matter for model selection.

title: Asymptotic Bayesian generalization error when training and test distributions are different

abstract: Similarity matrices generated from many applications may not be positive semidefinite, and hence can't fit into the kernel machine framework. In this paper, we study the problem of training support vector machines with an indefinite kernel. We consider a regularized SVM formulation, in which the indefinite kernel matrix is treated as a noisy observation of some unknown positive semidefinite one (proxy kernel) and the support vectors and the proxy kernel can be computed simultaneously. We propose a semi-infinite quadratically constrained linear program formulation for the optimization, which can be solved iteratively to find a global optimum solution. We further propose to employ an additional pruning strategy, which significantly improves the efficiency of the algorithm, while retaining the convergence property of the algorithm. In addition, we show the close relationship between the proposed formulation and multiple kernel learning. Experiments on a collection of benchmark data sets demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Similarity matrices from applications do not always satisfy the positive-semidefinite requirement of the standard kernel-machine framework. This paper studies how to train support vector machines when the supplied kernel matrix is indefinite. Its approach treats that matrix as a noisy observation of an unknown positive-semidefinite proxy that can be learned.

The regularized formulation computes the proxy kernel and support vectors together, connecting the adjustment of similarities to the classifier being trained. The authors express the optimization as a semi-infinite quadratically constrained linear program and provide an iterative solution method that reaches a global optimum. This gives a principled optimization route for the proposed formulation.

An additional pruning strategy substantially improves efficiency while preserving the algorithm's convergence property. The paper also establishes a close relationship with multiple kernel learning, connecting the proxy-kernel approach to another framework for learning similarities. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness, supporting the practical use of the joint formulation when the original similarity matrix is indefinite.
summary.tldr: A regularized SVM jointly learns a positive-semidefinite proxy for an indefinite kernel and its support vectors through globally solvable optimization.

title: Training SVM with indefinite kernels

abstract: Most existing sparse Gaussian process (g.p.) models seek computational advantages by basing their computations on a set of m basis functions that are the covariance function of the g.p. with one of its two inputs fixed. We generalise this for the case of Gaussian covariance function, by basing our computations on m Gaussian basis functions with arbitrary diagonal covariance matrices (or length scales). For a fixed number of basis functions and any given criteria, this additional flexibility permits approximations no worse and typically better than was previously possible. We perform gradient based optimisation of the marginal likelihood, which costs O(m2n) time where n is the number of data points, and compare the method to various other sparse g.p. methods. Although we focus on g.p. regression, the central idea is applicable to all kernel based algorithms, and we also provide some results for the support vector machine (s.v.m.) and kernel ridge regression (k.r.r.). Our approach outperforms the other methods, particularly for the case of very few basis functions, i.e. a very high sparsity ratio.
