paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian process methods reduce computation by using a limited number of basis functions. Common constructions obtain those functions by fixing one input of the covariance function. This paper makes the basis functions more flexible for Gaussian covariance functions, allowing each Gaussian basis function to have an arbitrary diagonal covariance matrix, or its own length scales.

For a fixed number of basis functions, the richer family permits approximations that are no worse, and typically better, under a given criterion. This is a statement about the flexibility of the approximation family. The authors fit the model through gradient-based marginal likelihood optimization, with a stated time cost of O(m²n), where m counts basis functions and n counts data points.

Comparisons with other sparse Gaussian process methods favor the proposed approach, particularly when very few basis functions are used. The paper also presents results for support vector machines and kernel ridge regression. Although Gaussian process regression is the main focus, the authors identify the flexible-basis idea as applicable more broadly to kernel-based algorithms.
summary.tldr: Giving sparse Gaussian basis functions independent length scales improves approximation flexibility and reported performance, especially with very few basis functions.

title: Sparse multiscale gaussian process regression

abstract: This paper investigates a new learning formulation called structured sparsity, which is a natural extension of the standard sparsity concept in statistical learning and compressive sensing. By allowing arbitrary structures on the feature set,this concept generalizes the group sparsity idea. A general theory is developed for learning with structured sparsity, based on the notion of coding complexity associated with the structure. Moreover, a structured greedy algorithm is proposed to efficiently solve the structured sparsity problem. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of structured sparsity over standard sparsity.

Moreover, a structured greedy algorithm is proposed to efficiently solve the structured sparsity problem. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of structured sparsity over standard sparsity.

paragraphs: Ordinary sparsity favors solutions that use only a small subset of available features. This paper extends that idea by allowing the chosen subset to have structure. Instead of describing a solution only through how many features it uses, structured sparsity also takes account of relationships or arrangements specified over the feature set.

The formulation permits arbitrary feature structures and generalizes group sparsity. The authors develop a general learning theory based on coding complexity associated with the chosen structure. This gives the theory a way to account for the structure of a sparse solution, rather than reducing all selections of the same size to the same description.

The paper also proposes a structured greedy algorithm to solve the learning problem efficiently. Experiments demonstrate advantages over standard sparsity in the evaluated settings. The contribution brings together a broader modeling formulation, a theoretical measure of structural complexity, and a computational method, making structure part of both the learning objective and the procedure used to find a solution.
summary.tldr: Structured sparsity generalizes sparse feature selection using arbitrary feature structures, coding-complexity theory, and a structured greedy algorithm.

title: Learning with structured sparsity

abstract: Multiclass classification is an important and fundamental problem in machine learning. A popular family of multiclass classification methods belongs to reducing multiclass to binary based on output coding. Several multiclass boosting algorithms have been proposed to learn the coding matrix and the associated binary classifiers in a problem-dependent way. These algorithms can be unified under a sum-of-exponential loss function defined in the domain of margins. Instead, multiclass SVM uses another type of loss function based on hinge loss. In this paper, we present a new output-coding-based multiclass boosting algorithm using the multiclass hinge loss, which we call HingeBoost.OC. HingeBoost.OC is tested on various real world datasets and shows better performance than the existing multiclass boosting algorithm AdaBoost.ERP, one-vs-one, one-vs-all, ECOC and multiclass SVM in a majority of different cases.

In this paper, we present a new output-coding-based multiclass boosting algorithm using the multiclass hinge loss, which we call HingeBoost.OC. HingeBoost.OC is tested on various real world datasets and shows better performance than the existing multiclass boosting algorithm AdaBoost.ERP, one-vs-one, one-vs-all, ECOC and multiclass SVM in a majority of different cases.

paragraphs: Output coding tackles multiclass classification by organizing the task into binary classification problems. Existing multiclass boosting methods can learn both a coding matrix and its associated binary classifiers for the problem at hand. The paper describes these approaches through a common sum-of-exponential loss defined over prediction margins.

The proposed algorithm, HingeBoost.OC, instead uses multiclass hinge loss within output-coding-based boosting. Hinge loss is also used in multiclass support vector machines. The contribution brings that choice of training objective into the output-coding boosting framework, creating a different way to learn a multiclass predictor from binary classification components.

The authors evaluate HingeBoost.OC on several real-world datasets against AdaBoost.ERP, one-versus-one, one-versus-all, ECOC, and multiclass SVM. It performs better in a majority of the cases considered. That qualification matters: the findings support the method across many tested comparisons without claiming that it wins every comparison. The results provide empirical evidence that changing the loss within this boosting framework can improve multiclass performance.
summary.tldr: HingeBoost.OC uses multiclass hinge loss in output-coding boosting and outperforms the compared methods in a majority of tested cases.

title: Multiclass Boosting with Hinge Loss based on Output Coding

abstract: In many reinforcement-learning (RL) systems, the value function is approximated as a linear combination of a fixed set of basis functions. Performance can be improved by adding to this set. Previous approaches construct a series of basis functions that in sufficient number can eventually represent the value function. In contrast, we show that there is a single, ideal basis function, which can directly represent the value function. Its addition to the set immediately reduces the error to zero---without changing existing weights. Moreover, this ideal basis function is simply the value function that results from replacing the MDP's reward function with its Bellman error. This result suggests a novel method for improving value-function estimation: a primary reinforcement learner estimates its value function using its present basis functions; it then sends its TD error to a secondary learner, which interprets that error as a reward function and estimates the corresponding value function; the resulting value function then becomes the primary learner's new basis function. We present both batch and online versions in combination with incremental basis projection, and demonstrate that the performance is superior to existing methods, especially in the case of large discount factors.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning systems approximate a value function using a weighted combination of fixed basis functions. Adding useful basis functions can improve that approximation. This paper establishes an ideal result: a single additional basis function can eliminate the value-function error without changing the existing weights. That ideal function is the value function obtained when the MDP's reward is replaced by its Bellman error.

The result motivates a practical construction using two learners. A primary learner estimates values with its current basis functions and supplies its temporal-difference error to a secondary learner. The secondary learner treats that error as reward and estimates the corresponding value function. Its estimate then becomes a new basis function for the primary learner.

The authors present batch and online versions combined with incremental basis projection. Experiments show better performance than existing methods, particularly for large discount factors. The exact zero-error statement applies to the ideal basis function; the practical method learns an estimate of it. The contribution connects remaining prediction error to a targeted way of expanding the value representation.
summary.tldr: A secondary learner turns temporal-difference errors into new value-function basis functions, motivated by an ideal basis that exactly corrects the current error.

title: Incremental Basis Construction from Temporal Difference Error

abstract: Social network websites, such as Facebook, YouTube, Lastfm etc, have become a popular platform for users to connect with each other and share content or opinions. They provide rich information to study the influence of user's social circle in their decision process. In this paper, we are interested in examining the effectiveness of social network information to predict the user's ratings of items. We propose a novel hierarchical Bayesian model which jointly incorporates topic modeling and probabilistic matrix factorization of social networks. A major advantage of our model is to automatically infer useful latent topics and social information as well as their importance to collaborative filtering from the training data. Empirical experiments on two large-scale datasets show that our algorithm provides a more effective recommendation system than the state-of-the art approaches. Our results also reveal interesting insight that the social circles have more influence on people's decisions about the usefulness of information (e.g., bookmarking preference on Delicious) than personal taste (e.g., music preference on Lastfm).

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether social connections help predict how users rate items. Social websites contain both material that users interact with and information about their social circles. The challenge is to combine these sources while learning how much each contributes to recommendations.

The authors propose a hierarchical Bayesian model that joins topic modeling with probabilistic matrix factorization of social networks. It learns hidden topics and social information from training data, along with their importance for collaborative filtering. This makes the contribution of social information something the model estimates, rather than a fixed judgment supplied beforehand.

Experiments on two large datasets report more effective recommendations than the state-of-the-art approaches compared. The results also suggest that social circles influence judgments about useful information more strongly than personal taste: bookmarking on Delicious and music preferences on Lastfm provide the examples. This is an empirical finding from the studied settings, highlighting that social information's predictive value can depend on the kind of preference being modeled.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian recommender jointly learns topics and social factors, improving recommendations while revealing differences in social influence across preference types.

title: Collaborative Topic Regression with Social Matrix Factorization for Recommendation Systems
